arxiv-2510-14725:
Al-Izzi and a large team of co-authors demonstrate, in a 2025 arXiv paper, free-standing filaments that keep changing shape on their own, with no tether and no outside controller. Active filaments drive propulsion and actuation in biology and soft robotics. Artificial versions usually stay robust only when externally controlled or anchored to a surface, which limits where they can work.

The team's trick is non-reciprocal interaction: the bending modes of a buckled beam are coupled anti-symmetrically, so action in one direction is not undone in the other. Ordinary snap-through buckling, where a beam jumps between two stable shapes, becomes a persistent cycle of self-snapping. The change is governed by a critical exceptional point, where the bending modes go unstable and merge at once. When the environment perturbs the filaments, they turn this cycling into useful behavior, including crawling, digging, and walking.
arxiv-2510-14825:
Poesia and Sampaio explore, in a 2025 arXiv paper, predictors that are made of readable code and decision trees instead of neural network weights. Classical models like decision trees are efficient and interpretable, but their quality depends entirely on hand-chosen input features. Neural networks learn their own features from raw data, at the cost of interpretability and specialized hardware. The authors ask whether language models can supply the features, keeping the predictor itself transparent.

Their LeaPR models stack features written as small programs, functions from a data point to a number, under a decision tree. Two learning algorithms are proposed. One adapts FunSearch to evolve features rather than predictors. The other extends the classic ID3 tree algorithm, generating features on demand when a leaf needs splitting. From chess position evaluation to image and text classification, the learned predictors often rivaled neural networks, with no network needed at prediction time.
arxiv-2510-14925:
Okutomi re-reads Kant's Critique of Pure Reason, in a 2025 arXiv paper, as an early theory of why reasoning systems become overconfident. For Kant, reason polices thought, keeping it within the bounds of possible experience. The author turns that picture into control theory: stable feedback on paper can still mislead in practice.

A composite instability index, H-Risk, combines four quantities: spectral margin, conditioning, time sensitivity, and innovation amplification. In linear-Gaussian simulations, higher H-Risk predicted sure-but-wrong errors even when the system was formally stable, exposing a gap between nominal and epistemic stability. Extended to large language models, internal fragility showed preliminary correlations with miscalibration and hallucination. Lightweight critique prompts modestly improved calibration in some small tests and worsened it in others. The author stresses the claims are early, but offers the Kantian lens as a principled way to diagnose overconfidence in reasoning systems.
arxiv-2510-15125:
Alexander Brady and Tunazzina Islam build an automated way to map the themes running through political advertising on social media. Their 2025 arXiv paper combines unsupervised clustering, which groups similar ads without preset labels, with large language models that name and refine the groups. Applied to Meta ads from the month before the 2024 United States presidential election, the method needs no seed topics or expert hand-labeling.

The analysis found voting and immigration ads dominating both spending and impressions, while abortion and election-integrity ads reached audiences beyond their budgets. Spending split sharply by viewpoint: conservative groups drove economic appeals, and abortion messaging divided between opposing coalitions. Brady and Islam also tagged ads with moral framing, finding, for example, that abortion ads leaned on liberty language while economic ads mixed care, fairness, and liberty themes. Targeting varied too, with younger Floridians seeing more housing ads.
arxiv-2510-15325:
Jonathan Bowden and Thomas Massoni prove that a geometric structure built from a foliation depends only on the foliation's topology, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A foliation slices a three-dimensional space into stacked surfaces, and a taut foliation has no dead-end leaves. Following work by Eliashberg and Thurston, the authors attach a Liouville structure, a kind of symplectic geometry, to a thickened copy of the space.

Their main result says foliations that are topologically the same yield matching Liouville structures, even if their smooth details differ. For the special case of flows with chaotic stretching, called Anosov flows, the result shows an older construction by Mitsumatsu is unchanged under orbit equivalence. The proofs rest on a careful smoothing scheme for rough conjugacies and a sharpened uniqueness result about contact structures near a foliation. An appendix by three other authors uses the smoothing to build new collapsed Anosov flows.
arxiv-2510-15525:
Weicen Dong and three colleagues map the magnetic phases of a two-dimensional magnet where a twist-promoting interaction is unusually strong. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, which cants neighboring spins and can create swirling textures. Topological magnons, spin waves with protected band structure, are prized for low-loss spintronic devices, but earlier work treated only weak versions of this interaction.

The team finds that strong interaction tips the ground state from simple ferromagnetism into a 120-degree noncollinear pattern, where spins point in three directions. Adding a magnetic field produces noncoplanar textures and a rich set of topological phases. Those phases can be read out through the anomalous thermal Hall effect, a measurable heat current. They also find that spin interactions in the strong regime let magnons hybridize with phonons, the lattice vibrations, creating mixed topological bands.
arxiv-2510-15625:
A dangling bond is an unsatisfied silicon atom that traps charge and disturbs electronic behavior. T. V. Pavlova and V. M. Shevlyuga examine single dangling bonds in this 2025 arXiv study. They work on silicon surfaces coated with chlorine or bromine, probed by a scanning tunneling microscope. The team observes a bond switching directly between positive and negative charge states. Notably, the neutral state plays no part in these observed transitions.

The switch happens when the bond and substrate fall out of equilibrium with each other. It ties to the charge neutrality level, where the bond changes from donor-like to acceptor-like character. The switching voltage also shifts with the bond's local electrostatic surroundings.
arxiv-2510-15725:
Old films are noisy and damaged, so software struggles to tell how the camera moved. Tingyu Lin and three colleagues improve camera movement classification for archival footage in this 2025 arXiv paper. They first unify modern datasets and the HISTORIAN collection into one balanced benchmark. Their model extends the Video Swin Transformer with directional grid motion encoding from optical flow. A small learnable fusion layer injects this motion signal late in the network.

Accuracy on modern clips rises from about eighty-two to eighty-six percent top-1. On World War II footage, accuracy improves from about eighty-three to eighty-five percent. Fine-tuning on modern data first adds over five points on historical material.
arxiv-2510-15825:
Lê Dũng Tráng, Juan J. Nuño-Ballesteros, and José Seade relate the topology of a Milnor fibre to a sliced version of itself for singular map-germs. A map-germ describes a holomorphic map near a point, here on a possibly singular complex variety. A second, well-behaved germ slices the first fibre, and the question is what the slice reveals about the whole.

Using stratified Morse theory, the three authors determine the fibre's topology up to homeomorphism from the slice and from Morse data of a perturbed restriction. That yields a general formula comparing the Euler characteristics of the two fibres. When the variety has only an isolated singularity, the difference formula becomes algebraic and easy to compute. It generalises the classical Lê-Greuel formula in two directions at once and unifies several known formulas as special cases.
arxiv-2510-15925:
Aleks Kleyn, writing alone, sets out the basic definitions for manifolds and Lie groups built over a Banach algebra. A chart is defined as a homeomorphism from a topological space into a convex set inside a power of the algebra. A simple manifold of a given smoothness class is one whose charts are linked by diffeomorphisms of that class.

A differential manifold is then a union of simple pieces whose overlaps are again simple. When such a manifold carries a group structure and the map sending a pair to the product with the inverse is differentiable, it is a Lie group in this setting. Kleyn equips the tangent module at the identity with a bracket product built from the group's structure coefficients, giving its Lie algebra. The note fixes the language for continuous transformation groups over general algebras.
arxiv-2510-16325:
Yuyao Zhang and Yu-Wing Tai present UltraImageGen, a framework for making images at ultra-high resolution from text. Top image models stall below two megapixels because their attention step grows far too costly as images grow. Sharp training data is scarce too. Their design splits the big picture into fixed local windows, where attention stays cheap.

A small, low-resolution copy of the image steers the whole, anchoring the layout so windows agree with each other. A light adapter, trained cheaply, links the global guide with the local detail work during cleanup. By reordering tokens window-first, the method runs dense, hardware-friendly math at any size. The result scales past eight thousand pixels across with more than ten times the speed and far less memory. Quality tests put it ahead, offering a practical path to poster-grade AI images.
arxiv-2510-16725:
Yongchun Bi and three co-authors prove stability tools for very large nonlinear systems whose rules change with time. Their target is integral input-to-state stability, which says a system's state stays controlled by its past inputs. The systems live in infinite-dimensional spaces and include terms that grow faster than linearly, a combination that resists standard methods.

The team first proves several comparison principles for ordinary differential equations with time-varying coefficients and superlinear terms. Those principles then support a local stability theorem in Banach spaces, using Lyapunov functions. In Hilbert spaces, they give conditions for such a function to exist and show how to build one. Two examples demonstrate the method in action.
arxiv-2510-17425:
Counting climate laws says little about what those laws actually push for, or what good they do. Aditi Dutta, writing alone, builds a number based measure of climate policy direction by reading official national policy documents with a multilingual language model. Each document is sorted by theme, such as cutting emissions, adapting to change, managing disaster risk, or covering loss and damage.

Dutta then links those theme scores to World Bank development data across countries and years. Policies centred on cutting emissions went together with higher national income measures. Disaster risk work linked to higher income and debt but lower foreign investment, while adaptation themes showed few measurable links. The framework offers a scalable way to compare climate governance between countries.
arxiv-2510-17625:
Jaehyup Seong, with Byungju Lee and two co-authors, improves satellite links for crowded beams in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their setting is a low Earth orbit satellite serving many users under shared beams. A method called rate splitting sends one common stream for all users plus private streams for each. Standard versions use one beam shape for the common stream, which limits quality when channel knowledge is poor.

The new design adds space time coding, meaning signals spread across antennas and time slots, to the common stream. Every user then gains full signal diversity, meaning protection against fading, regardless of load. An optimization routine balances power between common and private streams. The goal is raising the slowest user's rate. Simulations beat standard approaches clearly.
arxiv-2510-17725:
Haozhen Zhang and three co-authors built a new test for long-context language models. Their benchmark, AcademicEval, checks how well models write with very long inputs. Older tests use fixed lengths and costly hand labeling. They also risk leaking answers into model training data.

AcademicEval draws its tasks from real papers posted on arXiv. Models must draft titles, abstracts, opening sections, and related-work text. Sample answers come from a graph of co-author links. Fresh papers keep the test live and free of leaks. Results show models still struggle as tasks grow more layered.
arxiv-2510-17925:
George Ma, with eight co-authors, speeds up code completion by doing the hard lookup work before the coder asks. Retrieval systems that search a project at request time either return weak context or slow the tool down. SpecAgent instead explores project files during indexing and builds context that guesses future edits.

That early work hides the delay and improves the code the model writes. The authors also flag a leak in current benchmarks, where future context slips in and inflates scores. They build a clean synthetic test to avoid it. Tool builders get both a faster design and a fairer way to measure it.
arxiv-2510-18125:
Mohamed Warda and Ronojoy Adhikari find strange stability swings in a soft robot arm pushed by steady pressure under water. The arm bends, stretches, and shears like the Cosserat rods used to model it. Exact nonlinear equations, built with moving frames, govern its motion in the viscous fluid.

As pressure rises past a first threshold, the straight arm loses stability through an oscillating bifurcation. Push further, past a second threshold, and stability oddly returns. Nonlinear simulations confirm the pattern. Soft robot designers get a warning and a tool: pressure alone can switch a fluid-borne arm between calm and wobbling regimes.
arxiv-2510-18625:
Eric DeMarbre works with Jay Henderson, J. Felipe Gonzalez, and Rob Teather. They test how a controller should appear in extended reality. Participants selected targets in the tasks. Four display choices were compared. One showed a virtual controller. One showed a virtual hand. One showed both, and one showed neither. The tasks ran in two modes. One was full virtual reality. The other was mixed reality over the real room.

Performance came out much the same in both modes. Switching modes did not hurt basic task skill. Displays that mimicked the real controller helped in both modes. That is a practical design hint. Users judged their own performance in a distinct way in mixed reality. The scores did not match that feeling. The authors read this as a call for care. Mixed reality design needs its own focus on spatial awareness.
arxiv-2510-18725:
Josh McGiff and Nikola Nikolov make machine translation fine-tuning affordable for low-resource languages, using Irish as their test case. Adapting a huge multilingual model costs too much for many researchers, so efficient methods train only a small set of added parameters. The authors introduce two semi-supervised versions of that idea, SemiAdapt and SemiLoRA, designed to strengthen domain adaptation while staying cheap at inference time.

In their experiments, SemiAdapt beat even full-domain fine-tuning, while SemiLoRA matched or outperformed fine-tuning the entire model, a striking result for a method that trains only a fraction of the weights. Their embedding-based inference methods did especially well on larger and noisier text collections. All Irish translation models built in the study were released as open resources, aiming to lower the barrier for other low-resource language communities.
arxiv-2510-18825:
Yujie Xing and his four co-authors unify graph transformers, the attention-based models now central to learning on networks, under a single idea: the attention mask. Different designs for letting nodes interact look architecturally distinct, but the authors show an equivalence between architecture and mask construction, so diverse interactions can be captured just by designing masks carefully.

Their theory ties correct classification to two mask qualities, a large receptive field and high label consistency, and shows no single existing mask delivers both everywhere. Hierarchical masks, though, complement each other. Their model combines three theory-guided hierarchical masks and routes between expert subnetworks at two levels to integrate information across scales, with a dual attention computation to keep it scalable. The result is a flexible transformer whose design follows directly from the analysis rather than from trial and error.
arxiv-2510-18925:
Elias Al Ghazal and five co-authors present reduced-order methods for predicting systems that change on several time scales at once. Such systems are hard to model because they are nonlinear, react strongly to starting values, and include fast behavior that standard machine learning often misses.

Three approaches are offered. One splits dynamics into local parts with neural networks, one pulls out main modes that separate large and small scales, and one rebuilds those dynamics from sparse measurements. Together they aim to keep both slow trends and fast details while using far less data and compute.
arxiv-2510-19025:
Hamed Jelodar and three co-authors introduce FlexiDataGen, a framework that creates synthetic datasets for sensitive fields where real data are scarce, costly, or private. Healthcare, biomedical research, and cybersecurity all face that dataset problem, which slows models that need many labeled examples.

FlexiDataGen uses a large language model to generate data that is rich in meaning, coherent, and varied in language, adapting as it goes. By building usable training sets without exposing private records, the approach aims to help models generalize better in high-stakes areas where collecting real examples is the main barrier.
arxiv-2510-19125:
Harshita Gandhi and Huw Morgan link magnetic field measures in solar active regions with the three-dimensional speeds of coronal mass ejections, the huge plasma blasts that drive space weather. Measures taken above polarity inversion lines, such as the height where torus instability begins and the strength of the overlying field, should help predict how fast an eruption travels.

The authors show those measures predict speed just as well when taken over a broader nearby region, not only directly above the inversion line. They also judge a third measure, ribbon flux, for speed prediction. Better speed forecasts improve warnings for satellites and power grids.
arxiv-2510-19225:
Yongji Wu and seven co-authors present RLBoost, a system that harvests spare, preemptible computing capacity to cut the cost of reinforcement learning for large language models. Such training alternates between generating responses, which scales easily across many machines, and updating the model, which needs tightly linked graphics processors.

Older designs either force both stages onto the same hardware or split them and leave resources idle. RLBoost instead feeds the generation stage with cheap capacity that can be reclaimed at any time, keeping the expensive training hardware busy. Cheaper post-training matters as reinforcement learning becomes a standard step for reasoning models.
arxiv-2510-19525:
Vincent Savaux and four co-authors ask how well two modern wireless waveforms resist a passive eavesdropper. The waveforms, AFDM and OTFS, are candidates for demanding radio environments. An eavesdropper who intercepts the signal but lacks the waveform's secret settings must try demodulation matrices by brute force.

Their analysis shows the search grows far faster for AFDM than for OTFS as the number of subcarriers rises. Simulations of bit error rates back this up: with AFDM the intercepted signal stays nearly impossible to decode, while OTFS lets an attacker recover part of it. The results favor AFDM where secrecy against passive listening matters.
arxiv-2510-19625:
Gianni Manno and Filippo Salis carry a classical classification problem from Kähler geometry into its para-Kähler counterpart. The classical question, treated by Calabi and Chern among others, asks for a complete list of non-isometric Kähler-Einstein manifolds that can be immersed in a finite-dimensional Kähler space form. Para-Kähler geometry mirrors the same structures with a different signature.

Manno and Salis answer the analogous question for the toric case, where the manifolds carry a large torus symmetry. They produce a list of mutually non-isometric toric para-Kähler-Einstein manifolds that admit analytic immersions into a finite-dimensional para-Kähler space form.
arxiv-2510-19725:
Jingfan Meng, Tianji Yang, and Jun Xu design a communication protocol that lets two parties learn the intersection of their sets without revealing everything else. The better-studied cousin problem, set reconciliation, has both sides learn the differences, and existing intersection solutions simply reuse those costlier protocols. The authors point out that intersection is fundamentally cheaper and build a dedicated protocol around compressed sensing sketches.

In several rounds, each side sends a compact sketch that helps the other identify its unique elements, narrowing down until both agree on the shared elements. On real-world datasets the protocol cut communication costs by a factor of eight to ten compared with the standard reconciliation approach. The savings matter for privacy-sensitive data matching between organizations.
arxiv-2510-19925:
Philip Kirkeberg, Rixin Li, and Martin E. Pessah ask when the shearing box, a local simulation trick, can be trusted to follow black hole binaries embedded in the disks of active galactic nuclei. Such disks may host gravitational wave sources, and most studies simulate a small co-rotating patch around the binary to save computing power, cutting the binary off from the disk's global behavior.

The authors identify the conditions under which global disk timescales are slower than the gas-driven evolution of the binary's orbit, across a range of disk models. For the black hole masses of interest, there are radii beyond which global influence can be reasonably neglected, vindicating the local approach there. The framework also gives a general way to judge local simulations against the global problem.
arxiv-2510-20525:
Felix Sefzig works alone on deep links between two views of the same algebraic objects, building a clear form of the comparison map for objects known as one motives. These objects blend points on curves with torus like parts and serve as a test case for broad ideas in number theory.

Sefzig shows his construction gives back the classic comparison map and respects maps between the rigid forms of these objects. He then builds a new ring of motivic periods in the p-adic setting and explains how it ties to the classic period values. Worked cases for several motives and curves show the pairing in concrete terms, giving other scholars a firm base to build on.
arxiv-2510-20725:
Jasmine Bayrooti, Sattar Vakili, Amanda Prorok, and Carl Henrik Ek prove regret guarantees for Thompson sampling in short horizon decision problems modeled with Gaussian processes. Thompson sampling picks actions by sampling from current beliefs and is widely used, yet its theory for step by step tasks with time structure has stayed thin.

Working with joint Gaussian beliefs over rewards and transitions, the team bounds total regret across episodes in terms of horizon length and model complexity. Their proof handles value functions that are not Gaussian and the layered updates at the heart of dynamic planning. Tools from bandit theory are extended to multi output cases, clarifying how model shape and uncertainty drive sampling performance.
arxiv-2510-20825:
Gavin R Putland, working alone, gives an exact form of Huygens principle using generalized secondary sources that mix space and time offsets. The classic principle treats each point on a wave front as a fresh source, but exact matching in close regions and on general surfaces has remained delicate.

His generalized dipoles allow a smaller time delay than the travel time between paired points and allow one side to be weakened. Waves cancel exactly on a chosen circle at a finite distance. With these sources spread over a general surface, the Kirchhoff integral result for a single primary source is matched exactly, even in the near field. The construction widens Huygens principle beyond wave front surfaces alone.
arxiv-2510-20925:
Rattana Pukdee leads two co-authors on regression when only interval bounds on the target are known, because exact labels are costly or impossible to obtain. Standard losses need exact values, so interval data break the usual training recipe.

First, losses compatible with intervals receive generalization bounds based on smoothness of the model class, relaxing older demands of realizability and tiny ambiguity. Second, a min max learning formulation is proposed for the same setting. Together the results widen the range of problems where learning from coarse supervision carries firm guarantees, from medicine to sensing with censored readings.
arxiv-2510-21025:
Ahmed Saad Al-Karsani leads two co-authors on a in linked form stable and robust control scheme for standalone networks of small grids. Islanded operation must hold frequency and voltage steady despite variable clean sources and loads, without help from the main grid.

Shared averaging proportional integral control is a known approach for droop controlled resources, but it falters under operational and structural disturbances. The proposed variant aims to keep stability and robustness when lines switch, loads jump, or units drop out. Reliable standalone control underpins resilient local energy systems for campuses, bases, and remote communities.
arxiv-2510-21125:
Yuta Kochi leads four co-authors on boosting femtosecond photon echo signals from an ensemble of indium arsenide quantum dots using chirped pulses. Photon echoes are a leading route to optical quantum memory, but rare earth crystals offer narrow bandwidth while quantum dot ensembles span terahertz widths with ultrafast dynamics.

Detuning and field unevenness across that broad range cut echo efficiency badly. Adiabatic rapid passage with chirped pulses is demonstrated experimentally to restore coherent control across the dense ensemble. Ultrafast broadband memory would suit high rate quantum networks and signal processing far beyond slow crystal platforms.
arxiv-2510-21225:
Shouvik Sadhukhan and C. S. Narayanamurthy examine how air turbulence distorts optical fields, and whether clear plastic slabs can partly undo the damage. They rebuild the full light field from distorted intensity recordings, using a nonlinear equation that recovers the hidden phase of the light.

The rebuilt fields are studied with quantum phase-space tools, including Wigner functions and photon-count patterns. Four setups are compared: turbulence alone, turbulence with one plastic slab, turbulence with two slabs, and a calm free-space reference. A measure called the Fano factor tracks shifts between different photon statistics, giving a numeric view of how much the plastic elements calm the turbulence.
arxiv-2510-21325:
Hossein Nemati, Saskia Jacoba Elisabeth Suijkerbuijk, and Joost de Graaf model a contest between liver progenitor cells and colorectal cancer cells that meet in the liver. An earlier experiment showed signs of cell competition tied to the cell cycle, but no mechanism explained why one population gained ground.

Their model is deliberately simple: cells release a helpful signaling molecule and also take it up, while their growth follows cell cycle stages. Cancer cells take up the factor more efficiently, and that single edge, paired with secretion by the cells themselves, proves enough to reproduce the experiment's population patterns and cell cycle shifts. The result gives a minimal template for studying growth contests where rivals compete over a product they themselves supply.
arxiv-2510-21725:
Padraig Cunningham, Padhraic Smyth, and Barry Smyth read seventeen million research papers to watch scholarly writing change its habits since the year 2000. Their sweep covers how papers are authored and how they read, at a scale no manual review could approach, and several of the trends they surface worry them.

Author lists, reference lists, and abstracts all grow longer, and the author inflation is pervasive across major fields. While output per author falls, a pattern suggesting gift authorship, names added without real contribution. Papers also lean harder on hyperbole, inflating claims to compete for reviewer attention at the cost of readability. That drift sharpened after 2023 as AI writing tools spread, especially in computer science, engineering, and business, with risks to citation metrics and to objectivity itself.
arxiv-2510-22025:
Alfonso Zack Robles, Alexander I. Nesterov, and Claudia Moreno tackle a records problem in general relativity. The problem is how to define conserved energy, momentum, and angular momentum far from a heavy body. Far away, spacetime flattens out. Their tool is a quasigroup approach. It extends group symmetry for the slippery symmetries at a system's edge.

The team starts from the Newman-Unti family of symmetries at infinity. That family is infinite. They show how it reduces to the Poincaré quasigroup of standard relativity. They compute the Noether charges for its elements. In flat Minkowski spacetime, the total energy-momentum vanishes, as it should. So does the total angular momentum. The construction gives an angular momentum free of the supertranslation ambiguity. It also gives a working notion of intrinsic spin. It places the center of mass at future null infinity.
arxiv-2510-22325:
Nicolas Bongiorno counts rational points on split toric stacks, geometric spaces built from fans of cones but carrying extra stabilizer structure that makes their arithmetic richer than that of ordinary toric varieties. Counting points of bounded height is a flagship problem in arithmetic geometry, and here several heights must be bounded at once, one for each part of the structure.

Bongiorno's strategy lifts the count to an extended universal torsor, a covering space where points parametrize cleanly, and he proves the integral parametrization that makes the lift legitimate for stacks. On the torsor the stacky height becomes tractable. He then defines the Tamagawa number of the stack as an Euler product over primes. For each prime interprets the local factor through a mass formula that counts points over the finite field sector by sector, setting up the analytic machinery a full asymptotic count would need.
arxiv-2510-22525:
Collective theory describes many identical particles through shared variables, but finite particle counts change the space of possible states. Robert de Mello Koch, Antal Jevicki, Garreth Kemp, and Anik Rudra study that reduction in a 2025 paper on symmetric collective models.

Focusing on bosons, particles that can share states, mapped to matrix models, they give a complete algorithm for the independent relations. Null spaces, meaning solution sets that vanish, yield all trace relations and turn the construction into linear algebra. Their case study recovers expected primary quantities and finds secondary ones, forming a smaller emergent state space with finite occupation numbers.
arxiv-2510-22625:
Quantum information ideas may help answer basic questions about neutrinos, the nearly invisible particles that pass through matter. Raoul Serao, Gianpaolo Torre, and Antonio Capolupo review that meeting point in 2025, linking quantum theory tools with high energy physics.

Their review covers decoherence, meaning the loss of quantum effects through interaction, and unusual neutrino oscillation patterns. Those patterns could reveal whether neutrinos are Dirac or Majorana particles and whether a key symmetry called CPT is broken. Entanglement measures, which track linked quantum states, are also discussed as probes of axion mediated interactions and physics beyond the Standard Model.
arxiv-2510-22725:
Electric field noise heats trapped ions and limits how large ion based quantum computers can grow. Chon-Teng Belmiro Chu, with five co-authors, studies a three dimensional printed ion trap in 2025 whose skeleton shaped electrodes reduce the surface area sitting near the ion.

Compared with a conventional blade trap at the same confinement strength, the skeleton design cuts total heating by over half. Analysis patch by patch shows surfaces within a short distance of the ion dominate the heating. Realigning electrode gaps with the worst hotspots suppresses heating further, despite slightly more surface. A linear rule links ion distance to the peak heating location.
arxiv-2510-22925:
Karthik Duraisamy revisits a classic principle from mechanics and asks what it really fixes in a flow with no friction and no squeezing. At one frozen moment, he holds speed fixed and varies only how the flow speeds up. That step turns into a least-squares problem with rules the motion must obey.

The rules lead to a pressure field whose slope removes the parts of the motion that break the no-squeeze rule. Duraisamy shows this matches the well known projection method and brings back the Euler equations at that instant. The paper gives fluid scholars a cleaner view of why pressure acts as it does.
arxiv-2510-23125:
David E Ruiz-Guirola and four co-authors argue that dependable low-power Internet of Things networks must track their own context. Dependability means trusted, unbroken service despite uncertainty, a hard goal for huge fleets of battery-limited devices. Protocols that ignore local conditions waste energy or deliver stale data.

The authors name four context dimensions: energy status, information freshness, task relevance, and physical channel conditions. Each dimension supports core dependability traits. Building protocols around those signals, they show, can keep service reliable while respecting tight power budgets in large deployments across cities, farms, and factories.
arxiv-2510-23625:
Thomas D. DeWitt and Timothy J. Garrett test a textbook picture of the atmosphere against global weather balloon data. The standard view splits the air into layers of behavior by scale. Broad flows act like flat turbulence, mid-size motions ride gravity waves, and the smallest scales churn in three dimensions. If true, energy spectra should show clear breaks where one regime hands off to the next.

Using dropsonde and radiosonde wind records, the authors compute structure functions across vertical gaps from two hundred meters to eight kilometers, and horizontal gaps up to eighteen hundred kilometers. The measured scaling exponents match none of the three classic regimes. Instead, the data fit a less famous model by Lovejoy and Schertzer, where one anisotropic cascade runs across all scales. The authors argue this single framework could replace the traditional patchwork of scale-by-scale mechanisms.
arxiv-2510-23725:
Bilal Hawashin and a co-author examine a second phase transition in the Gross-Neveu model, a theory of interacting fermions in two dimensions. Rewriting the model with Majorana fermions reveals an SO(2N) symmetry when interactions are switched off. Mean-field theory then predicts, besides the chiral Ising transition, a second critical point where that symmetry breaks to a product of two groups.

Earlier work in three dimensions supported the transition but left its order in doubt as the copy number dropped to one. Hawashin and the co-author approach from above two dimensions, using an epsilon expansion. They build a renormalizable Lagrangian, compute the beta functions and anomalous dimensions, and sort out three fixed points. Two candidate classes stay critical as the copy number nears one, while one merges into another. An instability survives only in the susceptibility tied to the Gross-Neveu-Ising order parameter.
arxiv-2510-23825:
Markus J. Aschwanden reviews a decade of work on self-organized criticality in astrophysics, the idea that many cosmic systems drive themselves to a critical state where events of all sizes occur. The survey covers the literature from 2015 to 2025, found mainly through the NASA Astrophysics Data System, and complements earlier reviews that stopped at 2014.

The phenomena are grouped by setting. Solar topics come first: flares, the photosphere, chromosphere, and corona. Then come heliospheric systems such as coronal mass ejections, the solar wind, and solar energetic particles. Planetary systems follow, from asteroids and lunar cratering to Saturn's rings and magnetospheres. The tour ends with stellar flares and galactic events — pulsar glitches, gamma-ray bursts, magnetars, blazars, and black holes. As a review, the piece maps where the criticality framework has been applied across astrophysics and where the recent evidence stands.
arxiv-2510-23925:
Guohao Sun and seven co-authors rethink how large vision-language models learn to reason, treating the chain of thought as something to infer rather than imitate. Standard training recipes — supervised fine-tuning and reward-based methods like PPO and GRPO — can overfit the training tasks and lean on reward models. Generalization to unseen reasoning problems suffers.

Their approach recasts reasoning as posterior inference and trains with a variational method. A sparse reward function gives token-level signals that favor high-likelihood reasoning traces, dodging both dull fixed sampling and reward hacking. At test time, a Bayesian scaling strategy ranks candidate answers by marginal likelihood, replacing best-of-many sampling and beam search. Across seven reasoning benchmarks, the method improved vision-language models in accuracy, reach, and clarity. The authors present latent chain-of-thought as a sturdier foundation for visual reasoning than direct imitation of written steps.
arxiv-2510-24125:
Kiran Bacsa and four co-authors show that trained causal convolutional networks act much like classic signal filters for time series data. They study networks with nearly linear activation functions on data with many frequency parts. Such networks are widely used, but what they compute after training is not always clear.

Once trained, the networks behave like finite impulse response filters, especially when their kernels are longer than usual. The team shows the whole network can be collapsed, using a property of convolution, into a single layer filter akin to one fit by least squares. This view helps explain how the networks capture frequency traits and makes their action easier to interpret for dynamic systems.
arxiv-2510-24425:
Guangyu Xie leads a team of seven authors on small sentiment models. Sentiment models judge if text sounds glad, sad, or angry. Big teacher models do this well but cost too much to run. Distillation trains a small student model to copy the teacher. Two flaws block past attempts: few hand-written prompts, and huge text piles.

Their framework, CompEffDist, builds prompts on its own from trait lists. It also filters training text, keeping hard cases and dropping easy ones. Students with three billion weights matched teachers twenty times their size. The method reached that level on most tasks across three model families. It also matched rivals while using just one tenth of the data. Small, cheap sentiment tools for real products are the clear payoff.
arxiv-2510-24525:
Terry Generet and two co-authors provide the first differential predictions at next to next to leading order for producing a W boson together with a charm meson in proton proton collisions. This process probes quantum chromodynamics and the proton's internal content, especially its strange quark component. Precise predictions are needed before the data can sharpen proton structure fits.

The results are compared with recent ATLAS measurements, and the sensitivity to the strange content is studied by PDF profiling. The agreement is promising for including W plus charm meson measurements in global fits of parton distribution functions. The work raises the precision standard for heavy flavor plus vector boson production.
arxiv-2510-24625:
Anatolii Iu Egorov, Victor T Kim, Viktor A Murzin, and Vadim A Oreshkin look for signs of extra space traits in high energy hits. When two jets fly far apart in angle, the event may hint at gravity that works in more than the usual three space traits. Their work sets up both the sign and the plain back noise.

For the noise, they use a known strong force method that works when the hit energy is very high. They then gauge what big new machines could see, from the planned high use LHC run to later round and line machines. The gap rate is their key test.
arxiv-2510-24925:
Massimo Fornasier, Lukang Sun, and Rachel Ward track the long run acts of a noise driven search for low points of a cost. Such Langevin moves are used to find best fits in hard land shapes. They set firm ground for the search: its law is well set and smooth, with fresh prior bounds.

When the end state can be pooled, the law tends to that pooled state over time. When it can not, the law spreads out, at a rate they pin down. Under a named slope rule, they show sharp fast pull toward the set of best points. Both phases are joined in one read for a class not worked this way before.
arxiv-2510-25425:
Zhengrong Guo builds a strict math frame for how carbon nanotubes start to grow. His 2025 paper deals with chirality, the twist that sets how a tube acts with current. A tube is named by two whole numbers. Past work dealt mostly with growth after the start. Two gaps blocked a full view of the first step.

One gap was the shape of the cap at the tube end. The cap is the round start piece from which the tube grows. Guo gives a clear rule that links cap shape to twist. The link is a sum rule for the cap parts. Next, he argues the twist is fixed at the start, not in growth. Some caps form more readily on the face of the growth seed. For the tube named twelve and six, one cap has six-fold shape match. That match explains why that twist shows up so often.
arxiv-2510-25525: Olfa Draouil, Rahma Yasmina Moulay Hachemi, and Bernt Oksendal construct a multiparameter Levy white noise theory. Their 2025 mathematics paper builds a white noise calculus for the Levy sheet and its compensated Poisson random measures. The theory is aimed at stochastic partial differential equations driven by Levy noise. It is a short, specialized theoretical contribution for readers who work in stochastic analysis and white noise methods.
arxiv-2510-25725:
Eunju Kwon led seven co-authors presenting a humanoid dataset. Seungwon Oh, In-Chang Baek, and Yucheon Park helped. Gyungbo Kim, JaeYoung Moon, and Yunho Choi joined. Kyung-Joong Kim closes the eight-author team. Their 2025 paper gives visual-tactile-action data for manipulation. Contact-rich manipulation matters increasingly in robot learning. Prior datasets focused on rigid objects mainly.

Pressure setting diversity was underrepresented in prior data. Their dataset targets deformable soft object manipulation. Teleoperation with a humanoid robot collected it. Dexterous hands captured multimodal effects during tasks. Varying pressure settings were systematically included. Visual, tactile, and action signals are recorded jointly. Future models need advanced tuning for such data. Tactile signal hardness and diversity challenge learning methods. Humanoid embodiments match human-like manipulation settings closely. Soft object handling requires gentle, changing control strategies. Rich tactile feedback could teach those strategies. The dataset motivates research on tactile-aware robot learning.
arxiv-2510-26025:
Semyon Lomasov leads seven co-authors in a study of whether a strong chess model shares human concepts or only mimics patterns. They analyze a transformer model with two hundred seventy million parameters that plays at grandmaster level. Chess offers a clean test bed, since human strategy concepts such as center control and knight outposts are precise and well named.

Early layers of the model encode human concepts with up to eighty five percent accuracy in their probes, but deeper layers drift toward alien representations while playing better. On a new Chess960 data set, where starting pieces are randomized, concept recognition fell for all methods once memorized openings were removed. The findings expose a tension between winning play and human like understanding.
arxiv-2510-26125:
Runsheng Xu leads thirteen co-authors in a new Waymo data set built to test end to end self driving on rare, hard cases. End to end driving learns to drive directly from camera views, and it pairs well with multimodal language models, but current benchmarks mostly show normal scenes. Their data set holds four thousand twenty one driving segments, about twelve hours, chosen for long tail events that occur in less than a small fraction of daily driving.

Each segment includes routing directions, vehicle state, and full surround views from eight cameras. For scoring, they propose a Rater Feedback Score, based on human rater judgments, which better captures the multi modal nature of good driving than simple distance to a reference path. The set targets true robustness, not average case skill.
arxiv-2510-26325:
Hugues Meyer and Kay Brandner identify a regime where discrete time dynamics with weak memory can be reduced to a simple memoryless form. Discrete dynamics appear in systems whose time translation symmetry is broken, and they are usually written as first order recurrences for classical or quantum Markov chains. Hidden degrees of freedom, though, induce memory, which generally forces higher order evolution equations.

Meyer and Brandner delineate a weak memory regime where, on an intermediate time scale, such higher order equations reduce systematically to a unique first order counterpart on the same state space. They state the result as a mathematical theorem and work through two examples: stochastic Floquet dynamics under coarse graining, and quantum collisional models, showing how the reduction applies in practice.
arxiv-2510-26425:
Chen Chen, with ten co-authors, computes a key trait of the nucleon, the core particle of atoms, using lattice quantum chromodynamics. Lattice QCD puts the strong force on a grid of space and time points so computers can handle it. The team wants the unpolarized gluon parton distribution, which says how the nucleon's momentum is shared among gluons, its force-carrying particles.

Chen and the team run the work at the physical point, with real-world particle masses, and push toward the limit of a fine grid. They use five grid spacings, pion masses from near the real value upward, and nucleon momenta up to three giga-electronvolts in their units. Signal-boosting tricks, careful rescaling, and matching steps turn raw grid output into the final distribution. The paper presents it as a state-of-the-art result for this hard quantity.
arxiv-2510-26825:
Jiarong Du, with six co-authors, builds a speech enhancement system that uses the speaker's face as a guide. Audio-visual speech enhancement extracts a target voice from mixed audio with help from video. Real settings add interfering sounds and reverberation, which defeat most earlier methods and hurt the perceived quality of the result.

Du and the team design a pipeline that separates first and dereverberates second, a structure that can be grafted onto other enhancement networks. They validate it in the fourth COGMHEAR audio-visual speech enhancement challenge. Their system posted excellent results on the competition's three objective metrics. It ultimately took first place in the human subjective listening test, the measure the authors treat as decisive for real-world use.
arxiv-2510-27325:
Marius Feldmann, Tobias Nöthlich, and five other co-authors report results from the REDMARS2 project in this whitepaper. The project ran in 2021 and 2022 and looked at networks that must work across long delays. Such delay-tolerant networks serve places like deep space, where signals take minutes or hours. Their tool is the bundle, a packet that can carry other bundles inside it.

Nesting bundles lets the net split into scopes, zones with their own rules, following a recursive design idea the team borrows. The team built and tested the scheme in real field trials with the European Space Agency. One test mimicked a Solar System internet with drones and satellite relays. The trials showed the design can grow and still work across partners.
arxiv-2510-27525:
J. Poole, N. Dervilis, and five other co-authors cut the labeling cost of watching structures for damage, in a 2025 paper. Bridges and turbines need health checks, but labeled examples of damage are costly and rare. Population-based monitoring borrows data from sister structures. Their data differ in spread, though, so borrowed lessons can mislead.

Transfer learning aligns the spreads; most past work used no labeled target data at all. Their Bayesian framework starts from that unlabeled alignment, then improves it with a few labeled target cases. An active sampling strategy picks which cases are worth labeling, guiding inspections to the most telling spots. On a population of test structures, the method learned target classifiers with far fewer labels. That means cheaper monitoring campaigns with the same sharpness.
arxiv-2510-27625:
Andrew Leal studies hiring choices in 2025 through a lab job market where pay depends on choices. Bosses care about skill, but also about whether a worker will shirk, which means putting in low effort when not watched. Leal asks how bosses trade skill against prosocial conduct, which is a bent to help others and act fairly, when they rank candidates.

Workers first took part and left records of skill and conduct. Later, bosses saw those records and ranked and priced each worker for two distinct jobs. On average, bosses valued skill more than good conduct, most of all in science and tech fields. Bosses who were themselves highly prosocial valued good conduct more, at times above skill. Shared traits thus shape who gets hired.
arxiv-2511-00025:
Tadisetty Sai Yashwanth examines the data-based structure of floating-point noise in GPU matrix product, testing the common assumption that such errors are independent Gaussian noise. Floating-point adding order makes matrix product non-fixed, mainly across batch settings. Comparing outputs of single-input and batched products reveals pattern the independent model cannot explain.

The independent Gaussian picture predicts output instability where the observed pattern differs, so the assumption fails as a account of real hardware. Computing readers get a warning for repeat testing work in deep learning: numeric noise has structure. Understanding that structure matters for bug fixing, checking, and bitwise repeat testing efforts.
arxiv-2511-00325:
Jacek Gȩbala, Michał Tomza, and José D'Incao calculate what happens when two neutral atoms meet an ion near a special tuning point called a Feshbach resonance. In neutral three-atom systems, universal rules often predict bound states and collisions from very little detail. The team checks whether those rules survive when one partner carries a charge and pulls with long-range force.

They do not survive intact. The long-range pull bends behavior away from predictions based on short-range or van der Waals forces. At the same time, harmful inelastic transitions are strongly suppressed, so Efimov states, fragile three-body bound states, live far longer than in neutral systems. The dense spectra of these molecular ions could make a rich platform for few-body physics.
arxiv-2511-00525:
Gideon Yoffe, Fabian Klenner, Barak Sober, Yohai Kaspi, and Itay Halevy propose a new kind of biosignature for the search for life: molecular diversity. Classic biosignatures depend on naming specific molecules, isotopes, or handedness, measurements that space missions can only partly make. Their alternative looks at the statistical organization of whole molecular mixtures, scored with diversity metrics that need only relative abundances.

Across a dataset spanning Earth and space contexts, living samples proved consistently more diverse in amino acids than nonliving ones. The same gap held for fatty acids, suggesting the signal reflects how life builds molecules, not one lucky compound class. The distinction even survived modeled space-like degradation. Any mission composition data, archived or planned, can be screened this way.
arxiv-2511-00825:
Hanif Golchin, Hamid Bakhtiarizadeh, and Mohammad Reza Mehdizadeh present the first study of traversable wormholes inside Einstein-aether theory, a version of gravity with an added preferred time direction. Wormholes are tunnel like solutions that, in standard gravity, usually need matter that breaks basic energy rules.

By choosing three classes of values for the aether coupling constants and testing three shapes for the wormhole throat, they find three distinct geometries. For suitable parameters, the energy conditions can hold at the throat, unlike in Einstein gravity. In one class they hold across the whole spacetime. Requiring this also tightens the allowed ranges of the aether couplings beyond earlier theoretical and observational limits.
arxiv-2511-01425:
Yuhang Huang, Zekai Lin, Fan Zhong, and Lei Liu build a diagnostic agent whose explanations can be checked. In high stakes fields like medicine, model explanations often cannot be verified, which undermines trust. Their agent instead explains through an auditable sequence of actions, learning when to go and fetch external visual evidence for its reasoning.

Reinforcement learning trains that evidence seeking policy, making the agent both efficient and generalizable. In experiments the interactive process improved calibrated accuracy, cutting the Brier score by about eighteen percent against a non-interactive baseline. To test whether the explanations are faithful, the authors mask the evidence the agent chose and watch performance degrade measurably, confirming the evidence genuinely drives the decisions.
arxiv-2511-01525:
James Tian proves bounds on the size of combined quantum-style systems built from pairs of self-adjoint contractions, operators that never stretch a vector. The inequalities generalize the analytic structure behind the Tsirelson and CHSH bounds, famous limits on how strongly separated quantum systems can be correlated.

The estimates are dimension-free, meaning they do not grow with the size of the system, and they are written through norms of commutators and anticommutators. A graph-based version handles sparse interaction patterns, where each system touches only a few others, with constants depending only on how connected the graph is. The results connect operator theory with Bell correlations and network nonlocality, offering closed-form estimates alongside numerical semidefinite methods.
arxiv-2511-01825:
Ivy Chen and ten colleagues develop a gentler way to carve lithium niobate, the nonlinear optical crystal at the heart of thin-film integrated photonics for communications and quantum information. On-chip devices are held back by rough sidewalls and uneven geometry. Atomic layer etching removes material a layer at a time. It could polish past those limits, if it could etch directionally and avoid redepositing debris.

Their process alternates a hydrogen bromide, boron trichloride, and argon plasma that modifies the surface with an argon plasma that removes the modified layer. Bromine chemistry cuts redeposition compared with fluorine or chlorine plasmas, thanks to the higher vapor pressure of its products. A grating etched entirely by the process, 220 nanometers deep, showed no aspect-ratio-dependent etching down to gaps of 150 nanometers, where ion milling already fails at 300 nanometer gaps.
arxiv-2511-01925:
Safa Alsheyab models how natural gas's share of United States power production evolves. The tool is a new stochastic diffusion process. It is a random-walk-with-drift mathematical model, for quantities that wander over time. The variable tracked is gas-fired generation as a percentage of total electricity production.

The method works through trend function analysis, fitting both conditional and unconditional versions of the estimated trend. Parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood from discretely sampled paths of the annual series covering 1990 to 2021. The proposed process fits the historical data effectively and produces dependable medium-term forecasts, which the paper reports for 2022 and 2023. The contribution is one of method: a fresh diffusion model, with its estimation machinery worked out, applied to an energy series that planners watch closely as generation mixes shift.
arxiv-2511-02225:
Fan Feng, Phillip Lippe, and Sara Magliacane teach reinforcement learning agents to see a scene as objects that interact, rather than as one undifferentiated state. Agents with that structure should learn policies that are sturdier and transfer better, but most object-centric methods model each object separately and leave the interactions implicit. Their framework, FIOC-WM, learns a world model in which both object representations and their interaction structure are explicit and modular.

Starting from pixels and pretrained vision encoders, the system learns object-centred latent variables plus an interaction graph, then breaks tasks into composable interaction building blocks. A two-level policy picks which interactions to perform and in what order, while a lower level carries them out. On simulated robotics and embodied AI benchmarks, the method improved both how few trials policies needed and how well they generalised, compared with other world-model approaches.
arxiv-2511-02625:
Xinliang Liu, Tong Mao, and Jinchao Xu study shallow neural networks built on a sphere. Their 2025 paper looks at two matrices that come from these networks, called the mass and stiffness matrices. The main question is how hard those matrices are to work with in practice, a trait measured by the condition number.

When the network points sit in balanced pairs on the sphere, the authors find sharp values for the condition number. They also pin down the full set of eigenvalues, the special values tied to each matrix. Small eigenvalues link to simple low-degree patterns, while large ones link to high-degree patterns. The work ties a network's power to its stability in a precise way.
arxiv-2511-02825:
Artur d'Avila Garcez and Simon Odense argue that modern AI speaks a powerful new language of science but lacks semantics, a clear account of what its outputs mean. Without one, discoveries made by neural networks stay unsatisfying. Their 2025 paper claims logic can supply the missing framework, inside the neurosymbolic program that weds networks with symbolic rules.

The field today has many one-off encodings and extraction tricks, but no shared conditions for when good properties hold. The authors set out a framework for semantic encoding that makes the network-to-logic map explicit and names the common parts of past approaches. They define it formally, review leading methods, and discuss why finding such an encoding is hard in practice, drawing a parallel with problems in the philosophy of mind.
arxiv-2511-03025:
D. Vergani, S. Quai, and the Euclid Collaboration hunt a rare kind of galaxy in the telescope's first spectroscopic data. Their targets show highly ionized emission lines, signs of an active nucleus, violent shocks, or Wolf-Rayet stars. The sample sits in a redshift window, 2.48 to 3.88, where both neon and oxygen lines can be seen at once, a region past the usual hydrogen line range.

The team inspected spectra by eye and landed on sixty-five candidate neon emitters. Their colors resemble bright quasars, with a few very red cases. Against a control sample matched on oxygen lines and distance, the candidates held more stellar mass and a weaker break near 4000 angstroms, with similar shape profiles. The set is a first systematic probe for later releases.
arxiv-2511-03525:
Marco D'Elia, Irene Finocchi, and Maurizio Patrignani engineer faster ways to list well-isolated tight groups in large graphs. Maximal cliques, sets where everyone links to everyone else, explode in number even in sparse real networks. Isolated cliques, whose members link only lightly outward, are fewer and often more useful.

Building on a classic recursive enumerator, the team adds four pruning rules that cut search branches sure to fail the isolation test. Rules can run singly or stacked, and proofs confirm none discard a valid clique. Tuning the isolation dial filters out cliques tangled with the rest of the graph. Faster listing makes clique analysis practical for community and fraud hunting in big networks.
arxiv-2511-03625:
Shaan D Patel, Billy Quarles, Nevin N Weinberg, and Manfred Cuntz ask whether Earth-like planets around the smallest common stars can keep a large moon. Such planets in the habitable zone have become favorite targets in the hunt for moons beyond our system. Gravity among star, planet, and moon plus tidal drag decide a moon's fate, modeled here with a standard N-body simulator and its tidal extension.

Large moons around planets of mid-type dwarfs go unstable in under ten million years, far short of biological timescales. Even around the largest dwarfs in the class, most large moons fail within a billion years. If big moons help life, as Earth's Moon may, then habitable-zone planets of these stars face a hidden handicap for hosting complex biospheres.
arxiv-2511-03725:
Jongseo Lee and co-authors propose DANCE, a video action recognizer that explains itself through separated motion, object, and scene concepts. Heat-map explanations blur those strands together, leaving users unsure whether a call rested on movement or backdrop. Word-based explanations add structure, yet motion is tacit knowledge that words capture poorly.

Motion concepts are defined as human pose sequences, which carry movement without needing prose. A language model extracts object and scene concepts automatically to complete the trio. Predictions then flow through those named concepts, so an explanation can credit the swing itself rather than the court around it. Clearer video explanations matter for coaching, surveillance review, and any setting where a wrong reason is as bad as a wrong label.
arxiv-2511-04025:
Tianyi Huang, Chang Liu, and Bohan Wang present a compact design space for shellular metamaterials, thin periodic shell structures whose shape controls mechanical behaviour. Only a few dozen electric charges define a family running from flat sheets to complex minimal-surface-like forms, keeping the space small yet rich.

A graphics chip pipeline computes the elastic tensor of a candidate in near real time, making hands-on design practical. Built structures span wide shape and mechanical ranges. In the low-solid-volume regime, inverse-designed shells rival leading shell materials on several measures. Tiled prototypes built by 3D printing confirm the designs can be fabricated, backing real use beyond simulation.
arxiv-2511-04125:
Isaac M Hair and Amit Sahai prove that the shortest vector problem in Lp norms is deterministically NP-hard. That holds for every p above two. It stays hard even to approximate within a factor that grows almost exponentially in a fractional power of log dimension. Catalog evidence garbled the formula into the title; the arXiv record states the claim cleanly, and it is presented here as the authors' proved theorem.

Earlier finite-norm hardness needed the assumption that NP is not contained in RP, and only constant-factor approximation bounds were known. Their proof reduces directly from a regularized probabilistically checkable proof instance using elementary gadgets built on Vandermonde and Hadamard matrices. Exact hardness in a finite norm is also established for the first time.
arxiv-2511-04225:
Xuan Zhang, Xiao-le Li, Jingjing Niu, Tongxing Yan, and Yuanzhen Chen present a lean framework for nonadiabatic geometric quantum gates that delivers the robustness geometric gates promise in theory. Global path properties should resist control errors, yet real gates have often failed to keep that resilience.

Extra constraints suppress dynamical contamination, and noncyclic paths add design freedom. On superconducting transmon qubits, single-qubit gates reached high fidelity with error scaling far gentler than standard dynamical gates under Rabi amplitude error. Two-qubit gates under parametric driving exposed limits tied to phase compensation and waveform tuning. The scheme's plain design suits many quantum platforms, the authors argue.
arxiv-2511-04325:
Egor S Vyatkin and Sergey A Tarasenko build an analytic theory of second harmonic generation in hybrid setups that pair a nonlinear 2D crystal with a dielectric metasurface sheet. Resonant modes can strongly boost frequency doubling, and a theory in terms of material traits guides design better than blind runs alone.

At leaky resonances, output is set by radiative broadening tied to Fourier harmonics of the sheet response. At quasi-bound-state resonances, uneven broadening and absorption cap the gain instead. Diffracted second harmonic beams appear even when both parts are centrosymmetric, through a nonlocal route, with polarization traits spelled out. Basic limits for this platform are pinned down with the boost routes.
arxiv-2511-04825:
Luigi Caputi and two colleagues test reachability homology on directed graph data. The method tracks how reachability patterns persist across scales in a network. It refines older directed flag complex homology by working with condensed, smaller graphs.

The test case is epilepsy detection, a pressing brain research task. Betti curves and their integrals serve as shape features for the model. A support vector machine runs the test on brain network data. Reachability homology beats the older directed homology on the task. Smaller middle graphs also promise cheaper cost for network classification generally.
arxiv-2511-05025:
Hala Sheta built 8bit-GPT, a language model dressed as an old Macintosh system, to make users pause and think about chat bot use. Fast, smooth chat tools invite heavy reliance, which can dull recall and breed shallow bonds with the tool.

The design draws on slow technology and on making a tool less handy on purpose. By forcing clunky, slow steps, it breaks the smooth feel of modern bots and puts their role as tools back in view. The work asks what is lost when help feels too human and too easy.
arxiv-2511-05125:
Fei Li and co-authors test whether channel superposition can save quantum illumination from photon loss. In that method, an entangled probe photon and its twin boost the chance to spot a faint target in noise, per photon spent.

Loss of photons cuts that edge in practice. The authors try two superposition plans, one with no fixed order of channels and one with split paths. Using a quantum bound, their math and numeric work show both plans ease loss harm. The result points to more robust faint-target sensing with quantum light.
arxiv-2511-05225:
João Henrique Andrade and co-authors classify a family of singular Yamabe metrics on a sphere with two points removed. The Delaunay metrics are the known family here: flat under conformal change, with constant fractional curvature, symmetric, and periodic.

The authors prove that, for a parameter close to but below one, any full metric of that kind on the twice-punctured sphere is a Delaunay metric. On the way, they prove a sharp bound on the conformal factor. Such sharp bounds often serve far past their first use in geometric analysis more broadly.
arxiv-2511-05925:
M Mondelin and co-authors study the Perseus-Pisces supercluster, a vast chain of galaxies, to see how a galaxy's place shapes its form. Long threads in the cosmic web guide how structures grow. The team paired a catalog of galaxy spectra with deep images from a large telescope camera in Hawaii.

Galaxy shapes were judged by eye and from how their light fades with radius, which catches faint outer parts. A mapping tool rebuilt the thread network in 3D, giving each galaxy's gap to the nearest thread and dense node. The map shows thin threads braiding toward the Pisces cluster. Heavy, old-style galaxies hug the thread spines and nodes, while spiral and ragged ones spread more broadly.
arxiv-2511-06025:
Derya Sürgit leads a team measuring the southern eclipsing binary star DG Mic for the first time from spectra. The pair is a detached Algol-type system, where two stars orbit without touching and take turns eclipsing each other. Their program observes such southern systems to pin down exact stellar properties.

Spectra from mid-resolution instruments set the hotter star's temperature and checked the model against the system's overall light output. Combined fits to those spectra and light curves from three sky surveys show two near-twin stars in circular orbits. The masses and radii of both stars were measured with modest errors. Standard evolution models say both are main-sequence stars, with a system age of roughly seven hundred million years.
arxiv-2511-06125:
Nathan Scales, Nathanael Schärli, and Olivier Bousquet dissect why retrieval-based question answering fails on a hard benchmark. Retrieval-augmented generation grounds answers in fetched documents, yet it struggles when the needed facts are scattered across many documents or demand complex reasoning. The QUEST part of the LOFT benchmark showed the largest headroom of all.

The authors analyze the factors behind the poor scores and publish updated numbers grounded in careful human evaluation. They then show retrieval can be tuned to beat long-context approaches by a wide margin. The winning recipe uses a structured output holding reasoning and evidence, with an optional second pass that re-verifies the answer. The analysis separates fixable pipeline flaws from true model limits.
arxiv-2511-06225:
Shu Zhao and co-authors handle a common failure of vision-language models: one input type goes missing at test time. A model trained with both images and text may receive only one, due to privacy limits or collection problems. Prompt-based fixes miss the ties between the two input types and add computing cost.

Their method, MoRA, fine-tunes the model with very few new parameters. Shared parameters link the vision and text encoders so knowledge flows both ways, while separate parameters keep each input type flexible. On standard benchmarks, MoRA improved missing-modality accuracy by about five percentage points over the prior best, using a fraction of its inference time.
arxiv-2511-06625:
Yifei Zhang and colleagues read cardiovascular risk out of low-dose chest scans taken for lung screening. One scan images both lungs and heart, yet most tools judge each organ system alone and ignore how they interact. Their framework reasons across diseases while showing its work in plain language.

Four parts cooperate: a frozen lung-risk prior, a lung perception module, an agentic reasoning step grounded in medical knowledge, and a cardiac feature extractor over a heart subvolume. Fused outputs blend local heart evidence with mechanism-level lung context. On a national screening cohort the system beat heart-only, single-disease, and foundation-model rivals at screening and mortality prediction, with controls ruling out simpler explanations.
arxiv-2511-07125:
Andre Opris tightens the theoretical understanding of NSGA-III, a widely used evolutionary algorithm for optimization with many objectives. Its population dynamics, especially how many individuals can share one fitness value, have resisted analysis, and almost no runtime bounds existed. Opris proves tight bounds on the bi-objective OneMinMax benchmark, a standard test problem where each bit string is scored by its numbers of ones and zeros.

The expected number of generations is shown to grow like a certain function of problem size and population size. This gives the first proven lower runtime bound for NSGA-III on a classic benchmark besides one recent exception. For the general multi-objective version he improves the known upper bound by a large factor. A surprise follows: NSGA-III beats its predecessor NSGA-II in expected runtime by a factor tied to population size.
arxiv-2511-07325:
R Kumar and four co-authors build a camera-based system that catches illegal waste dumping at garbage vulnerable points in Indian cities. These chronic dumping spots burden municipal services, and the proposed system pairs Internet of Things infrastructure with computer vision: a street-level camera watches the point. An object detection model flags dumped waste as it appears. Data was collected in the Sangareddy district of Telangana.

Four detection models, YOLOv8, YOLOv10, YOLO11m, and RT-DETR, were tested in depth on the collected dataset. YOLO11m won, reaching about ninety-two percent accuracy and a mean average precision of 0.91 at the standard threshold. Beyond detection, the system logs hourly, daily, and weekly dumping patterns around the clock, giving municipalities both enforcement alerts and the trend data needed to plan cleanups.
arxiv-2511-07625:
Ola Kenji Forslund and colleagues watch a magnet flip from metal to insulator while changing its topology. K2Cr8O16, a chromium oxide, orders as a magnet and then stops conducting. Whether lattice softening drives the change, as in a Peierls shift, was the open question.

X-ray and neutron scattering plus first-principles math finds no phonon softening at the transition. The switch therefore comes from electron interactions and band topology rather than a lattice distortion. Its topology changes across the same edge. A material that toggles conduction and topology together inside a magnetic state interests makers of future quantum switches.
arxiv-2511-08125:
Askin Altinoklu and Leila Musavian design power splitting and beamforming for wireless systems that send information and energy jointly. Dynamic metasurface antennas serve several single antenna users who must each harvest enough energy while keeping signal quality. Metasurfaces cut the need for radio chains and phase shifters, but their tuning follows a strict Lorentzian constraint.

An alternating tuning method based on semidefinite programming handles the coupled choices. Several holography schemes are weighed, including an adaptive radius variant, alongside nonlinear harvesting models and circuit noise. Model runs show the proposed design lowers transmit power clearly compared with baselines, confirming the value of optimal splitting.
arxiv-2511-08425:
Zeyang Li, Kaveh Alim, and Navid Azizan introduce HardFlow, a method for making flow matching generative models obey hard constraints on their outputs. Diffusion and flow models generate richly varied samples, but applications like robot motion demand exact constraint satisfaction, such as never hitting an obstacle. Projecting the whole sampling path onto the constraint set is overly restrictive and damages sample quality, the authors argue.

HardFlow instead recasts constrained sampling as trajectory optimization, steering the path with numerical optimal control so constraints hold precisely at the final time. Model predictive control ideas turn the problem into an efficient surrogate problem. Extra integral and terminal costs can reduce distribution shift and raise quality inside the same framework.
arxiv-2511-08525:
Shu Yang and co-authors in full study whether the thinking traces of large thinking models can be watched for trouble. Long chains of thought expose shortcuts or pleasing, suggesting a safety chance, but two blocks stand in the way. Models do not always state the real factors behind a decision, and monitors reading long traces can be oversensitive, insensitive, or simply deceived by elaborate wording.

The study separates those problems into verbalization quality and monitor reliability. Empirical evidence and correlation analyses connect how faithfully a model explains itself, how reliably a monitor can detect trouble, and final task performance. The authors frame their work as the first systematic map of chain of thought monitorability.
arxiv-2511-08725:
Katy Aruachan and four co-authors model how molecular spin qubits lose their quantum coherence, a limit that decides whether such qubits can ever compute well. Their test system is copper porphyrin molecules held in a crystal, where the qubit's magnetic tensor wobbles as the lattice moves.

Molecular dynamics runs supply the wobbling, which feeds quantum master equations that predict the relaxation and dephasing times. Physics at the atomic level alone predicts relaxation times far longer than those measured. Adding a magnetic field noise model for the lattice's nuclear spins restores agreement at every field strength. The combined picture explains why relaxation follows one field scaling while dephasing follows another. The authors present the method as a general tool for molecular qubits.
arxiv-2511-08925:
Marius Lemm, Simone Rademacher, and Jingxuan Zhang prove that disorder slows a Bose-Einstein condensate's ripples to a crawl. Their system holds interacting bosons in the mean-field regime, sitting in a potential that is either random or quasi-periodic, and starts from a condensate localized in one spot.

The fluctuations around that condensate, which carry sound and transport, propagate with only a small velocity because the disorder keeps tripping them. The result holds in any spatial dimension, giving a rare example of a disordered many-body system with rigorously proven slow transport. The technical novelty is an interaction-picture analysis built directly on the Anderson-localized one-body dynamics, the single-particle states that disorder pins in place. Such proofs matter because slow transport in interacting disordered systems is usually argued from numerics, not theorems.
arxiv-2511-09425:
Yicheng Li and Qian Lin gather evidence for a theoretical program aimed at explaining why neural networks learn useful features. The adaptive feature program analyzes feature learning abstractly, stripping training down to its essential dynamics. Their strategy leans on Le Cam equivalence, a classical idea for comparing statistical experiments.

They advocate over-parameterized sequence models as a simplified arena for studying the program's training dynamics. A quantity called the feature error measure tracks how good the learned features are. Across several concrete models, including linear regression and single- and multiple-index models, that measure decreases during training, they show. The pattern supports the program's promise as a route to a real theory of feature learning.
arxiv-2511-10025:
Noam Koren, Ralf J. J. Mackenbach, Ruud J. G. van Sloun, Kira Radinsky, and Daniel Freedman present SVD-NO, a neural operator that learns solution operators for partial differential equations directly from data.
