Jingwen Fu, Ming Xiao, and Mikael Skoglund present DriftDecode, a one-step decoder for wireless image transmission that restores detail rather than generating an image from scratch. Generative receivers can raise reconstruction quality, but diffusion and flow decoders need many iterative steps and add latency. A received wireless signal already keeps the coarse structure of the source image, so the hard part is recovering channel-damaged detail.

DriftDecode conditions a one-step U-Net decoder on the signal-to-noise ratio and adds a drift-inspired texture loss at the instance level. That loss, set in perceptual feature space, pulls each rebuilt local feature toward its aligned true counterpart and suppresses mismatches. The design aims for diffusion-like quality at single-step speed.
arxiv-2605-02625:
Davide Valentinis derives how local quantum fluids respond when a probe varies in both time and space. In strongly linked electron systems outside the slow, diffusive regime, a probe's energy stirs time-dependent forces. Its spatial pattern also makes the response spread beyond the probe point. A sound theory must still respect charge and mass conservation, which constrains the math tightly.

Valentinis assumes self-energies and interaction terms that are local but depend on frequency. He then builds corrected interaction terms inside the standard response frame, using coupled integral equations. That covers density, currents, momentum, and stress at once. Clear symmetry rules then state when the corrections vanish in full. The rules turn on how energy bands and bare interaction terms behave under operations such as inversion and mirror reflection.
arxiv-2605-03025:
Shauvik Biswas asks whether a wormhole can show no tidal response, in the form of vanishing magnetic-type Love numbers. Love numbers measure how a compact object deforms under an outside tidal field, and for black holes in general relativity some of them famously vanish. Wormholes, as rival geometries to black holes, invite the same test: does their tidal signature match, or give them away?

The test case is a wormhole solution in a spacetime with vanishing Ricci scalar, under a steady axial gravitational perturbation. Keeping the master equation's solution to first order in the geometry's regularization parameter, the magnetic Love number for the quadrupole mode vanishes, and numerical solutions with physical boundary conditions back the result. A second wormhole family, of Damour-Solodukhin type, gives the same conclusion.
arxiv-2605-03325:
Haiping Hu builds a scattering theory for time boundaries. A time boundary is the temporal analogue of a spatial interface. At such a boundary, a system's rules change suddenly in time. Spatial scattering is well developed, but no unified quantum framework for time boundaries existed.

Hu defines a temporal scattering matrix. It links incoming and outgoing Bloch channels. Special points in it give perfect band-to-band transfer and frozen dynamics. A bulk-time-boundary rule ties their count to the jump in a bulk invariant. In one dimension, this yields a time-domain Levinson theorem. Robustness depends strikingly on whether the dimension is even or odd.
arxiv-2605-03425:
Duc Dm, Thao Do, Minh Son Hoang, Anh Le Duc Tran, Daeyoung Kim, and Huy Nguyen present FiBeR, a differentially private optimizer built for temporally filtered gradients. Filtering privatized gradients cuts variance. But it also changes the noise statistics that adaptive optimizers assume. Standard bias corrections then become miscalibrated.

FiBeR filters in innovation space. It decouples observation geometry from filter gain, for independent tuning. It subtracts a filter-aware noise term, computed in closed form. Across vision and language benchmarks, under equal privacy budgets, it consistently beat state-of-the-art private optimizers. The gains show that optimizer design must match the filtering actually applied.
arxiv-2605-03825:
Xiamiao Zhao, Yichen Wang, and Mei Lu settle a conjecture about paths between equal-degree vertices in dense graphs. Erdős and Hajnal asked whether every graph with a certain number of vertices and edges must contain two vertices of equal degree joined by a path of length three. The edge bound is sharp because of the complete bipartite graph. Chen and Ma answered that question affirmatively for large cases in 2026.

Chen and Ma further conjectured that, for sufficiently large graphs, the statement stays true when the path of length three is replaced by a path of any fixed odd length. Zhao and his co-authors confirm that conjecture, extending the equal-degree phenomenon from short paths to all fixed odd lengths.
arxiv-2605-04125:
T. Azevedo and four co-authors calculate the magnetic counterpart of the Uehling correction, a quantum electrodynamic effect in which virtual particle-antiparticle pairs polarize the vacuum around a charge. Their target is the field of a classical point-like idealized magnet, corrected by the relativistic quantum effects of vacuum pair creation. The vacuum, under this correction, behaves like a paramagnetic medium.

They find the induced currents that stem from vacuum polarization around the magnet. They also compute the correction to the electric dipole potential and show that the familiar symmetry between the classical fields of point electric and magnetic dipoles is broken at the quantum level. Possible applications are briefly discussed, including neutron-neutron scattering and the hyperfine splitting of hydrogen-like atoms.
arxiv-2605-04325:
Nicholas J. Cooper and five co-authors introduce a framework for analysing the architectural complexity of deep neural networks, down to the structure of the tensor operations that most theory leaves abstract. Their aim is both to understand how designs have evolved and to build new ones in a principled way.

Studying networks introduced over forty years, they find that landmark designs coincide with jumps in distinct kinds of complexity. They also identify large families of higher-complexity designs that nobody has explored yet, and they release a public data set of more than three thousand such architectures for others to test.
arxiv-2605-04725:
Zhibin Du and Xuli Qi bound how small the average distance of a spanning tree can be. The bound uses a graph's independence number. That number is the size of its largest set of mutually nonadjacent vertices. A spanning tree's average distance averages the path lengths between all vertex pairs. Finding the best such tree is known to be computationally hard. Guarantees therefore matter.

A 2014 result showed a tree with average distance at most the independence number plus two always exists, under a mild size condition. Du and Qi first improve that bound, to below the independence number plus one. They then sharpen it further for larger independence numbers. The sharper bound grows more slowly.
arxiv-2605-04825:
Taiga Hayashi and five co-authors improve a black-box search method that pairs a factorization machine with annealing hardware. When whole numbers are encoded as one-hot binary choices, random starting data can leave some choices never switched on. Those parts of the model then get no direct learning signal from the first data.

The authors design starting data so every binary choice appears at least once, using Latin hypercube sampling and Sobol sequences. They test both versions on shaping a wing for a human-powered aircraft, with seventeen and thirty-two design choices. Both versions reached higher average cruising speeds than the standard method, with a clearer gain on the larger problem.
arxiv-2605-05025:
Gijs van Dijk proposes detecting language model hallucinations from the model's own attention patterns in a single pass. Many uncertainty methods need repeated sampling or extra models, which adds cost. His method measures how far each attention head's distribution sits from a uniform one, using a divergence measure, and feeds those values to a simple logistic probe.

Across datasets, task types, and model families, that signal predicted answer correctness well and rivalled established uncertainty methods. The signal sits in middle layers and on factual tokens such as names and numbers. That pattern makes those dynamics a cheap and readable white-box sign of when a model is unsure.
arxiv-2605-05125:
Olivia Jullian Parra and nine co-authors estimate treatment effects from incomplete electronic health records, where missing biomarkers may be missing for reasons tied to their values. Trial emulation lets researchers ask causal questions of observational data when a real trial is impossible. Time-varying confounding and heavy missingness make such records especially hard.

Their two-stage pipeline first runs a causal normalising flow, constrained by an explicit causal graph and fed with patient history, to make exact counterfactual inferences. A language-model-driven evolutionary imputer then fills gaps by proposing reusable imputation rules rather than single values. Tests on synthetic benchmarks show the graph constraints and exact inference each fix distinct failure modes.
arxiv-2605-05725:
Spotting anomalies in a time series is expert work: points, structures, seasons, and patterns each fail differently. Hyeongwon Kang, Jeongseob Kim, Jinwoo Park, and Pilsung Kang build SAGE, a multi-agent framework that mimics that division of labor. A single general model asked for anomaly locations directly proves hard to control or interpret.

SAGE fields four specialized analyzers, one per anomaly family, each with numerical tools and diagnostic plots. An evidence-grounded detector then consolidates their findings into confidence-scored judgments. The design aims for diagnoses a human expert can audit, not bare index predictions.
arxiv-2605-05925:
Hyesung Lee and three co-authors address a hard problem in robot learning: teaching dexterous hands from human motion data. Human object interaction records are sparse and purely kinematic, so copying them onto a robot often fails. Body mismatch and rich contact forces make direct retargeting unreliable in the real world.

Their framework, DexSynRefine, treats human motion as a guide rather than as ready robot action. It first builds hand and object paths from a learned motion prior, then grounds them with reinforcement learning in task space. A final step reads contact clues from the robot's own sensor history. Across five tasks, real world success rose by 50 to 70 percentage points over kinematic copying.
arxiv-2605-06225:
Andy Zeyi Liu and five co-authors steer language models by editing the latent attention cache instead of the visible prompt. Prompting gives strong control but stores guidance tokens at every layer and clutters long conversations. Activation steering is compact, yet usually weaker and poor at carrying large structured reminders over time.

Memory Inception inserts text derived key value banks at selected layers only, treating steering as selective cache allocation. On matched personality steering tasks it gave the best balance of control against drift, rivaling prompting and beating a leading activation method. It also supports mid conversation behavior shifts without rewriting the transcript. On structured reasoning tests it beat visible prompting in most settings while cutting matched cache storage by up to 118 times.
arxiv-2605-06725: Veronica Phan extends the graph blow-up operation to a broader combinatorial setting and discusses what it could be used for. In graph theory, blowing up a graph replaces each vertex with several copies of itself, and copies are joined exactly when the original vertices were joined. Phan generalizes that copying idea beyond graphs and explores potential applications of the extended construction.
arxiv-2605-06825:
Rohan Patil, Jai Malegaonkar, and Henrik I. Christensen show that randomness is sometimes needed for same agents to act as a team. Cooperative learning teams usually share one policy, but under symmetric views a shared deterministic policy gives every agent the same action spread, making role split impossible. Symmetry breaking among unnamed chips is known to require randomness, and their Diamond Attention architecture builds it in.

Each agent samples a random number per step, creating a brief ranking that hides lower-ranked peers from agent-to-agent attention while task attention stays open. A team trained with four agents deploys as-is to teams of two through eight. On a symmetric test game it succeeds fully where deterministic rivals stall near chance.
arxiv-2605-06925:
Christina W. Lindberg and sixteen co-authors map dust extinction across the Small and Large Magellanic Clouds at parsec detail, the finest yet for these neighboring galaxies. Dust dims starlight and traces the raw material of star formation, but gauging its column density needs background stars as probes. Their method combines kriging, a geostatistical fill-in method, with mixture models that isolate background sources and handle depth effects along the line of sight.

Applied to sixty-eight Hubble fields, tests show recovery accurate to about a tenth of a magnitude where sources are common. The maps track other interstellar tracers strongly, most in star-forming regions like 30 Doradus. Extinction-based dust masses differ by a set pattern from emission-based ones, a key calibration benchmark.
arxiv-2605-07025:
JaeWon Kim and Alexis Hiniker build a design framework for social media that supports young people's friendships. Their work draws on five studies with 331 participants aged 13 to 25, using interviews, co-design, surveys, diaries, and a field deployment. From 209 design-relevant points, three pillars emerge.

Social Understanding covers norms, cues, and accountability in interaction. Placeness covers community feeling, boundaries, and shared presence, while Identity Alignment covers how people present who they are. The framework maps nine design spaces, giving designers a shared vocabulary for comparing ideas and spotting areas that future work has left underexplored.
arxiv-2605-07125:
Haoyu Han and eleven co-authors audit recommendation benchmarks with a deliberately simple graph trick. Starting from only a user's last one or two items, their heuristic walks a small item-transition graph and ranks candidates by feature similarity. It uses no sequence encoder, no generative training, and no learned model at all.

Despite that simplicity, the heuristic matched or beat many modern systems on major datasets, with large gains on two Amazon categories. The authors trace the effect to shortcut structures in the data, such as predictable local transitions. Across fourteen datasets, the heuristic stayed competitive on ten, warning that strong benchmark scores need not show advanced modeling.
arxiv-2605-07525:
Luciano Baresi and five co-authors ask whether large language models can do real science or only produce code that runs. Their study centers on quantum solvers, programs that solve scientific problems on quantum computers. Writing code that executes is not enough in this field, because the numbers it returns must also be right.

The team built Q-SAGE, a method that runs a model's script, compares its output with a classical solver, and keeps refining the script until the results match closely. They tested five problem families with five language models, both open and commercial. Repeated refinement raised success rates a lot, but at high computing cost, and stronger models failed through wrong numbers rather than crashes.
arxiv-2605-07925:
Arnav Arora and three co-authors trace the side effects of teaching language models values. Assistants are post-trained to express traits like curiosity and empathy and values like helpfulness and honesty. But values are inter-related, so pushing one may move others, and some induced language could make models more addictive or flattering.

Fine-tuning models on curated value subsets of preference datasets, they measured spillovers onto other values, safety, anthropomorphic language, and question-answering benchmarks. Inducing a value also raised expression of related, sometimes contrasting, values. Inducing positive values increased safety. And every value increased anthropomorphic language, making models more validating and sycophantic, a side effect with direct consequences for users.
arxiv-2605-08025:
Henry Marichal, Diego Passarella, and Gregory Randall built software to speed up tree ring work. Marking rings in wood cross-section images is usually done by hand, which is slow and varies between experts. Their open-source suite, TRAS, combines automatic detection with tools for manual correction.

TRAS runs three detectors: a classical image method and two deep learning methods. Users can fix false rings, add missed ones, and measure earlywood and latewood areas, ring perimeter, and ring width. On eighteen expert-marked pine images, the best detector reached an F-score of eighty-one percent and cut the manual correction work sharply.
arxiv-2605-08125:
Rushil Saraswat, Aditya Prasad Dash, Huan Zhong Huang, Gang Wang, and coauthors probe how jets lose energy in the hot matter made in heavy-ion collisions. Energy-energy correlators summarize how energy is shared inside a jet and are sensitive to both hard splittings and soft medium effects. Medium interactions add particles to the cone, which can distort the measured correlator.

The authors build an augmentation method that uses momentum balance between near-side and away-side regions in photon-jet events, simulated with the CoLBT-hydro model for central lead-lead collisions. The reconstructed correlator agrees better with the true jet-shower signal, opening a cleaner way to test jet energy loss scenarios.
arxiv-2605-08325:
Rajdeep Singh Hundal, Yan Xiao, Jin Song Dong, and Manuel Rigger use segmentation masks to make vision models look at the right places for the right reasons. Two qualities matter: attention should land on the truly discriminative regions, and the decision should actually depend on that attention.

Their method, CAMAL, extracts a model's class activation maps during training and compares them against ground-truth regions taken from the segmentation masks that many datasets already provide. Training then pushes the attention toward those regions. Because the supervision comes from existing annotations, the approach stays efficient and scalable while targeting both spatial accuracy and causal faithfulness of attention.
arxiv-2605-08525:
Francisco Gonçalves, Conor Trygstad, and Néstor Pérez-Arancibia tackle flight control for a robot that weighs only ninety five milligrams and flies by flapping its wings. Tiny fliers face deep model error, wire tension, gusts, and forces from slightly uneven wings. Their answer pairs adaptive control that follows a reference model with a filter that estimates spin rates during flight.

Tests cover real hovering and path following in all six directions of motion. The filter calms shaking around roll and pitch and lifts overall flight quality. Engineers building insect scale aircraft gain a tested way to fly complex moves despite faults and noise.
arxiv-2605-08625:
Md Atik Ahamed and seven coauthors inject language model reasoning into time series forecasting without turning numbers into text tokens. Splitting numbers into tokens breaks math relations and inflates length, while pure forecast models explain nothing. Their STRIDE framework distills reasoning traces into a light language model and projects its pooled inner states as a continuous signal inside the numeric encoder.

The add on attaches to several forecasting architectures and trains with both forecast and reasoning losses. Combined with a partner system, STRIDE tops a major forecasting leaderboard, and on a reasoning benchmark it improves both accuracy and explanation quality. Forecasting gains forecasts that a reader can follow, not just numbers to trust blindly.
arxiv-2605-08725:
Chih-Hua Ke examines memory modules that fill only one of the two independent halves of a DDR5 channel. Halving the chip count enables smaller eight gigabyte modules the standard layout cannot build, a trick overclockers have used since 2021 to set frequency records across three Intel generations. Ke derives the transaction identity behind the sub channel design, where each burst moves exactly one standard cache line.

A roofline analysis finds heavy throughput losses for bandwidth bound work but small losses for latency bound work, plus a speed inversion point against older DDR4. One major platform proves incompatible by design, while the official specification already encodes such modules. Memory standards work gains a clear map of the remaining gaps.
arxiv-2605-08925:
Xueyang Kang, Zijian Yu, Kourosh Khoshelham, and Liangliang Nan segment three dimensional point clouds interactively from just a few user clicks per object. Labeling 3D data by hand is costly, and most interactive tools handle one object per pass with binary masks or lean on camera aligned two dimensional models. ClickSeg3D works directly on sparse sampled points and answers all object clicks in one forward pass.

A point transformer encoder and hierarchical mask decoder reason jointly over the clicks through learned semantic embeddings, refining masks and class guesses together. Accuracy jumps by over twenty percent against strong baselines, with further gains across datasets, often from a single click per object. Robotics and annotation gain fast, general 3D labeling.
arxiv-2605-09525: Testing many hypotheses at once risks a flood of false discoveries; steering the false finding rate simultaneously across location groups is the goal. Zijun Gao, Wenjie Hu, and Qingyuan Zhao solve it with new approach. The 2026 paper is multiple-testing theory with simultaneous assures.
arxiv-2605-09725: Distilling a big teacher model into a small student works best on-policy — but which teacher rollouts deserve distilling? Ke Zhang, Yunjie Tian, Dongdi Zhao, and others select the best-of-N teacher rollouts. The 2026 paper distills only the teacher's finest moments.
arxiv-2605-09825: Four-bit floating point — MXFP4 — on native FP4 hardware could slash the cost of training. Musa Cim, Poovaiah Palangappa, Miro Hodak, and others pretrain large language models exactly that way. The 2026 paper is hardware-aware training at extreme low precision.
arxiv-2605-10125: AI tools in academic research — useful for exploration, risky for precision. Anthea Dathe, Kiran Hoffmann, and Aline Mangold test the tradeoff. The 2026 paper is meta-science on the AI assistant. It grades the machine honestly as a capable research partner.
arxiv-2605-10325: Process rewards for agentic reasoning — verifiable, not just plausible. Huining Yuan, Zelai Xu, Huaijie Wang, and others design the reward scheme. The 2026 paper is LLM agents with accountability. It rewards every single reasoning step with fully verifiable process rewards today.
arxiv-2605-10525: Video depth that stays 3D-consistent — via shapes-embedded features: GemDepth. Yuecheng Liu, Junda Cheng, Longliang Liu, and others build the estimator. The 2026 paper is video depth. shapes embedded in features keeps depth consistent. Depth stays consistent. shapes guides every frame.

arxiv-2606-04125:
David Pankaczy and Conrard Tetsassi Feugmo benchmark in 2026 eleven physics-informed neural network designs on a notoriously stiff problem: the coupled equations governing ions and electric potential in a lithium cell. Such networks need no mesh, but they often fail where layers turn razor-thin.

The eleven configurations fall into four strategy families, chiefly differing in how competing training losses are weighted. Errors against a trusted finite-volume reference spanned a wide range across designs. One scheme, balanced residual decay rate, matched the accuracy of the much heavier neural tangent kernel approach on concentration fields while taking far less time. Loss-landscape shapes backed the ranking. The team released its implementation openly for reuse on other stiff coupled systems.
arxiv-2606-04225:
Bart Rosenzweig and Jonathan Stanfill answer a question posed by V Maz'ya in 2026. It concerns a heat-like equation built from a logarithmic Laplacian on a circle.

The operator is nonlocal: each point feels the whole circle at once. That makes even basic questions, such as whether smooth solutions exist, hard to settle. The pair exploit links to a classical problem about cavities and to known formulas for the operator's eigenfunctions. They show the solution extends in a clean way and derive exact sums for its parts. One sum involves Bernoulli numbers, a classic sequence. The work gives a rare exact handle on a nonlocal equation.
arxiv-2606-04425:
Yuanbo Xie leads a team naming in 2026 a new attack class against AI agents: cross-session stored prompt injection. Agent systems keep persistent state, memories, files, and tool records that survive between sessions, and hostile instructions planted there can fire long after the attacker has left.

Modeled on stored cross-site scripting, the attack extends prompt injection across time, persisting and activating in later sessions, and across space, spreading from the chat into the agent's stored state. The team formalizes the attack's lifecycle, builds a taxonomy of persistence channels and incorporation mechanisms, and releases a sandbox toolkit for evaluation. Their conclusion reframes agent security: the hard problem is governing how outside information gains authority inside persistent state, not just filtering inputs.
arxiv-2606-04525:
Ledneva, Nuridinov, and Kuznetsov build a common yardstick for genomic foundation models, in a 2026 arXiv paper. They argue that today's comparisons cannot be trusted. Benchmarks are fragmented. Each model reports on its favorite tasks. So claims of superiority are rarely comparable. Their benchmark, GENEB, evaluates frozen representations from 40 genomic models. It covers 100 tasks in 13 functional categories under one probing protocol. It includes settings with only a few labeled examples.

Aggregate leaderboards prove unstable. Rankings swing sharply across task categories. Larger scale brings only modest and inconsistent gains. Alignment of architecture and pretraining with a task often outweighs raw parameter count. It replaces a single league table with a diagnostic profile. The profile shows where each genomic model actually works.
arxiv-2606-04725:
Gondosiswanto and Pulsipher make nonlinear model predictive control fast enough for harder real-time problems by exploiting repetition, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their framework uses a parametric interior-point formulation that reuses structure-dependent computation across re-solves.

Symbolic factorization in the sparse Cholesky solver, for example, is done once and reused. On distillation column and two-dimensional heated plate benchmarks, against state-of-the-art CPU and GPU configurations, the framework cut total NMPC run times by more than a factor of ten. The gains come mainly from reduced per-iteration solve times, with GPU execution reducing them by up to 94 percent against the baseline.
arxiv-2606-05125:
Si-Cong Ji and colleagues test the quantum physics of the inverted harmonic oscillator in this 2026 arXiv paper. When a quantum system passes an unstable fixed point, its dynamics reduce to this oscillator, which stretches one quadrature while squeezing the other. That grows large quantum states out of tiny zero-point fluctuations. The same mathematics describes how inflation stretched quantum ripples in the early universe.

The team realized the dynamics with a Bose-Einstein condensate on an AtomChip, using radio-frequency dressing to flip the confinement into the inverted form. Phase-space imaging let them follow the full Wigner function of the evolving state. They observed sub-vacuum squeezing of 10.6 decibels, give or take 1.3 decibels. Time-reversing the evolution tested whether the process runs coherently in reverse. Matter-wave interference between the two daughter clouds confirmed coherence far beyond the initial expansion.
arxiv-2606-05425:
Ziad Ghanem returns to the Ize Conjecture in this 2026 arXiv paper, replacing a disproved claim with an exact test. The conjecture claimed that every irreducible representation of a compact Lie group admits a maximal isotropy subgroup with an odd-dimensional fixed-point space. Ghanem defines Ize pairs: a group and representation where some maximal isotropy subgroup makes a dimension difference odd.

He proves this dimension-parity test captures the obstruction to a nontrivial change of the degree at maximal orbit types, the point where bifurcation guarantees live or die. Combining the test with a mod-2 equivariant spectral flow yields local and global bifurcation guarantees without Burnside ring arithmetic.
arxiv-2606-05525:
Kuangshi Ai and colleagues present SciVisAgentSkills in this 2026 arXiv paper, reusable skill packages that make coding agents good at scientific visualization. General-purpose agents can write code, but scientific visualization demands tool-specific expertise: long multi-step workflows in tools such as ParaView, napari, VMD, and TTK, each with its own assumptions and idioms. The skills encode that knowledge: environment needs, tool usage patterns, and domain heuristics.

The team evaluated the skills on two agent harnesses using SciVisAgentBench, a benchmark of 108 expert-designed tasks. Adding the skills improved mean task scores across the suites. Structured procedural knowledge, not just a stronger base model, drives reliable work. Token-efficiency benefits were real but depended on the harness and setting used. The authors caution that skills should be studied together with the harness that runs them, not as portable magic. The skills are publicly available.
arxiv-2606-05725:
Shuze Liu, Guo, and Dong catch model theft from API traffic with a strikingly plain tool in a 2026 arXiv paper. Extraction attackers query a hosted model to clone it; each query alone looks harmless. The team watches windows of traffic instead. Queries are embedded as points of meaning, and the window's spread is compared with past benign traffic. A maximum mean discrepancy test flags windows that drift too far.

Thresholds come only from benign-versus-benign checks, so no attack examples are needed. Fourteen attacker-normal pairings tested the detector. Five adapted rival systems served as baselines. The simple test kept false alarms near a third of one percent. It caught every pure-attacker stream and reached about ninety-five percent balanced accuracy overall. Mixed traffic, where attackers hide among normal users, also gave way. The authors call plain distribution testing the baseline to beat.
arxiv-2606-05825:
Alutto, Zino, Johansson, and Fontan model how leaders emerge from opinion exchange in a 2026 arXiv paper. In real groups, people with firm views often gain sway. Lasting sway, though, demands staying near the group's drift. The team extends the Friedkin-Johnsen model of opinion dynamics. Leadership becomes a moving trait: each person's openness to influence evolves by a game-like rule.

Decisive yet socially coherent opinions build leadership in the model. Drifting away from the collective state bleeds it away. The coupled math tracks opinions and leadership feeding each other over time. The authors prove sufficient conditions that sort agents in advance. Under those conditions, some agents must emerge as leaders and others as followers. The results give network designers a first map of who will lead. They also suggest how seeding views might steer that outcome.
arxiv-2606-05925:
Guangyu Wang and a twenty-five-author team argue biomedicine needs models that simulate futures, not just label data in a 2026 arXiv paper. Today's biomedical AI mostly recognizes static patterns in scans, sequences, and records. Clinicians and biologists instead ask what happens next: after a drug, a mutation, a surgery. Biomedical world models would learn hidden states from molecule to patient scale. Intervention-conditioned dynamics would let users rehearse actions in simulation before touching a real system.

The authors sketch roles across the field. World models could serve as data engines, environment simulators, and planning substrates. Virtual cells, organoids, virtual patients, and surgical rehearsal are the flagship applications. None of it works without data infrastructure, honest benchmarks, safety limits, and governance. The paper maps those requirements rather than claiming a finished system. Closed-loop discovery, where simulation proposes experiments that refine the model, is the endgame.
arxiv-2606-06125:
Riccardo Poiani, Martino Bernasconi, and Andrea Celli study online contract design in this 2026 arXiv paper at the boundary of economics and learning theory. In a principal-agent problem, a principal offers payments tied to outcomes to persuade an agent to exert costly effort. Here the principal repeats the interaction over many rounds, without knowing each agent's private cost type or seeing the actions taken. Learning relies only on each round's outcomes.

For agents who either act or do not, the authors prove tight regret bounds, where regret measures the loss against the best fixed contract known in hindsight. Against adversarial type sequences, regret grows with the two-thirds power of the number of rounds, independent of the number of outcomes. When one hidden type stays fixed, an explore-then-commit strategy using stochastic binary search improves the rate to roughly the square root of the rounds.
arxiv-2606-06225:
Anh Truong and co-authors solve the cold start problem for a streaming service's recommendations in this 2026 arXiv paper. Collaborative filtering recommends content from patterns in what similar users watched, but a brand new title has no watch history at all. Tubi's production system also needs an embedding, a numeric fingerprint, for new content the moment it arrives. The team reframes cold start as filling in missing links in a device and content graph.

Their architecture, Shallow RHS, is deliberately asymmetric. The device side reads watch history through graph message passing to absorb collaborative signals. The content side stays shallow and builds its embedding only from the title's intrinsic features, never from interactions it may not have. After training, that content encoder maps any new title into the collaborative space, and retrieval finds warm surrogate neighbors for it. Online experiments showed gains for both new content and new devices.
arxiv-2606-06325:
Julia Blyumen and Eitan Farchi price data products where no money changes hands in this 2026 arXiv paper. Inside a company, teams trade datasets through internal platforms, and ordinary pricing fails twice over. Data is non rival, since one team's use does not consume it, and no market sets a price anyway. Managers still need to know which offerings deserve investment and attention.

Their metric values a data product purely from user choice behavior, modeling attention and preference as staff pick among offerings. They show the metric is a cooperative game whose Shapley value, a fair division rule from game theory, has a closed form. The formula rewards uniqueness and discerning use instead of raw popularity. That steers creators toward distinctive long tail products rather than more copies of what everyone already downloads. Worked examples show the valuation matches economic intuition while staying equitable.
arxiv-2606-06525:
Ziheng Geng and co-authors let language models do a structural engineer's paperwork in this 2026 arXiv paper. Analyzing a 3D frame, the skeleton of beams and columns in a building, normally means hours of manual model building. Their framework takes a plain language description instead. A team of agents handles it: one parses the problem into structured data. Others lay out floors and place nodes, girders, slabs, and columns. The last agents assign supports and loads and emit scripts for SAP2000 analysis software.

The key enabler is representation. An irregular 3D frame is projected onto a 2D plan of gridlines, with a matrix recording how many stories rise from each grid cell, so the geometry stays consistent and machine readable. On ten representative 3D frames, the system averaged ninety percent accuracy across repeated trials. The authors present it as a step toward trustworthy automation of routine engineering modeling.
arxiv-2606-06725:
Outlining the heart muscle in ultrasound scans is slow hand work, yet it is needed to measure how well blood feeds the muscle. Gonzalez and co-authors borrow a trick from large language model design in this 2026 arXiv paper. Neural scaling laws, rules that predict how a model's error falls as it grows, let them pick the right network size before full training.

Working with a public heart scan set and a contrast ultrasound set from twenty five patients, the team found that trends measured on small data slices predicted full scale performance well. Their chosen networks matched or beat the best published results with far fewer parameters, in one case two hundred forty times fewer. The automatic outlines also produced blood flow measures that agreed closely with those of a senior cardiologist, suggesting the sizing method suits small medical data sets.
arxiv-2606-07125:
Red giant stars ring like bells, and their tones reveal how fast their cores spin. De Vries and co-authors simulate those tones directly in this 2026 arXiv paper. The tones are mixed modes, waves that behave partly like sound and partly like buoyancy waves. They matter because they may carry angular momentum outward through the star.

Two dimensional hydrodynamic simulations followed a red giant of about one point three solar masses. Two runs cut the star's surface layer at different depths. Frequencies matched linear theory excellently for pressure dominated modes. Gravity dominated modes disagreed slightly in one frequency band. Surprisingly, the largest kinetic energies sat in slow modes below fifty microhertz, not near the expected peak. The deeper run produced surface velocities comparable to empirical predictions. Those slow, energetic modes are hard to observe yet may dominate momentum transport inside the star.
arxiv-2606-07225:
Ermolina, Danilkin, and Vanderhaeghen jointly analyze two particle collision processes to pin down exotic charm states in this 2026 arXiv paper. The data come from the BESIII experiment, where electrons and positrons annihilate into a J/psi particle plus pion or kaon pairs. A Dalitz plot, a map of how energy is shared among the three outgoing particles, reveals intermediate states. The analysis covers collision energies from about 4.1 to 4.4 giga-electronvolts.

Their model combines two resonant structures with a smooth background and treats pion and kaon scattering with a method that enforces consistency with scattering theory. One shared parameter set described both total production rates and mass distributions measured by BESIII. A purely resonant picture failed, so the background term proved necessary. From the fit they extracted mass and width values for three exotic states, including the charged Zc(3900) candidate.
arxiv-2606-07325:
Kim derives fundamental limits on forecasting how a probability distribution evolves, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting treats each distribution as a point in Wasserstein space, a geometric space where distance measures the work to reshape one distribution into another. Given finitely many noisy past snapshots, how accurately can any method estimate a future distribution? Kim assumes the flow changes smoothly, bounded by an adiabatic condition on its velocity field.

The central result is a minimax lower bound, the best worst-case error any estimator must suffer, blending temporal and spatial difficulty. It interpolates between an irreducible extrapolation cost, present even with a perfect record of the past, and the spatial estimation curse that worsens with dimension. Matching upper bounds are proved for the smoothness case and in a translation submodel. For smoothness the upper bound remains conditional, which Kim flags as an unresolved problem for the field.
arxiv-2606-07525:
Allein and Moens reconstruct the middle steps of causal claims in text, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Writers state a cause and its effect while leaving the intermediate events unstated, assuming readers share the knowledge. That gap matters when causal claims are wrong, correlational, or deployed to mislead, as in climate debates. The authors treat each cause-effect pair as the endpoints of a causal graph. They use language models to infer the missing links, comparing whole-graph generation against building graphs from discovered causal chains.

Chain-based methods either aggregate many inferred chains or expand chains through iterative search. Wisdom-of-the-crowd variants combine models' knowledge, either after generation or during inference. To judge quality without ground-truth graphs, they evaluate inferred relations against a database of over 1,500 validated causal pairs. That database check is proposed as a cheap evaluation transferable to domains where causal graphs are never available.
arxiv-2606-07625:
Huang and co-authors quantify how much city buildings shelter each other from the wind, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Shielding by upstream buildings controls urban drag, the resistance cities exert on airflow, yet it is barely measured in practice. Their large-eddy simulations reproduce the University of Bristol campus, 110 buildings of height, shape, and orientation, under 24 wind directions, so each building faces shielding conditions. Campus drag varied little with direction, while individual building drag swung widely.

About a fifth of the buildings accounted for four fifths of drag, led by a few large structures. To characterize shielding, the authors introduce two dimensionless ratios: the distance to the nearest upstream obstacle scaled by its height, and that obstacle's height relative to the target building. Together they separate near-wake from far-wake, sheltered from exposed. The framework suits any city, pushing shielding-aware definitions of effective frontal area and drag coefficients.
arxiv-2606-07725:
Teutschmann and colleagues pretrain GNSS-FM, a reusable base model for satellite positioning time series, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Stations in global navigation networks record daily ground movement, revealing slow tectonic drift, seasonal shifts, and sudden earthquake steps. Labelled examples for training are scarce, even though unlabelled records are abundant and free.

GNSS-FM learns without labels by predicting masked parts of its own compressed codes, an approach adapted from speech modelling. It was pretrained on records from more than seventeen thousand stations worldwide, feeding in both displacement and day-to-day change. Analysis of its learned codebook shows it separates the main signal types, including seismic offsets, steady drift, and seasonal cycles. Fine-tuned afterwards, it beat strong task-specific baselines at both ninety-day forecasting and locating seismic steps, suggesting this label-free training suits such data well.
arxiv-2606-07925:
Vijayaraghavan and co-authors summarise hardware code with a search procedure borrowed from game-playing AI, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Engineers write chips in hardware description languages such as VHDL and Verilog. Good summaries of what a module does are scarce, slowing maintenance and reuse. Language models can draft summaries, but a single greedy pass often misses the code's actual function.

Their system, RoSum-Mcts, explores summary candidates with Monte Carlo tree search, the lookahead strategy behind strong game agents. A composite reward guides the search, combining functional correctness, how well the summary covers the local content, and fluency. A verification loop checks candidates against the code. On the VHDL-eval and Verilog-eval benchmarks it beat baseline summarisation on standard quality metrics. It also proved robust to variable renaming, a cosmetic change that degraded baseline summaries sharply. Treating summarisation as search, not one-shot generation, is the main lesson.
arxiv-2606-08125:
Derya Acar, Metin Azmaz, Vural Cam, and Ömer Küçüksakallı rule out a family of polynomials from a rare club, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A polynomial is arithmetically exceptional if it permutes a finite field's elements for infinitely many primes. In one variable the exceptional polynomials are fully classified: built from linear maps and Dickson polynomials. The question here concerns generalised Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind, a multivariable family attached to the root system A2.

The verdict is negative: these polynomials are not arithmetically exceptional. The wider question is which such maps can shuffle a finite field perfectly. The proof studies the norms of certain cyclotomic elements, special numbers tied to roots of unity. Tracking those norms shows the permutation behaviour cannot persist across infinitely many primes. Negative results matter as much as positive ones: each family excluded sharpens the boundary of what such behaviour is possible.
arxiv-2606-08225:
Salman and colleagues propose an adaptive filter that handles two difficulties at once in this 2026 arXiv paper. An adaptive filter adjusts its own coefficients to track a signal, and many real systems are sparse, meaning most coefficients are zero. Separate methods exist for sparse systems and for impulsive noise, sudden large spikes that corrupt measurements, but combining both strengths in one algorithm was an open gap. Their design, called DP-SAF, updates cheaply, with cost proportional to filter length.

Two gain matrices do the work. One scales each step in proportion to coefficient size, so large coefficients learn faster. The other pulls small coefficients toward zero, most strongly for inactive taps, sharpening the sparsity. A sign-error update, which uses only the direction of the error, adds resistance to impulsive spikes. Simulations under random impulsive noise showed steadier final accuracy than rival algorithms, at matching or better speed.
arxiv-2606-08825:
Cheng, Jin, and Zhang ask when a molecule's 3D shape improves property predictions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Drug hunters predict properties like solubility from molecular structure. The cheap input is a 2D fingerprint, a summary of which chemical fragments a molecule contains. The expensive input is a conformer ensemble, the set of 3D shapes the molecule folds into, summarized by statistics from their Distribution Kernel Operators. They ran roughly 1,000 experiments across 13 model setups and 16 prediction targets.

The answer is selective. Conformer statistics cut prediction error on solvation properties, which depend on how molecules meet water: error fell 11 percent on the ESOL benchmark and 13.5 percent on FreeSolv. They gave no benefit for electronic or steric tasks. The gains grew for large, flexible molecules and with more training data, pointing to a physical cause. Still, end-to-end 3D neural networks beat fingerprints by 21 to 42 percent, far beyond what ensemble features add.
arxiv-2606-09125:
Chen and colleagues show that AI models which see images can leak private information in ways text-only models cannot, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multimodal models process text and pictures together. A photo may contain a name or medical detail, and the model can repeat it, or retain it in memory. The team built MM-Privacy, a dataset assessing such risks across tasks, split into disclosure risks, leaking image content, and retention risks, leaking stored content.

Evaluating several models, they found leakage: models exposed sensitive data embedded in images and held in memory. A striking factor was task inconsistency: a model could guard information in one framing and spill it in another, so single-task tests overstate protection. Mitigation is harder here, because safeguards must track information across modalities and turns. The authors release the dataset and code to spur defenses.
arxiv-2606-09225:
Buil and colleagues bring software containers, cloud packaging, to microcontrollers that could never run Docker, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multi-tenant chips run several apps with varying permission levels, useful for IoT devices. Current tools for such hardware lack runtime configuration: scheduling policies and each one's access to host resources are fixed at build time, limiting use in dynamic deployments.

TinyContainer is middleware with per-container scheduling and fine-grained access control through metadata describing each container's rights. A runtime layer supports multiple runtimes. The team tested CS4WAMR, a small WebAssembly runtime, on RIOT OS, across IoT boards with various Cortex-M chips. Regulating access and host services cost an overhead of up to 4 ms per call. A TinyML demo showed the value: containers hold data and model weights, delegating inference to native host services, so untrusted code never touches the model, and permissions change while the device runs.
arxiv-2606-09325:
Thomsen and colleagues show that the bewildering variety of spectra from stars torn apart by black holes reduces to one knob: how ionized the debris gas is, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Tidal disruption events flash as a star's remains accrete, and their optical spectra fall into four classes: hydrogen-dominated, helium-dominated, mixed, and featureless. The mixed class shows Bowen fluorescence lines, rare in other sources and long unexplained. The team built the first unified radiative transfer model covering all four classes, simulating optically thick, outflowing envelopes.

The controlling parameter is the ratio of injected luminosity to envelope mass, which sets the ionization state. As ionization decreases, the classes emerge in sequence: featureless, helium, Bowen, hydrogen. Electron scattering in the thick outflow explains the extreme line widths directly. The model also reproduces links with luminosity and black hole mass, and why each event's class stays stable.
arxiv-2606-09425:
Veena and her many co-authors hunt for methanol masers where gas streaming along the Milky Way's bar crashes into its centre in this 2026 arXiv paper. Masers are natural amplifiers that beam out intense microwave emission from excited molecules. The target region is where inflowing gas meets the Central Molecular Zone.

Using the Yebes forty-metre telescope, the team searched for class I methanol maser lines near thirty-six and forty-four gigahertz, alongside thermal emission and archival survey data. They found widespread emission at the lower frequency across several parsecs. The brightest source ranks among the most luminous galactic class I masers known, with an isotropic luminosity just under a thousandth of the Sun's output. Because the masers trace an extended high-velocity gas feature, the authors link them mainly to shock-processed gas at the bar interface, not only to local star formation.
arxiv-2606-09525:
Nadya Yuki Wangsajaya, Haeun Yu, and Isabelle Augenstein trace how language models learn their habits of using provided context during instruction fine-tuning in this 2026 arXiv paper. A model's decision to trust a supplied passage depends on traits like its length, fluency, and similarity to the question.

The authors tracked sensitivity across the successive stages of instruction tuning: supervised fine-tuning, direct preference optimisation, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Experiments covered four models and three datasets. Supervised fine-tuning consistently made models favour contexts that are easy to understand, meaning long, fluent passages closely matching the query. Later stages could either reinforce or undo those preferences, depending on the training dataset's own balance of characteristics. Context use is reshaped at every stage, so dataset design decides how robustly a system uses the evidence it is given.
arxiv-2606-09725:
Jhonny Velasquez Olivera, Christo Thomas, and Walid Saad untangle the factors inside data with a symbolic twist in this 2026 arXiv paper. Disentanglement means splitting a sample's traits, like shape, hue, and pose, into clean parts. Past tools leaned on smooth number codes and tuned losses. This team treats the code as a bundle of symbols instead.

Their tool uses holographic reduced representations, vectors that can be bound and summed like tied notes. Each latent unit is itself a vector, and units add up to form the whole code. An unbinding step peels one symbol-value pair from the bundle. Tests with latent walks and standard scores matched rival methods. A theory side shows unbinding yields near-free pairs, and caps how many clear concepts each slot can hold. The codes also shook off noise well, losing sense in a slow, graceful way.
arxiv-2606-10125:
Pourhabib tackles the cost of labeling cases for text-to-SQL systems, which turn natural language questions into database queries, in a 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning. Few-shot prompting with a bank of annotated cases is the dominant approach, but expert annotation is expensive and the bank's quality governs quality of answers. He casts choosing which cases to label as a bounded design problem over the small manifold of query meanings.

His stratified greedy algorithm maximizes a heteroscedastic mutual information objective, which accounts for the uneven reliability. He proves the goal stays submodular and roughly monotonic, giving a constant-factor approximation guarantee. A spectral bound shows the guarantee degrades gently, not badly, when the assumed kernel diverges from the true data-generating process. In tests, the strategy sharply reduces tagging effort while keeping high retrieval accuracy for the downstream system.
arxiv-2606-10425:
Kim and Kim study when a partial differential equation still has exactly one solution in this 2026 arXiv paper in analysis. The equations are second-order evolution equations, describing how a quantity changes over time, and their coefficients can degenerate, vanish, or blow up. Standard theory demands the coefficients stay locally integrable, their accumulated size near any moment finite. This paper drops that demand, allowing blow-up even at the starting and ending times.

The key that makes this possible is a zero initial condition: the system starts from nothing, so singular behaviour at the start has nothing to destroy. Working in weighted Lp spaces, the authors prove existence and uniqueness of weak solutions for exponents from one upward. Open problems remain, including uniqueness for bounded solutions.
arxiv-2606-10725:
Shakhmatova and colleagues mine discharge reports to predict atrial fibrillation in this 2026 arXiv paper on medical informatics. Atrial fibrillation is the commonest heart rhythm disorder, but risk scores lean on factors, age and hypertension, that nearly every cardiology patient has. The team studied 17,562 cardiology patients without prior fibrillation; 1,438, or 8.19 percent, developed it during follow-up. A language-processing pipeline turned discharge reports into 73 features, feeding models predicting risk over twenty-four months and the whole follow-up.

The full model reached a ROC area of 0.735 for the twenty-four-month target; a 13-feature simple model, Pre-AF 13, scored 0.725, against 0.53 to 0.64 for four scores. A linear 9-feature bedside score separated patients whose two-year incidence ran from about 7 to about 36 percent. Age and left atrial volume carried the most weight. Routine hospital text, mined well, stratifies risk better than the scores clinicians use.
arxiv-2606-10825:
El Asri and colleagues improve diffusion policies for robot control in this 2026 arXiv paper. A diffusion policy, which plans actions by gradual denoising, is usually trained by copying demos and cannot beat them. Direct reinforcement learning on such policies is awkward, since each action comes from a multi-step process. MODIP instead plans inside a learned world model with model predictive control, then trains the policy on the planned paths as fresh targets.

Two choices keep it fast: a terminal state value replaces policy-dependent action values, and critics train on policy-independent targets. On D4RL and RoboMimic tasks, MODIP lifts diffusion policies beyond plain copying and matches or beats both RL fine-tuning methods and strong model-based baselines such as TD-MPC2. The authors note that all tests use state vectors, not images.
arxiv-2606-11025:
Ping and co-authors introduce a 2026 arXiv method for fine-tuning flow matching models, the generators behind many image and video tools. Online reinforcement learning, where a model improves from scored trial outputs, can raise quality, but PPO-style ratio clipping limits updates using a noisy single-sample estimate of how far the policy moved.

Flow-DPPO swaps clipping for a divergence proximal constraint built on the KL divergence, an exact distance between old and new policies that is cheap here because each step is Gaussian. An asymmetric mask blocks only updates that both leave the trusted region and break the divergence limit. Across several base models, Flow-DPPO earned higher rewards, forgot less, and stayed stable over many passes where clipping degraded. Paired with CPS sampling, it reached 92.6 percent on a GenEval2 image test, ahead of the 84.5 percent scored by Flow-GRPO in the same setting.
arxiv-2606-11525:
Shen, Chuck, Feng, and Huang diagnose why contrastive learning struggles with robot manipulation in a 2026 arXiv paper. Contrastive Reinforcement Learning has succeeded at goal-conditioned tasks like locomotion, but it falters on interaction-rich manipulation. The authors argue the difficulty is object-centric interaction: contacts and grasps switch the underlying dynamic modes. They model manipulation as a piecewise-smooth Markov process, showing mode changes create reachability structures standard energy functions represent poorly.

Their fix, Interaction-weighted Resampling, resamples around phases before, during, and after interactions, so representations capture the complexity near contacts. Across two-dimensional control, manipulation, and robot air hockey, it improves sample efficiency and performance over prior methods, by about 19.8 percent on average in simulation. A sim-to-real pipeline yields the first real-world goal-conditioned robot air hockey agent that scores goals, raising success from twenty-five to sixty percent.
arxiv-2606-11725:
Mayur Abhisheki and Prasanta Kumar Das test a model of the infant universe in this 2026 arXiv paper on cosmology. Inflation is the brief burst of rapid expansion thought to have smoothed the early cosmos. Their model uses an inverse-tangent potential, a curve describing the energy driving inflation. After inflation ends, reheating converts that energy into hot matter, and its details are usually guessed.

Using Bayesian inference, weighing evidence for parameter values, they confront the model with Planck and ACT satellite data. Where reheating's character stays fixed, preferred settings imply reheating temperatures spanning a huge range and durations of a few to a few dozen e-folds, units of expansion. A dynamical version, where the decay rate evolves, tightens things sharply. Demanding inflation and reheating agree restricts the spectral index, how clumpiness varies with scale, to a narrow band.
arxiv-2606-11825:
Fabio Cavalletti and Andrea Mondino prove a new singularity theorem in this 2026 arXiv paper on mathematical relativity. The classic Hawking-Penrose theorems show that spacetime must contain incomplete paths, interpreted as singularities, under broad conditions. Their engine is a focusing hypothesis: gravity pulls bundles of paths together strongly enough, usually expressed through a starting surface's mean curvature.

The authors replace that local hypothesis with a condition on asymptotic volume growth, how the volume of space expands far from a compact starting surface. Under the strong energy condition, a uniform positive lower bound on their new expansion invariants forces past timelike incompleteness. They also give an explicit upper bound on how far the past can extend. The theorem is proved not only for smooth spacetimes but also for non-smooth Lorentzian length spaces, with no differentiability assumed. Companion results include an area comparison theorem and a volume-based singularity theorem.
arxiv-2606-11925:
Zsolt Robotka and four colleagues manufacture training data for sign language translation in this 2026 arXiv paper. Translation systems need parallel sign video and text pairs for fine-tuning, but such data is scarce, especially for rare vocabulary. Starting from a gloss-annotated corpus, where glosses label individual signs, they cut training videos into per-gloss clips using forced alignment.

A large language model, anchored to the corpus, invents new gloss sequences and matching sentences; synthetic videos are assembled by sampling clips for those sequences. Counterintuitively, polishing clip transitions for smoothness hurts, while abrupt boundaries seem to help training implicitly. In a strict controlled comparison, five recent methods gained at most about one BLEU point over baseline. Augmentation gains nearly three BLEU points, with no change to model architecture or training protocol. The authors also warn the synthetic data harms vision-language pretraining despite improving its own objectives.
arxiv-2606-12325:
Dúcz settles how few colors a certain geometric pattern needs by coloring all of it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The fractional chromatic number of the plane asks how few colors paint the plane so equal-distance points differ, allowing colors to be shared fractionally. Earlier work pushed the lower bound to four using a twenty-seven-point unit-distance graph inside the Moser lattice, a four-dimensional grid of points. That graph's geometric fractional chromatic number is exactly four. Whether four colors suffice for the whole lattice stayed open.

Dúcz exhibits geometric four-colorings of the entire Moser lattice, proving the bound tight for lattice graphs. Geometric means the coloring respects distances: isometric point sets receive matching color patterns. The same colorings extend to the Moser ring, a larger structure. The result explains why computerized searches inside this lattice stalled at four: nothing better was there to find.
arxiv-2606-12525:
Davenport and co-authors derive how bound states of particles drift through crystals, and find the rule needs replacing, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Excitons and trions are composite excitations: an electron bound to a hole, or to two partners. Single electrons feel Berry curvature, a geometric field that bends their motion sideways. The team asks what geometry governs composites.

For neutral composites, an electric field does not couple to Berry curvature at all, defying the naive expectation. Instead a different quantity steers them: the gap between distinct Berry connections definable for the composite, a generalized quantum geometric dipole. Charged trions do get a Berry curvature term, but there is an endless family of candidate curvatures. The right choice depends on how the composite's center is defined. In magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, trions drift sideways under a field driven by both effects, and their dipole moment oscillates in time.
arxiv-2606-13025:
Čiginas offers a diagnostics-guided, variance-inflated Fay-Herriot estimator for small area estimation from non-probability samples, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Non-probability sources such as administrative records and platform data are used to estimate totals for small domains, often via inverse probability weighting. Those weighted values are model-dependent, and their reliability varies across domains.

The method starts from calibrated inverse-probability-weighted domain estimators, sums up their quality through a set of domain diagnostics, and adds a variance-inflation component to the Fay-Herriot equation. Domains whose diagnostics show weaker weighted information are smoothed more strongly toward the regression mean. In a validation on a pseudo-real population of Lithuanian firms, it reduces estimation error relative to calibrated weighting alone, showing that domain diagnostics carry uncertainty information the variance estimates miss.
arxiv-2606-13325:
Yu, Lyu, and Li test an exotic deformation of black hole geometry against Solar System data in this 2026 arXiv paper. The deformation, controlled by a parameter called B, arises when a magnetised black hole solution is stripped of its field. What remains is not the usual flat-at-infinity Schwarzschild spacetime but a spindle-shaped geometry. No known astrophysical process would create such a deformation. The authors ask how large it could be if it extended across the weak gravity around the Sun.

They compute its effects on two classical tests: the advance of planetary perihelia, an orbit's closest point slowly rotating, and the Shapiro delay of light near the Sun. Requiring the extra perihelion advance to hide within uncertainty gives the strongest limits, pinning B to a tiny range. A Cassini-style time-delay estimate provides a check on the bound.
arxiv-2606-13425:
Rameshan and Messmer propose a framework for assessing cryptographic agility in this 2026 arXiv paper. The coming switch to post-quantum cryptography will force every program to replace its algorithms. Today's programming interfaces were not designed for such swaps, and there is no systematic way to judge how agile a system really is. The term itself bundles distinct abilities: replacing algorithms, selecting among them by policy, and substituting one version for another. Without splitting these, evaluation and design both stall.

Their component-based scheme scores application-level agility along seven dimensions. Three coupling dimensions measure what the code itself knows about schemes and providers. A decoupling mechanism and a governance axis capture how change is controlled. Two enabler axes measure migration capability, whether a swap can be performed in practice. It gives developers shared terms for scoring systems.
arxiv-2606-13525:
Bouzenada and Moreira generalise quantum information measures to fractional quantum mechanics in this 2026 arXiv paper. Fractional quantum mechanics replaces derivatives with nonlocal fractional ones, which encode memory effects: the system's present state depends on its past. The authors adopt the Riemann-Liouville formalism and first revisit the standard definitions of Shannon entropy, the standard measure of uncertainty, and Fisher information. Fisher information measures how sensitively a distribution responds to parameter changes. They then construct fractional versions of both and examine their structure.

Applying this to the quantum harmonic oscillator, the workhorse model of a vibrating system, yields formulas as functions of the fractional parameter. The results show that fractional forms change how probability densities bunch and produce real variations in information content and response. That parameter becomes a dial controlling the strength of memory effects. The paper offers a model for researchers studying such quantum systems.
arxiv-2606-13725:
Ataberk Olgun and colleagues describe their large-scale laboratory for characterising real memory chips in this 2026 arXiv paper. Testing DRAM chips yields insights into how memory behaves, enabling mechanisms that improve performance, robustness, security, and energy efficiency. The laboratory's key building block is DRAM Bender, an infrastructure for running characterisation experiments on real devices. This paper introduces its updates: support for new types of characterisation experiments, and broader coverage of DRAM interface standards. Further changes make the platform easier to use at large scale.

The authors, from a computer architecture research group, release the work as infrastructure. Their hope is that wider access to real-chip characterisation helps researchers discover new problems and solve memory scaling issues. The memory bottleneck, the growing gap between processor speed and memory capability, plagues systems from phones to AI clusters. Such laboratories have historically produced results that simulated studies missed.
arxiv-2606-13825:
Oshin, Ghosh, and Theodorou make learned optimization practical for large cone-shaped problems in robotics. Deep unfolding speeds up an iterative solver by adding trainable parts taught through the solver's own steps. For semidefinite programs, though, training hit two walls: memory use grew with the square of problem size, and a key projection step turned unstable when values repeated. Their 2026 arXiv paper removes both obstacles.

A matrix-free differentiation rule works only through matrix-vector products, cutting memory from quadratic to linear in problem size. A second rule, based on the Dalečkii-Krein formula, keeps the projection step well defined even with repeated eigenvalues. The team learns small policies for solver settings and warm starts. Across covariance steering, max-cut, and control problems, the learned solver beats leading rivals. Speedups reach fifty times in some classes. Inside a sequential programming loop, it runs over thirty times faster than COSMO.
arxiv-2606-13925:
Ilin and Nugent argue that finishing a proof is not the hard part of AI mathematics. Their 2026 arXiv paper is a case study of a semi-autonomous formalization. A language model agent, guided by humans, formalized Grothendieck's vanishing theorem in the Lean proof assistant. The theorem concerns when sheaf cohomology, a tool for gluing local data, must vanish. The first version compiled with no gaps left open.

Expert review then found serious problems elsewhere. Definitions were poorly chosen. Theorem statements lacked the right generality. File organization and the public API, the surface future users build on, were weak. A review-driven refactor followed, with a second expert review. The split was sharp. The agent handled local, mechanically checkable feedback well. It stayed weak at global design: choosing definitions and shaping an API. The authors propose judging such systems by survival under expert review.
arxiv-2606-14325:
Cazzaro, Lennon, and Quattoni teach small language models to query graph databases accurately, without annotated fine-tuning data. Property graphs store richly connected data, but reading them requires Cypher, a query language few users know. Regulated industries need small local models for data sovereignty, and such models need training data that barely exists. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents CYQUARK, an automatic synthetic data generator grounded in the target graph.

CYQUARK builds on the authors' earlier SPOT pipeline, which generated grounded queries from tree patterns and paraphrased them into questions. It expands the Cypher syntax coverage of generated queries, a known weakness, while guarding quality. Experiments ran on all major benchmarks. With this data, small local models improved significantly, performing very close to much larger proprietary models. The claim is sovereignty without sacrifice: keep data on-premises and still query accurately. A limitation is English-only questions and Cypher-only output.
arxiv-2606-14625:
Wichiramala and Panraksa settle a covering conjecture in plane geometry in a 2026 arXiv paper. John Wetzel conjectured that one specific triangle covers every unit arc. It is a thirty-sixty-ninety triangle, built by placing a small square on its hypotenuse. It must contain any curve of length one in the plane, however it wiggles. Covering problems ask for the smallest shape containing a whole family of curves.

The authors give a computer-assisted proof. It carries independently checkable interval certificates. Any supposedly uncovered arc reduces to a finite family of models. The family has five hundred ninety-nine second-order cone models. In each model, interval arithmetic validates a length lower bound above one. Since every bound clears a margin, a slightly shrunk triangle still covers all unit arcs. Its area provably beats the sector cover.
arxiv-2606-14825:
Qin and co-authors realize a full map of Anderson localization in a 2026 arXiv paper. Anderson localization is the trapping of waves by disorder. Theory predicts seven phases of wave behavior. Waves may spread freely, stay trapped, sit at the edge between the two, or mix these states in pairs or all three at once. No single experiment had shown all seven.

The team built a one-dimensional photonic lattice whose hopping pattern varies in a quasiperiodic way. Engineered zeros in the hopping create the critical, edge-like states. Each regime showed its own motion pattern. Some light spread ballistically, some oscillated in place, some stayed put. All seven phases appeared, including the elusive triple mix of spread, critical, and trapped states. The authors also tracked the transitions between phases. It is the first complete experimental map of this landscape.
arxiv-2606-15025:
Zeller and Cordery compute how a finite scattering slab reflects and transmits light in a 2026 study. Such slabs matter in atmospheric, snow, and biomedical optics, where Henyey-Greenstein scattering is standard. Classic routes use random Monte Carlo sampling or heavy analytic machinery. The authors instead build a first-passage transfer operator on photon depth and direction.

Confining the operator to the slab with absorbing boundaries yields order-resolved reflection and transmission laws in one evaluation. Reflectance then factors into a half-space return law times a truncation term, summed over scattering orders. Emergent angular patterns come out at no extra cost. The results match three-dimensional Monte Carlo closely across asymmetry, thickness, and albedo ranges. Energy conservation holds to close tolerance in the conservative case. The deeper point is structural: as slab thickness grows, the slab law recovers the half-space first-return law order by order.
arxiv-2606-15425:
Saef studies stochastic parabolic equations with gradient nonlinearities in 2026, asking when such equations have solutions that exist, are unique, and depend cleanly on their starting data. These equations mix diffusion, a nonlinear drift involving the gradient, and random forcing, so noise can destroy a solution in finite time. Saef works in critical function spaces using recent maximal-regularity methods.

The advance is to control the drift and the noise coefficient separately rather than under one joint assumption. That separation allows rougher driving noise when the dispersion is subcritical, widening the class of treatable equations. By gluing local ones together, Saef also obtains new continuation criteria that say exactly when a solution can be extended or must blow up. Applied to stochastic phase-field models of moving boundaries, they give global well-posedness for all time.
arxiv-2606-15725:
Zhumekenov and colleagues examine score-based martingale posteriors in 2026, a fast alternative to Markov chain Monte Carlo for Bayesian uncertainty in deep neural networks. Standard Bayesian inference over millions of network weights is punishing to compute, and sampling methods crawl. The martingale approach instead runs a gradient recursion whose parameters form a martingale, a sequence with a simulable random limit.

Because the limit simulates quickly, the method promises posterior-like uncertainty at a fraction of the usual cost, and it parallelises well. The catch is sensitivity to the preconditioner. On large convolutional networks, the unpreconditioned version is safe but yields no epistemic uncertainty at all, the very quantity practitioners want. Real uncertainty likely needs curvature tools such as KFAC, or friendlier designs with normalisation layers and smooth activations. The survey maps where the method works today and what must change for it to compete broadly.
arxiv-2606-16125:
Konoplya, Stashko, and Stuchlík study in 2026 how an extra scalar field changes the ringing and evaporation of black holes. A new family of asymptotically flat black holes with primary scalar hair was recently found in beyond-Horndeski gravity, a modified gravity theory. Hair means extra structure beyond mass and spin. The authors compute quasinormal mode spectra, graybody factors, and Hawking radiation for this class.

Scalar hair leaves clear imprints on the ringdown, the decaying vibrations after a disturbance. It shifts quasinormal frequencies, rearranges overtones, and can produce echoes in the signal. Fundamental modes tied to the light ring change only moderately, while higher overtones react strongly to the small near-horizon deformation the scalar field creates. In some parameter regimes, graybody factors show resonant tunneling, making the Hawking emission rate oscillate with frequency. The corresponding naked singularities are shown to be quantum mechanically singular, admitting no well-defined dynamics.
arxiv-2606-16425:
Hsieh and co-authors prove in 2026 that constant-depth quantum circuits form a true hierarchy: each extra layer of depth buys computational power no shallower circuit can match. Classical bounded-depth circuits have known hierarchy theorems, but constant-depth quantum computation was mostly compared against classical models, its internal structure unexplored. The authors construct, for every depth level d of at least 12, a family of two-round interactive problems.

No quantum circuit of depth d minus 1 can achieve near-perfect success on these problems, whatever its gate set, size, or number of ancillary qubits. Simple bounded fan-in quantum circuits of depth modestly above d, however, implement honest strategies that succeed. Moreover, every bounded fan-in classical circuit of sublogarithmic depth fails to reach perfect success, for every d. The result yields an unconditional quantum advantage of the class QNC0 over its classical counterpart NC0, in hierarchy form.
arxiv-2606-16825:
Jaggi ties expert layers together in a 2026 machine learning paper on Mixture-of-Experts language models. These models hold many expert sub-networks but activate only a few per token, so most parameters sit idle in memory. Memory, not computation, becomes the scaling bottleneck.

Expert Tying shares the same expert parameters across consecutive transformer layers, while each layer keeps its own routing choices and attention. Tested across several current open architectures, tying cuts the memory footprint nearly in half. Perplexity and downstream quality barely move, the pretraining experiments show. A control study finds per-layer attention, not routing, is what keeps tied layers behaving distinctly, so the biggest parameter pool is also the cheapest to share. Saved memory can be reinvested as extra experts, making width and depth trade against each other at a fixed budget. Tests stop at moderate scale, leaving frontier-size training open.
arxiv-2606-17125:
Gumel and Safsten present a 2026 arXiv paper on controlling Anopheles mosquitoes with the sterile insect technique. The method floods an area with sterile males, so matings yield no offspring. It appeals because insecticide resistance and outdoor biting weaken standard malaria tools. The authors ask how releases can be timed and sized best.
