For Theosophists of the 1920s, this was the standard map of the unseen rule of the world. The book states that age's esotericism at its fullest.
lewis-arrowsmith-1925:
Sinclair Lewis published Arrowsmith in 1925, turning from small-town business to American science. He researched the novel with a young bacteriologist, Paul de Kruif, who supplied the laboratory life. The book was awarded the Pulitzer Prize, which Lewis famously refused.

Martin Arrowsmith fights his way from a prairie town to medical school, country practice, and a great research institute. Everywhere, commerce, publicity, and careerism press him to sell his science short. A plague outbreak in the Caribbean tests his principles at the highest cost. Lewis makes the researcher's purity both heroic and impossible to keep clean. Arrowsmith made the scientist a tragic American hero and remains the classic novel of the profession.
lexa-magie-egypte-antique-vol-1-1925:
Frantisek Lexa published the first volume of his great French study of Egyptian magic in 1925. The work traces magic in Egypt from the Old Kingdom to the Coptic period. Volume one lays out the whole system in an extended survey.

Lexa asks who practiced magic, how rites worked, and what words could do. Priests, private magicians, and the gods themselves all have roles here. He treats magic as a serious Egyptian science rather than mere superstition. The survey was the fullest of its time on the subject. Egyptologists still respect its learning and scope. Volume two supplies the translated texts behind the survey.
lexa-magie-egypte-antique-vol-2-1925:
Volume two of Frantisek Lexa's study of ancient Egyptian magic appeared in 1925, in French. The first volume explained the system; this companion gathers the actual texts. Magical writings from across three thousand years stand side by side here.

Pyramid spells, coffin texts, and everyday charms appear in French translation. Readers move from theory to raw material in the magicians' own words. Lexa selects texts that show magic at work in temple, tomb, and home. The sourcebook remains unmatched for following his survey volume. Students of ancient spells can test every claim in volume one here. Together the pair forms a landmark of Egyptology.
locarno-pact-1925:
Germany, France, Belgium, Britain, and Italy signed these treaties in 1925. Their rulers acted through named envoys with full powers. The preamble recalls the scourge of the war of 1914 to 1918. Peoples who suffered it desired security and protection afterward.

Belgium's old neutral status had been ended before this pact. Europe's frequent conflict area needed fresh guarantees of peace. Article One guarantees the land status quo together and separately. Germany's frontiers with Belgium and France stand declared inviolable. The League of Nations framework bounds the supplementary guarantees. Frontiers fixed by existing treaties remain untouched by Article One. Each side signed in the names of its king or its republic.
locke-new-negro-1925:
The New Negro, published in 1925 and edited by Alain Locke, is the landmark anthology of the Harlem Renaissance. Locke, a Howard philosopher, gathered the movement's fiction, poetry, essays, and art. His aim was to present a people remade in its own image.

His title essay declares that the Negro is no longer an object of history but a maker of it. The people, he argues, are moving from the rural South to the modern city. Work from the era's rising writers and artists fills the volume with argument and display. The book served as the movement's manifesto and showcase in one. Its influence on American culture is still unfolding.
mathnawi-nicholson-vol-1-1925:
R. A. Nicholson was the great English sage of Persian verse. His Mathnawi of Jalaluddin Rumi, Book One, came out in 1925. The book gives Books One and Two of the Mathnawi with the Persian text at hand. Rumi was a Sufi sage of the 1200s in Turkey.

The Mathnawi is a vast poem of tales, told to bare the soul's path to God. A reed's wail for its lost home opens the whole grand work. Kings, fools, and saints crowd its tales of love and loss. Nicholson's set is the stock full dress of the poem in English.
mellon-ms-28-alchemical-miscellany-1525:
Mellon MS 28 is a small paper manuscript from north Italy. The copy is dated about 1525, and may come from Bologna. White leather, stamped in blind tooling, covers its paste boards.

John Dastin's Rosarius of the philosophers leads the texts inside. A short piece on the four elements adds a chart for mixing colors. A work ascribed to Hermes, Merlin, or Rasis closes the set. One scribe wrote the main texts in a small, neat humanistic hand. Pale red marks set off heads, tables, and some verse. Linen ties once held the small book shut on all sides.
mellon-ms-29-lumen-luminum-etc-1525:
Mellon MS 29 holds the Lumen Luminum, or Light of Lights. Elias of Cortona, a Franciscan friar, is named as its author. This north Italian paper copy is dated about 1525.

The record says the work was said to be made in 1315. That date, the record warns, is wrong for the piece. Its matter came from Saracen and Hebrew sources, turned into Latin. A text in cipher and some recipes in Italian stand with it. Gilt edges with a knot work stamp mark this copy's care. Part of the text hides its sense in a cipher code.
mendel-experiments-plant-hybridisation-b:
Gregor Mendel was an Austrian monk who crossed pea plants and counted how their traits passed to the next crop. He read his results to a local science society in 1865, but few people noticed them at the time. William Bateson later translated the paper into English, and this edition came out in 1925.

Mendel found that traits such as tall or short stems appear in clear ratios, not blended halfway. He argued that hidden factors, now called genes, carry each trait from parent to child. The paper was ignored for decades, then rediscovered around 1900. It is now read as the founding work of genetics, the science of heredity.
moore-defence-of-common-sense-1925:
George Edward Moore published A Defence of Common Sense in 1925, and it became his most famous short work. Moore, a Cambridge philosopher, wrote against skeptics who doubted the plain truths of everyday life. His method was disarmingly direct: state what we all know, and hold it more firmly than any theory that denies it.

The essay lists truisms Moore claims to know with certainty, such as that the earth existed long before his birth. In its best-known passage, tied to his lectures of the period, he proves an external world by holding up one hand, then another. The plain statement shook philosophy because it refused the skeptic's terms altogether. The piece is often called the shortest revolution in thought ever written, and it still anchors debates about knowledge.
nasa-tm-19710007896-simulated-space-envi:
Engineers at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland ran this test, reported in February 1971. A module of twenty-five cadmium sulfide thin-film solar cells faced a simulated space environment. The run lasted for almost two thousand hours.

The test checked the strength of the module's mechanical and electrical links. It also taught the team how the module behaves as a power source. During the run, the module was loaded as it would be on a spacecraft. No breakdown could be found in the links between cells, the report states. Its power output and current traits were tracked through the test.
openalex-w1966648825:
George Schoneveld, Laura German, and Eric Nutakor studied biofuel farms. Their paper appeared in Ecology and Society in 2011. Africa's biofuel sector grew fast in those years. Plantations promised jobs and rural development to villages. Opinion on the sector was sharply divided, they note.

The team grounded its analysis in local field evidence. It measured real impacts of feedstock plantations in Ghana. Land deals can shift food, work, and forest access. Promises of development must face village reality, they argue. Their findings weigh gains against losses for local people. The study guides fairer land investment policy in Africa.
openalex-w2046416025:
Marisa Repetto and Susana Llesuy reviewed natural compounds used in folk medicine for stomach ulcers. Their paper appeared in the Brazilian Journal of Medical and Biological Research in 2002. Harmful oxygen species play a role in many diseases. They are also linked to stomach inflammation and ulcers. Natural antioxidants might protect the stomach lining.

The review explains how antioxidant claims should be tested. Lab tests must come before claims of benefit. The authors survey compounds from traditional remedies. They discuss how these substances may neutralise harmful molecules. They also consider protection of affected tissues. Clear testing standards matter before medical use. The paper maps a research path for natural anti-ulcer agents.
openalex-w2113310925:
Sophie Fauset, Michelle Johnson, Manuel Gloor and colleagues asked how a few tree species dominate Amazon carbon cycling. Their paper appeared in Nature Communications in 2015. Amazon forests hold extraordinary species diversity. Yet tree numbers skew toward few hyperdominant species. Those trees also drive much carbon uptake and storage.

The team used data from forest plots across Amazonia. They compared species' shares of stems and carbon flows. The hyperdominant species handled a large share of carbon uptake. They also held a large share of stored carbon. Rare species contributed little to totals despite their numbers. Protecting common species matters for the carbon balance. Diversity still matters for other forest functions.
openalex-w2286612125:
Silvia Serrano-Gomez, Mazvita Maziveyi, and Suresh Alahari published this review in Molecular Cancer in 2016. They explain how the epithelial-mesenchymal transition is regulated at the epigenetic and post-translational levels. In this transition, stuck-down epithelial cells loosen into wandering mesenchymal cells, a shift behind embryo growth, scarring, and cancer spread.

The switch's hallmark is losing E-cadherin, the glue protein of epithelial sheets, while gaining mesenchymal markers. Master switch proteins silence the E-cadherin gene by gripping its promoter. They also team with enzymes that chemically tag DNA and proteins, locking the new state in. The review ends with treatment ideas meant to block the transition and slow metastasis.
openalex-w2593913025:
Simón Guendelman, Sebastián Medeiros, and Hagen Rampes reviewed mindfulness and emotion regulation in Frontiers in Psychology in 2017. Mindfulness-based programs are increasingly used to treat conditions marked by poor emotion control. Brain imaging studies show they change activity in regions handling attention, self-reference, and feeling. The authors gather findings from brain science, psychology, and clinical research.

They compare several research models: everyday mindfulness, brief inductions, full programs, and expert meditators. From brain science they discuss how top-down and bottom-up control of emotions interact during practice. Clinicians, they argue, have not clearly separated mindful emotion regulation from other strategies. The authors propose splitting these strategies into top-down and bottom-up kinds. They also offer an embodied framework linking body, brain, and behavior. The review aims to sharpen how mindfulness treatments are understood and tested.
openalex-w2760911225:
Laura Jane Sonter, Diego Herrera, and D. J. Barrett, with colleagues, measured mining's forest footprint in Nature Communications in 2017. Mining is a known risk to tropical forests, but its damage was thought to stop near mine sites. In Brazil's Amazon, leases, concessions, and permits already cover huge areas. Nobody had counted the deforestation mining causes beyond its own fences.

The team found mining significantly increased forest loss up to seventy kilometers beyond lease boundaries. Mining drove over eleven thousand square kilometers of deforestation in the study period. Roads, towns, supply chains, and displaced farming spread the damage outward. Current licensing, though, ignores off-lease and cumulative impacts. The authors argue impact assessments must widen their view dramatically. Otherwise the Amazon keeps paying for minerals with forest that official accounts never record.
openalex-w2794463825:
Richard Patterson, Eoin McNamara, and Marko Tainio lead a team pooling sitting-time research in the European Journal of Epidemiology in 2018. Sitting for long hours is now a normal part of work and leisure. Whether it kills, and how risk grows with each added hour, needed a dose-response answer. The authors adjusted for physical activity, which often confounds such studies.

They combined thirty-four prospective studies covering over 1.3 million people. For total sitting, the link to early death was non-linear: risk crept up, then rose faster past about eight hours daily. Heart disease mortality followed a similar bend. Type 2 diabetes risk rose steadily and linearly with sitting time. Cancer mortality showed no significant link. Television time carried stronger risks than total sitting at the same hours. The message is not simply move more; very long sitting days carry their own penalty.
openalex-w3044545425:
Don Husereau, Michael Drummond, Stavros Petrou, and colleagues issued the CHEERS statement in Cost Effectiveness and Resource Allocation in 2013. CHEERS sets reporting standards for economic evaluations of health interventions, the studies that weigh a treatment's costs against its benefits. Reporting such studies poses special challenges.

A survey of medical editors showed the need for fresh, unified guidance. The task force gathered candidate items from a review of earlier guidelines, then ran a two-round expert panel drawn from universities, clinics, industry, government, and journals. Of forty-four candidates, twenty-four items survived into a user-friendly checklist. The statement speaks to researchers writing evaluations and to the editors and reviewers who judge them.
openalex-w4281762625:
Manon Fallet, Caroline Montagnani, Bruno Petton, and colleagues show that early microbial exposure protects oysters from disease for life. Their study of the Pacific oyster appeared in 2022. Pacific oyster mortality syndrome is a pathogen-driven disease that devastates farms. Whether the microbes around young oysters shape their adult immunity was an open question.

Oysters exposed to microbes early in life survived later infection far better. Remarkably, their offspring were protected too. The team combined microbe, gene activity, and epigenetic analyses to explain the effect. Early exposure left lasting marks on immune genes, reprogramming how they switch on. The authors suggest such training could become a new strategy for protecting oyster farming.
openalex-w4386522125:
Mariana Leguía, Alejandra Garcia-Glaessner, Breno Muñoz-Saavedra, and colleagues track highly pathogenic bird flu, H5N1, in Peru's wildlife, in Nature Communications in 2023. The virus swept down the Americas and began killing seabirds and marine mammals in Peru. Genetic family trees placed the Peruvian outbreak's start in the autumn of 2022. The same virus cluster appeared in pelicans, a cormorant, a sandpiper, a dolphin, and sea lions, showing jumps between birds and mammals.

Some sea lion viruses from southern Peru grouped with Chilean viruses, evidence of spread across the border. Two carried a mutation linked to easier spread among mammals. One sat close on the tree to a virus later found in a person in Chile. Such tracking shows why wildlife die-offs are watched as pandemic early warnings.
openalex-w7204840425:
Ana Maria Dias dos Santos and Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva released a Portuguese-language philosophy paper in Brazil in 2026 on the function of will and intelligence in human freedom. Reading the Aristotelian, Augustinian, and Thomist tradition, the study asks how intellect and will together ground human freedom and moral responsibility. Their hypothesis is that freedom is not merely choosing between alternatives, but the will's capacity to orient itself rationally toward the good the intellect knows.

Intelligence plays the determining role by making truth and the good known, the authors find. The will freely adheres to that good, making responsible moral action possible. The integration of intellect, will, and virtues grounds authentic freedom, they conclude, offering resources for thinking about moral responsibility amid today's ethical problems.
openalex-w7212691425:
Kayani Micheli Bevilaqua leads a team that weighs a cage-free egg farm for a small plot in Ourinhos, Sao Paulo. Cage-free hens roam a shed floor in place of stacked wire pens. Shoppers now ask for such eggs more and more. The team sized a flock of one thousand brown hens, and costed the start-up, the feed, and the cash the eggs would bring in, with and sans a green stamp.

The count weighs more than outlay and price. A green stamp can lift what a box of eggs earns, but it adds checks and costs of its own. Small farms live or fall on sums like these. The study gives one farm a full set of counts: what it takes to start, what it takes to run, and what must hold for the flock to pay its way.
openalex-w7213553525:
Augusto Ndumbo Canutula Cativa and Armando Manuel Miguel Louro analyse sustainable tourism in Moçâmedes, Namibe province, Angola. Their 2026 qualitative study joins tourism research with library work on audit in business management. Ten participants linked to local tourism informed the tourism side of the study.

Having tourist resources does not by itself bring lasting development, the authors find. Planning, efficient management, internal control, and reliable information are also required. Risk management, transparency, and sound decisions complete the conditions. Good management and audit practice can raise business efficiency and stakeholder trust, they argue. Value then stays in the territory longer, giving Moçâmedes a better chance to turn potential into durable local development.
openalex-w7213964825:
Vanessa Freire Silva Claudino leads a team reviewing psychomotricity and learning, with motion as the central element. Their 2026 library review consults books and papers through SciELO and Google Scholar. Psychomotricity joins neurology, psychology, and pedagogy, and views the person as a whole.

Body schema, body image, muscle tone, coordination, fine motion, rhythm, laterality, and balance form its elements. Psychomotor disorders, such as inhibition, instability, and dyspraxia, are described without a neurological cause assumed. School should integrate motion into learning in a way, the authors conclude. Specific actions and policies joining motion to the pupil's learning process are their practical recommendation.
openalex-w7214234825:
Thiago de Sales Miranda, Carolina Lima de Souza, and José Carlos de Sales Ferreira reviewed, in 2026, how the drug tirzepatide changes appetite and eating in people treated for obesity. The drug makes people feel full sooner and quiets constant thoughts about food. That helps weight loss, but it also raises the risk that patients eat too little of what they need.

Their narrative review covers how the drug acts on gut and brain signals, side effects such as nausea, and the danger of hidden poor nutrition and muscle loss. Drug treatment alone, they argue, rarely keeps weight off. Individual nutrition guidance is presented as essential: it eases stomach problems, protects protein intake and lean mass, and helps new eating habits last.
openalex-w7214457325:
Thalyne Nayara Barbon, João Paulo Ribeiro Eduardo, and Micheli Patrícia de Fátima Magri studied type 2 diabetes care in a Brazilian town in 2026. They asked why patients do or do not take their medicine as prescribed. Their work mixed a literature review with field research among patients at local family health units, including people with diabetic foot problems, and examined the nurse's role in the process.

Most patients used their medication, the team found, but few kept to diet and exercise plans. Forgetting doses and side effects hurt adherence, and many patients also lived with high blood pressure or thyroid problems. Foot self-care was only partly satisfactory. The authors argue nurses matter through health education, a trusting bond with patients, and care fitted to each person, sustained over time rather than given once.
openalex-w7221094725:
Pedro Leandro Siqueira dos Santos and Keila Aparecida de Lima reviewed the literature on physical exercise and childhood obesity, publishing in 2026. Childhood obesity is tied to behavior, surroundings, food, and low activity, and the authors ask what regular exercise can do both to prevent it and to treat it once present.

Across the studies they survey, exercise helped control body weight and improved fitness, metabolic health, and quality of life. Sedentary habits and lifestyle patterns stood behind much of the problem's growth. The authors present exercise as a central strategy, strongest when joined with adequate food and healthy daily habits. Their review gives families and schools a compact case for moving more, earlier.
panchatantra-ryder-1925:
Arthur W. Ryder gave English readers the Panchatantra in 1925, in the University of Chicago Press edition. The Sanskrit original is a famed book of beast fables from old India. A sage uses its tales to teach three dull princes how to rule.

Five books sort the tales by theme, from lost friends to war and peace. Lions, jackals, and doves act out greed, trust, and quick wit. Short verses state the morals, and tales nest inside tales. Ryder's sprightly prose keeps the humor and bite of the source. Its frame puts statecraft first and mere fun second.
pirenne-medieval-cities-halsey-1925:
Henri Pirenne's Medieval Cities appears in Frank D. Halsey's translation of 1925. The book prints Pirenne's Princeton lectures. Pirenne argues that the Arab conquests closed the Mediterranean and stalled Europe's trade. Cities faded until commerce revived in the 1000s. Merchants then built new towns and won charters of freedom.

This is the Pirenne thesis in its urban form. Burghers, guilds, and communes remade European society from below. The lectures are short, bold, and clearly argued. Later research qualified the thesis, yet its frame still organizes debate. The book is the best short entry into Pirenne's thought. It shows economic history at its most vivid.
pistis-sophia-schmidt-1925:
Carl Schmidt edited the 1925 critical edition of Pistis Sophia, a Gnostic gospel. The text, written in Coptic, survived in a single old codex. It claims to record secret talks of the risen Jesus.

Mary Magdalene asks most of the questions in the dialogue. Jesus explains the fall and rise of Pistis Sophia, a spirit who repents. Strange heavens, powers, and passwords fill the teaching. Schmidt's edition gave scholars a firm text to study. The work remains a key, hard source for anyone tracing early Christian mystics and their rivals. Few texts show that world so fully.
plaw-118-213-2025: Purcellville, Virginia gained a renamed post office building under Public Law 118-213, approved on January 2, 2025. The law states that the postal facility at 220 North Hatcher Avenue shall be known as the Secretary of State Madeleine Albright Post Office Building. Any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-118-228-2025: Public Law 118-228 is the Gabriella Miller Kids First Research Act 2.0, approved on January 4, 2025. The law extends a children's research program at the National Institutes of Health. It amends the Public Health Service Act to move the program's funding years forward. Funding that once ran from 2014 through 2023 now runs from 2024 through 2028, paid through a planning division of the institutes.
plaw-118-230-2025: Public Law 118-230 is the Accelerating Appraisals and Conservation Efforts Act, or the AACE Act, approved on January 4, 2025. The law sets a policy for land value work on deals under the Secretary of the Interior. A covered appraiser needs a license or certificate in only one state to value land in any state for such a deal. When the Secretary hires outside help, local licensed appraisers get first call where practical.
plaw-118-240-2025: Public Law 118-240, approved on January 4, 2025, renames a post office building in Titusville, Pennsylvania. The law states that the postal facility at 135 West Spring Street shall be known as the Edwin L. Drake Post Office Building. Any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, record, or other paper counts, under the law, as a mention of the new name.
plaw-119-1-2025:
Public Law 119-1 is the Laken Riley Act, approved on January 29, 2025 by the 119th Congress. The law orders the Secretary of Homeland Security to take certain people into custody. It amends the federal rules on who must be held after arrest.

The duty covers a person who entered the country without valid papers and is charged with certain crimes. The listed crimes include burglary, theft, larceny, and shoplifting. They also include assault of a law enforcement officer, and any crime that ends in death or grave bodily harm to another person.
plaw-119-10-2025: Public Law 119-10 is a joint resolution approved on May 9, 2025, in which Congress cancels a federal rule. The rule came from the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection and dealt with overdraft lending. Its subject was overdraft loans at very large banks and similar firms. Under the resolution, that rule, issued in December 2024, has no force or effect.
plaw-119-11-2025: Public Law 119-11 is a joint resolution approved on May 9, 2025, in which Congress cancels a federal rule. The rule came from the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection. It defined the larger firms in the market for general-use digital payment apps, the phone apps people use to pay each other. Under the resolution, that rule, issued in December 2024, has no force or effect.
plaw-119-12-2025:
Public Law 119-12 is the TAKE IT DOWN Act, approved on May 19, 2025 by the 119th Congress. Its full name is the Tools to Address Known Exploitation by Immobilizing Technological Deepfakes on Websites and Networks Act. The law requires covered online platforms to remove intimate images shared without consent.

One part makes it a crime to share such images on purpose, under the Communications Act of 1934. The law defines consent as a free and clear yes, given without force or fraud. It also defines digital forgery, meaning a fake intimate image made with software or artificial intelligence.
plaw-119-14-2025: Rubber tire manufacturing is the subject of Public Law 119-14, a joint resolution approved on May 23, 2025. Congress used it to cancel a rule from the Environmental Protection Agency. The rule set national emission standards for harmful air pollutants from tire plants. Under the resolution, that rule, issued in November 2024, has no force or effect.
plaw-119-15-2025: Public Law 119-15 is a joint resolution approved on June 12, 2025, in which Congress cancels a federal decision. The decision came from the Environmental Protection Agency and covered California motor vehicle pollution standards. It dealt with heavy-duty truck emission warranties, the Advanced Clean Trucks program, and a waiver that let California set its own rules. Under the resolution, that decision has no force or effect.
plaw-119-18-2025: Public Law 119-18 is the Aerial Firefighting Enhancement Act of 2025, approved on June 12, 2025. The law renews a power first granted in the Wildfire Suppression Aircraft Transfer Act of 1996. The Department of Defense may again sell aircraft and parts for use in fighting wildfires. Planes sold under the law may be used only for wildfire work, and the law adds water alongside fire retardant as a load they may drop.
plaw-119-2-2025: Public Law 119-2 is a joint resolution approved on March 14, 2025, in which Congress cancels a federal rule. The rule came from the Environmental Protection Agency and set a waste emissions charge for oil and gas systems. It spelled out steps for following the charge, including netting and exemptions. Under the resolution, that rule, issued in November 2024, has no force or effect.
plaw-119-21-2025:
Public Law 119-21, approved on July 4, 2025, is a budget reconciliation act passed under title II of House Concurrent Resolution 14. Laws of this kind carry out the budget plan of Congress by changing spending and tax rules across many programs. This act is built from titles sent in by House and Senate panels.

The first title comes from the panels on agriculture, nutrition, and forestry. Its parts rework the food aid program known as SNAP, including work rules for able-bodied adults. Other parts take back forestry funds and update farm support rules for crops, sugar, and dairy farms.
plaw-119-22-2025: Public Law 119-22 is the Alaska Native Settlement Trust Eligibility Act, approved on July 7, 2025. The law amends the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act. For a five-year period, money or benefits from a Settlement Trust paid to an aged, blind, or disabled Alaska Native or descendant do not count against that person. Such payments are left out when officials decide who qualifies for certain aid programs.
plaw-119-24-2025: Public Law 119-24 is the Apex Area Technical Corrections Act, approved on July 15, 2025. The law amends a 1989 act on land transfer for the Apex Project in Nevada. It adds two parties to that older act: the City of North Las Vegas and the Apex Industrial Park Owners Association. The added names join Clark County in parts of the land plan set out in 1989.
plaw-119-25-2025: Public Law 119-25 is the Salem Maritime National Historical Park Redesignation and Boundary Study Act, approved on July 15, 2025. The law gives a new title to the Salem Maritime National Historic Site in Massachusetts. The site is now the Salem Maritime National Historical Park. The law also orders a study of nearby sites tied to sea trade, coastal defense, and military history, to judge if they fit in the park.
plaw-119-27-2025:
Public Law 119-27 is the GENIUS Act, approved on July 18, 2025. Its full name is the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act. The law provides for the regulation of payment stablecoins, a kind of digital asset tied to a steady value.

Early sections define the terms the law uses, from the federal banking agencies to the digital asset itself. A digital asset is a record of value kept on a secure shared ledger, the law says. The act then builds a federal rulebook for firms that issue payment stablecoins.
plaw-119-28-2025: Public Law 119-28 is the Rescissions Act of 2025, approved on July 24, 2025. A rescission cancels budget authority that Congress had granted earlier. The law acts on cuts the President proposed in special messages sent to Congress on June 3, 2025. The listed cuts take effect at once and draw on funds not yet spent. The first items cover money set aside for contributions to world bodies through the Department of State.
plaw-119-29-2025: Public Law 119-29 is the Filing Relief for Natural Disasters Act, approved on July 24, 2025. The law amends the Internal Revenue Code, the federal tax code. It changes the rules for pushing back tax deadlines when a disaster strikes. The tax Secretary may now grant that relief for a state-declared disaster, at the written request of a governor. The Secretary must first consult the head of the Federal Emergency Management Agency.
plaw-119-30-2025: Public Law 119-30 is the Jocelyn Nungaray National Wildlife Refuge Act, approved on July 24, 2025. The law renames the Anahuac National Wildlife Refuge in Texas as the Jocelyn Nungaray National Wildlife Refuge. Congress states in its findings that Jocelyn Nungaray, age twelve, was killed in Houston in June 2024. The findings also note an executive order of March 4, 2025 that gave the refuge her name.
plaw-119-31-2025: Public Law 119-31 is the VA Home Loan Program Reform Act, approved on July 30, 2025. The law amends title 38 of the United States Code, which covers veterans' benefits. It gives the Secretary of Veterans Affairs new tools when a veteran falls behind on a home loan backed by the Department. The Secretary may pay the loan holder an amount needed to stop a foreclosure, and gain a secured claim on the home.
plaw-119-32-2025: Public Law 119-32 is the ACES Act of 2025, approved on August 14, 2025. The law orders a study of cancer among people who served as active duty aircrew in the Armed Forces. Within thirty days, the Secretary of Veterans Affairs must seek a deal with the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. That body will study how common cancer is in that group, and how often it leads to death.
plaw-119-33-2025: Public Law 119-33 is the Protecting Regular Order for Veterans Act of 2025, or the PRO Veterans Act, approved on August 14, 2025. The law guards the normal budget process for the Department of Veterans Affairs. For three years, the Secretary must brief the proper panels of Congress in person every three months. The briefings cover the budget of the Department and any shortfall it faces, plus plans to fix a shortfall.
plaw-119-34-2025: Public Law 119-34 is the Maintaining American Superiority by Improving Export Control Transparency Act, approved on August 19, 2025. The law amends the Export Control Reform Act of 2018. Each year, the Commerce Secretary must report to Congress on export license requests tied to covered foreign parties. Each report lists the firm that applied, the item and its control code, the end user, and the choice made on the request.
plaw-119-35-2025: Public Law 119-35, approved on September 5, 2025, names a veterans clinic in Toms River, New Jersey. The clinic at 1055 Hooper Avenue, newly opened, becomes the Leonard G. 'Bud' Lomell VA Clinic. Congress states in its findings that Lomell was a Second Lieutenant who served with the 2nd Ranger Battalion in World War II. The findings note that local veterans backed naming the clinic for the long-time Ocean County resident.
plaw-119-36-2025: Public Law 119-36 is the Homebuyers Privacy Protection Act, approved on September 5, 2025. The law amends the Fair Credit Reporting Act. It limits when credit reporting agencies may hand out a consumer report tied to prescreening. When a person asks for a report in connection with a home mortgage loan, the agency may not pass that report on in the ways the law bars.
plaw-119-37-2025:
Public Law 119-37 is the Continuing Appropriations, Agriculture, Legislative Branch, Military Construction and Veterans Affairs, and Extensions Act, 2026, approved on November 12, 2025. The law keeps the federal government funded for fiscal year 2026. It pairs short-term funding with full-year spending acts for some parts of the government.

Full-year parts fund farm and food programs, the Food and Drug Administration, and the legislative branch. Another part funds military building projects and the Department of Veterans Affairs. Later parts extend farm programs and health programs whose authority was set to lapse. Such bridge laws keep agencies running while full-year spending acts are finished.
plaw-119-38-2025:
Public Law 119-38 is the Epstein Files Transparency Act, approved on November 19, 2025. The law orders the Attorney General to release records held by the Department of Justice that relate to Jeffrey Epstein. The release must come within thirty days of the law's passage.

The records must be posted in a form that people can search and download. They cover all unclassified files from the Department, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and United States Attorneys' Offices. The files include probes, court cases, flight logs, and material on Ghislaine Maxwell. Flight logs and travel records for aircraft, vessels, or vehicles tied to Epstein are named in the list.
plaw-119-40-2025: Public Law 119-40 is the Wetlands Conservation and Access Improvement Act of 2025, approved on November 25, 2025. The short law changes one date in the Pittman-Robertson Wildlife Restoration Act. Interest earned on sums held in the federal aid to wildlife restoration fund becomes ready to divide among the states at the start of fiscal year 2033. The prior date in the law was the start of fiscal year 2026.
plaw-119-41-2025: Public Law 119-41 is the Bottles and Breastfeeding Equipment Screening Enhancement Act, approved on November 25, 2025. The law deals with airport security screening by the Transportation Security Administration. Within ninety days, and every five years after, the agency must issue or refresh guidance on clean handling. The guidance guards breast milk, baby formula, and infant water and juice from dirt during screening, along with the packs used to keep them cold.
plaw-119-43-2025: Public Law 119-43 is the Medal of Honor Act, approved on December 1, 2025. The law amends title 38 of the United States Code, which covers veterans' benefits. It raises the rate of the special monthly pension paid to Medal of Honor recipients. Congress calls the medal the highest and most honored military decoration of the United States in its findings, and notes that living recipients on the Medal of Honor Roll receive the pension.
plaw-119-44-2025:
Public Law 119-44 is the SUPPORT for Patients and Communities Reauthorization Act of 2025, approved on December 1, 2025. The law renews federal programs on opioid use disorder. Those programs cover prevention, treatment, and recovery help for people who struggle with opioid drugs.

The first title deals with prevention, from care for mothers and newborns to training for first responders. It also funds state and tribal responses to opioid disorders. A second title turns to treatment for people in care. Later titles carry the renewed programs forward and set their new funding years. Its contents also name aid for families hit by fetal alcohol spectrum disorder.
plaw-119-46-2025: Public Law 119-46 is a joint resolution approved on December 2, 2025, about displays in Washington, D.C. Congress asks the Secretary of the Interior to allow one-time displays for the nation's two hundred fiftieth birthday events. The displays would run from December 31, 2025 to January 5, 2026, on and near the National Mall. They include images projected onto the Washington Monument for five nights of public viewing.
plaw-119-47-2025: The National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska is the subject of Public Law 119-47, a joint resolution approved on December 5, 2025. Congress used it to cancel the Bureau of Land Management's record of decision for the reserve's integrated activity plan, issued in April 2022. A watchdog opinion later held that the decision counts as a rule. Under the resolution, it has no force or effect.
plaw-119-48-2025: The Miles City Field Office plan falls under Public Law 119-48, a joint resolution approved on December 11, 2025. Congress cancelled that Bureau of Land Management plan, which joined a record of decision with a resource management plan amendment issued in November 2024. A Government Accountability Office opinion of June 25, 2025 held that the plan counts as a rule. Under the resolution, that plan has no force or effect.
plaw-119-49-2025: North Dakota land planning is the subject of Public Law 119-49, a joint resolution approved on December 11, 2025. It cancels the Bureau of Land Management's record of decision and approved resource management plan for the North Dakota Field Office, issued in January 2025. Under the resolution, that plan has no force or effect.
plaw-119-50-2025: Alaska's Central Yukon region is covered by Public Law 119-50, a joint resolution approved on December 11, 2025. It disapproves the Bureau of Land Management's record of decision and approved resource management plan for that area, issued on November 12, 2024. A Government Accountability Office opinion of June 25, 2025 held that the plan counts as a rule under the Congressional Review Act. Under the resolution, the plan has no force or effect.
plaw-119-51-2025: Public Law 119-51, approved on December 11, 2025, strikes down a land plan amendment from the Bureau of Land Management's Buffalo Field Office in Wyoming. The amendment, issued on November 20, 2024, joined a record of decision with changes to the office's resource management plan. The Government Accountability Office called it a rule in an opinion dated September 18, 2025. Congress disapproved it, so the amendment has no force or effect.
plaw-119-52-2025: Oil and gas leasing on Alaska's Coastal Plain is the subject of Public Law 119-52, a joint resolution approved on December 11, 2025. Congress used it to cancel the Bureau of Land Management's record of decision for the Coastal Plain leasing program, issued in December 2024. Under the resolution, that decision has no force or effect.
plaw-119-53-2025: Public Law 119-53 is the Miracle on Ice Congressional Gold Medal Act, approved on December 12, 2025. The law awards three Congressional Gold Medals to the members of the 1980 United States Olympic men's ice hockey team. Congress finds that the team, made of college players, beat the Soviet Union by four goals to three on February 22, 1980. The games were held in Lake Placid, New York.
plaw-119-54-2025: Public Law 119-54 is the Fairness for Servicemembers and their Families Act of 2025, approved on December 12, 2025. The law amends title 38 of the United States Code, which covers veterans' benefits. It orders the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to review, every five years from January 1, 2026, the top automatic coverage under two life insurance programs. One program serves troops, and the other serves veterans after service.
plaw-119-55-2025: Public Law 119-55 is the Montgomery GI Bill Selected Reserves Tuition Fairness Act of 2025, approved on December 12, 2025. The law amends title 38 of the United States Code. It tells the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to reject courses at a public college that charges more than the in-state tuition rate to certain veterans. The shield now covers veterans using aid under the Selected Reserve program in title 10.
plaw-119-56-2025: Public Law 119-56 is the Veteran Fraud Reimbursement Act of 2025, approved on December 12, 2025. The law amends title 38 of the United States Code. When a fiduciary, a person trusted to handle a veteran's benefit money, misuses that money, the Secretary of Veterans Affairs must repay the full amount to the veteran. The Secretary must also try in good faith to recover the money from the fiduciary.
plaw-119-57-2025: Public Law 119-57 is the Foundation of the Federal Bar Association Charter Amendments Act of 2025, approved on December 12, 2025. The law revises the federal charter of the Foundation of the Federal Bar Association in title 36 of the United States Code. It leaves who may join, and the rights of members, to the group's own bylaws. It also states that the board of directors governs the group and that the group may not issue stock.
plaw-119-58-2025: Public Law 119-58 is the Secure Rural Schools Reauthorization Act of 2025, approved on December 18, 2025. The law extends the Secure Rural Schools and Community Self-Determination Act of 2000. That older act pays states and counties that hold large areas of federal land. The new law moves the payment years forward, from 2023 to 2026, and orders the Treasury to send payments for recent years within forty-five days.
plaw-119-59-2025: Guthrie, Oklahoma is the town covered by Public Law 119-59, approved on December 18, 2025. The law states that the postal facility at 201 West Oklahoma Avenue shall be known as the Oscar J. Upham Post Office. It adds that any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-119-60-2025:
Public Law 119-60 is the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, approved on December 18, 2025. The law grants funds for military work of the Department of Defense for that year. It also covers military building projects, defense work of the Department of Energy, and the set size of the armed forces.

The act is built from eight divisions, starting with defense funding and military construction. Later divisions cover energy security work and funding tables. The last divisions fold in yearly acts for the Department of State, for intelligence work, and for the Coast Guard.
plaw-119-61-2025: Public Law 119-61 is the Wounded Knee Massacre Memorial and Sacred Site Act, approved on December 19, 2025. The law orders the Secretary of the Interior to finish the steps needed for certain land to be held in restricted fee status. The holders are the Oglala Sioux Tribe and the Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe. The land stays owned by the tribes, forms part of the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation, and cannot be taxed by a state or local government.
plaw-119-62-2025: Public Law 119-62 is the Modernizing Access to our Public Waters Act of 2025, or the MAPWaters Act, approved on December 26, 2025. The law deals with data on public outdoor use of federal waterways. It calls for that data to be made uniform, joined together, and published by the federal land and water agencies. The named agencies include the National Park Service, the Bureau of Land Management, and the Forest Service.
plaw-119-63-2025: Public Law 119-63 is the Alaska Native Vietnam Era Veterans Land Allotment Extension Act of 2025, approved on December 26, 2025. The short law changes one phrase in an older land act. It stretches the land allotment program for Alaska Native veterans of the Vietnam era. The span in the law grows from a five-year period to a ten-year period, giving more time to claim an allotment.
plaw-119-64-2025: Public Law 119-64 is the Disaster Related Extension of Deadlines Act, approved on December 26, 2025. The law amends the Internal Revenue Code, the federal tax code. When a tax deadline is pushed back because of a disaster, that delay now counts as an extension of time for filing a return. That change matters for the time limit on claiming a credit or refund. The law also counts such delays when tax collection notices are sent.
plaw-119-65-2025: Public Law 119-65 is the Save Our Seas 2.0 Amendments Act, approved on December 26, 2025. The law improves how two ocean cleanup efforts are run. One is the Marine Debris Foundation, set up under the Save Our Seas 2.0 Act. The other is the Marine Debris Program of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, under the Marine Debris Act. The changes tidy the rules for grants, contracts, and other deals.
plaw-119-66-2025: Public Law 119-66 is the Congressional Award Program Reauthorization Act, approved on December 26, 2025. The law renews the Congressional Award Act, which honors young people for service and personal growth. It moves the end date of the program from October 1, 2023 to October 1, 2028. The change counts as if it had passed on October 1, 2023, so the program shows no gap.
plaw-119-67-2025: Public Law 119-67 is the Great Lakes Fishery Research Reauthorization Act, approved on December 26, 2025. The short law changes one year in an older funding law. It renews funding to watch, assess, and study the Great Lakes Basin. The end year for that funding moves from 2025 to 2030, so the fishery research work in the basin can go on for five more years.
plaw-119-68-2025: Public Law 119-68 is the La Paz County Solar Energy and Job Creation Act, approved on December 29, 2025. The law orders the Secretary of the Interior to hand certain federal land in Arizona to La Paz County. The land covers about three thousand four hundred acres run by the Bureau of Land Management, as shown on a map from June 2023. The transfer takes place once the county asks for the land.
plos-pbio-0020225:
Livia de Hoz, Stephen J. Martin, and Richard G. M. Morris explored lost memories in rats for PLOS Biology in 2004. A rat that learns where things are can seem to forget over time. The team asked whether the memory is truly gone or just hard to reach.

A reminder cue brought the lost spatial memory back. That means forgetting was a failure of retrieval, not of storage, at least in this case. The result matters for how memory loss is understood. If traces persist but cannot be reached, then prompts and cues may restore more than expected. The study gives a neat animal model for telling stored memories apart from reachable ones.
plos-pone-0000025:
Bahjat Al-Ani, Peter Hewett, Suborna Ahmed, and co-authors reported in 2006 on a chemical route to growing new blood vessels. Angiogenesis, the sprouting of fresh vessels, is wanted for healing wounds and starved hearts, and unwanted when it feeds tumors. Nitric oxide, a small signaling gas, was already known to be involved.

The team showed that nitric oxide released from compounds called S-nitrosothiols promotes angiogenesis. Pinning the effect to a releasable source matters, because a drug that donates nitric oxide at the right place could coax vessels to grow where they are needed. The finding adds a usable lever to a process medicine has long wanted to control.
plos-pone-0000125:
Neil J. Gemmell and Jon Slate published this short genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2006. It addresses heterozygote advantage, the idea that carrying two different copies of a gene can beat carrying two matching copies. Here the trait under study is fecundity, how many offspring an organism produces.

Heterozygote advantage is one classic way that genetic variety stays in a population instead of being weeded out. The authors weigh the evidence for this effect on reproductive output. The question matters well beyond one species, because it helps explain why populations keep diversity that looks, at first glance, like it should disappear.
plos-pone-0000225:
Annika C. Karlsson, Astrid K. N. Iversen, Joan M. Chapman, and colleagues published this HIV study in PLOS ONE in 2007. CTL responses are attacks by killer T cells on virus-infected cells. The authors track how these responses broaden, one target after another, in early HIV-1 infection. They link that broadening to viral escape, mutations that let the virus dodge attack.

Early immune responses shape the whole course of HIV infection. As each new T cell target appears, the virus mutates away from it, in a chase the authors document. Understanding that race informs vaccine design, which aims to aim the immune system at targets the virus cannot easily change.
plos-pone-0000325:
Xiang Jia Min and Donal A. Hickey published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. DNA barcodes are short, standard gene stretches used to identify species. The authors show that barcodes also provide a quick preview of a species' mitochondrial genome composition. One small piece summarizes features of the whole molecule.

A preview from a barcode saves the cost of sequencing whole mitochondrial genomes for every specimen. The authors test how much information the barcode region carries about the rest. The result adds value to the vast barcode libraries being built for species identification.
plos-pone-0000425:
Sol Efroni, Carl F. Schaefer, and Kenneth H. Buetow sorted cancers by the biological pathways active in them, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Two tumors can look alike under the microscope yet behave differently. Instead of cataloging single genes, the team analyzed pathway activity to identify the key processes underlying cancer phenotypes, the observable traits of each tumor.

Grouping cancers by the processes they depend on could reveal shared weaknesses that cut across tumor types. A drug aimed at a process, rather than at one gene, might then serve several groups at once. The approach reflects a shift in cancer research from lists of mutations toward maps of how cells are rewired.
plos-pone-0000525:
R. David Hawkins and colleagues profiled gene activity in healing ear tissue, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Some animals can regrow inner ear sensory tissue, the hair-cell-bearing epithelia whose loss causes deafness in humans. The team produced large scale gene expression profiles of regenerating inner ear sensory epithelia.

A profile taken during regrowth lists the genes the tissue switches on to rebuild itself. Comparing that list with the mammalian ear, which does not regenerate, highlights what is missing. Deafness research uses such profiles as a parts list for attempts to wake the same program in human ears.
plos-pone-0000625:
Farooq Kiani, Sonja Schwarzl, Stefan Fischer and colleagues built three-dimensional models of a faulty enzyme, published in PLOS ONE in 2007. The enzyme is G6PD, and losing its function is the most common inborn error of metabolism in the world. The authors cite an estimate of 400 million people affected. In Germany, though, the condition is very rare.

Working from known G6PD crystal structures, the team modeled variants found in people of German ancestry. A 3D model shows how a changed enzyme part might break its working shape. Such models help explain why some variants cause severe disease while others stay mild.
plos-pone-0000725:
Odile Launay, Christine Durier, Corinne Desaint and colleagues compared two routes for delivering an HIV vaccine in the ANRS VAC16 trial. Their 2007 PLOS ONE objective was safety and cellular immune response. Healthy, HIV-uninfected volunteers received a candidate vaccine called LIPO-4, built from HIV lipopeptides. One group got it intradermally, into the skin; the other intramuscularly, into muscle.

The trial was randomized and open-label, run in France at six sites with 24 weeks of follow-up. Intradermal delivery is dose-sparing, stretching limited vaccine further. If skin delivery with less vaccine matches muscle delivery, vaccination campaigns gain reach. Cellular responses, T cell reactions, were the measure that mattered here.
plos-pone-0000825:
Ann-Charlotte Lundstedt, Shane McCarthy, Mattias C.U. Gustafsson and colleagues proposed a genetic reason some people suffer the worst urinary infections. For unknown reasons, urinary tract infections cluster in certain individuals. Their 2007 PLOS ONE paper proposes a new, gene-based cause of susceptibility to acute pyelonephritis. That is the most severe form of UTI, the kind that reaches the kidneys. The IL-8 receptor, CXCR1, was identified as a candidate.

A receptor for IL-8 helps summon white blood cells to fight bacteria in the urinary tract. If inherited variants blunt that summons, kidneys may be left undefended. A genetic basis would explain family clustering, and could flag patients who need aggressive prevention.
plos-pone-0000925:
Richard Ortega, Peter Cloetens, Guillaume Deves and colleagues pictured iron stored inside dopamine vesicles at nano scale, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Disturbed metal balance in the brain is suspected in nerve cell death. Until now, no tool could map metals inside neurons finely enough to test that idea.

The team developed a chemical nano-imaging setup for the job. With it, they could see iron held within the tiny vesicles that store dopamine, a key brain signal chemical. A clear picture of where iron sits in healthy cells sets the baseline. Later work can then ask what changes when neurons begin to fail.
plos-pone-0001025:
Qi Wang and Yuan-Ping Pang offered a safer way to relax small molecules into their bound shapes on a computer, in PLOS ONE in 2007. When a drug molecule settles into a protein pocket, it takes a bound conformation, a specific folded shape. Computer minimization finds such shapes by lowering the molecule's energy.

The catch: a shallow energy dip may not stop the process, and the molecule folds wrongly. Their procedure watches the minimization with normal mode analysis, a check on the molecule's vibration patterns. A monitored stop should give shapes that match how molecules really sit in pockets. Drug modelers need exactly that reliability.
plos-pone-0001125:
Stress during development can leave lasting marks on the brain. Xia Wang, David Green, Stephen Roberts, and co-authors tested one form of stress, heat, in the fruit fly Drosophila, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They focused on the mushroom body, a brain region flies use for smell-based learning.

The study asks whether thermal stress disrupts how the mushroom body develops and how well adult flies learn odors. Earlier work had shown that many kinds of stress disturb brain development in every model system tried. This paper ties a specific stress to a specific brain structure and a measurable behavior, smell learning.
plos-pone-0001225:
Some blood cancers hide chromosome damage that standard tests cannot see. Lukasz Gondek and colleagues applied SNP arrays to patients with atypical myeloproliferative and myelodysplastic syndromes. Their study appeared in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. SNP arrays are chips that read hundreds of thousands of single-letter DNA variants.

The authors show that SNP array karyotyping detects uniparental disomy. In that condition, both copies of a chromosome segment come from one parent. It also detects cryptic chromosomal abnormalities that older methods miss. They studied patients with and without the JAK2 V617F mutation, a common driver in these diseases. Finer karyotyping can change diagnosis and treatment choices.
plos-pone-0001325:
Certain short peptides can assemble themselves into coatings and scaffolds, making them attractive nano-biomaterials. Hong Yang, Shan-Yu Fung, and Mark Pritzker studied one model peptide, EAK16-II, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Ionic-complementary peptides carry alternating positive and negative charges that drive their assembly.

The authors present evidence that the peptide can assemble on and coat both hydrophilic and hydrophobic surfaces, water-loving and water-hating alike. Such coatings could engineer biosurfaces for implants, sensors, and cell culture. A single peptide that coats both surface types is a versatile tool. The peptide assembles on its own once applied.
plos-pone-0001425:
Enrique Caviedes-Vidal and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how bats take up food from the gut. Bats tend to have less gut tissue than like sized mammals that do not fly. A small gut saves weight, which helps flight. The team asked how bats still get enough food from that small gut.

They show that bats let a large share of food pass between gut cells, not just through them. That route breaks the usual mammal pattern. It lets a small gut act like a much larger one. The finding recasts how flight shaped the bat body, gut included, over time.
plos-pone-0001525:
Joshua Herbeck and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on whether HIV is growing more or less harsh. Past cohort data and lab tests had given clashing answers, with claims of falling, flat, and rising harm. The team tested the change claim in North American data. They used set marks of virus strength over time.

They found a lack of proof for a shift in HIV strength in this region. A flat verdict from sound data still counts. It means care and spread plans need not chase a moving target on this front. It also shows how weak methods can breed false trends.
plos-pone-0001625:
Cédric Patthey, Lena Gunhaga, and Thomas Edlund studied how the brain, spinal cord, and sense organs begin to form in the early embryo. Their 2008 PLOS ONE research article focuses on two signal families, Wnt and BMP, that cells use to tell nearby cells what to become. The central nervous system grows from the neural plate, while the peripheral system grows from cells at its border.

For the senses to work, these two systems must grow in step, so that circuits form in the right places. The authors trace how Wnt and BMP signals coordinate the growth of neural plate, neural crest, and placodal cells. The full text gives the embryo experiments and the signals they recorded. The work helps explain how a flat sheet of early cells turns into a wired nervous system.
plos-pone-0001725:
Gregory P. Bisson, Tendani Gaolathe, Robert Gross, and their co-authors warned that HIV treatment success may be overstated, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Tracking how well global antiretroviral therapy scale-up works is a health priority. In resource-limited settings, though, many patients are lost to follow-up after starting treatment, and their true outcomes are unknown.

If many of those lost patients have died, published survival figures will look too good. The authors examined definitive outcomes of lost patients and what they imply for reported survival after HAART. The full text gives the tracing results and the corrected survival estimates. Honest numbers decide whether scale-up is truly working or needs fixing.
plos-pone-0001825:
Daniel A. Beard, Kalyan C. Vinnakota, and Fan Wu worked out detailed enzyme kinetics for a core metabolic enzyme in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Citrate synthase runs the first step of the citric acid cycle, the cell's central energy pathway. The paper analyzes the compulsory-ordered ternary mechanism used by two-substrate, two-product enzymes.

Their treatment accounts for inhibitors binding to each of the four enzyme states and keeps the kinetic constants consistent with the reaction equilibrium constant. The full text gives the derivations and the worked example. Rigorous kinetics of this kind, called biochemical species kinetics, improves computer models of metabolism used in drug and biofuel research.
plos-pone-0001925:
Mathias Gehrmann and co-authors asked why tumor cells, but not healthy cells, show a stress protein on their surface, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The protein, Hsp70, is the main stress-induced member of its family. When it sits on a tumor's outer membrane, it flags a worse or better outlook in some cancers, such as leukemia.

The team traced the display to a fat-like molecule in the membrane called Gb3. As the title states, Gb3 enables the tumor-specific placement of Hsp70 on the surface. That detail matters because surface Hsp70 can draw immune attack. A drug that shifts Gb3 might make more tumors show the flag.
plos-pone-0002025:
Lina Dahl and co-authors studied a gene that keeps young blood cells dividing, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. How the blood system expands in the fetal liver, stem cells and all, is largely unknown. The gene Lhx2 was a candidate driver, since it is active in that setting.

The team grew embryonic stem cells into embryoid bodies, small balls that mimic early development, and switched Lhx2 on. As the title states, its expression promoted self-renewal of a distinct early blood progenitor cell. A gene that keeps blood precursors young could help labs grow blood stem cells for therapy.
plos-pone-0002125:
Phuoc Tran and co-authors asked what happens when two cancer genes are switched off at once. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Lab models had shown that tumors need a cancer gene to stay switched on, a trait called oncogene addiction. Most real cancers, though, are driven by several gene changes at once, which makes it hard to tell which ones the tumor truly needs.

Working with lung adenocarcinomas and lymphomas in mice, the team turned off both MYC and K-Ras together. Doing so reversed tumor growth in their models. The finding supports the idea that hitting more than one driver gene at once could be a stronger way to treat cancer.
plos-pone-0002225:
Allan Reiss and co-authors scanned the brains of people whose laughter can knock out their muscles. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Cataplexy affects some people with narcolepsy, roughly 1 in 2,000 people overall. Strong feelings, above all laughter, can trigger a brief loss of muscle tone that leaves a person limp but awake.

The study aimed to find how the hypothalamus, a small brain region tied to sleep and emotion, responds to humor in these patients. Its responses looked anomalous next to those of healthy subjects. The work helps explain how an emotion can flip a switch in the brain and cut the body's strength.
plos-pone-0002325:
Wei Zhang, Song Liu, and Yaoqi Zhou presented an improved program for recognizing a protein's fold, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Predicting which known shape a new protein sequence will fold into is a central challenge in protein science. The team had built a series of methods, called SPARKS and SP2 through SP4, that score how well a sequence fits a known structure.

Their new method, SP5, adds torsion angle profiles, the twist patterns along the protein backbone, and a smarter penalty for gaps. Better fold recognition means more proteins of unknown shape can be assigned a likely structure from sequence alone, guiding experiments that follow.
plos-pone-0002425:
Faça and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Vitor M. Faça, Aviva P. Ventura, Mathew P. Fitzgibbon, among others. Its subject is proteomic Analysis of Ovarian Cancer Cells Reveals Dynamic Processes of Protein Secretion and Shedding of Extra-Cellular Domains. Elucidation of the repertoire of secreted and cell surface proteins of tumor cells is relevant to molecular diagnostics, tumor imaging and targeted therapies.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002525:
Takata and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Norio Takata, Hajime Hirase, among others. Its subject is cortical Layer 1 and Layer 2/3 Astrocytes Exhibit Distinct Calcium Dynamics In Vivo. Cumulative evidence supports bidirectional interactions between astrocytes and neurons, suggesting glial involvement of neuronal information processing in the brain.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002625:
Jürgen Konczak and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of haptic perception of object curvature in parkinson's disease. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Jürgen Konczak, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The haptic perception of the curvature of an object is essential for adequate object manipulation and critical for our guidance of actions. A further point appears in the abstract. This study investigated how the ability to perceive the curvature of an object is altered by Parkinson's disease (PD). Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002725:
In 2008, Karlijn I. van Aerde and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about prelimbic and infralimbic prefrontal cortex interact during fast network oscillations. The catalog record names Karlijn I. van Aerde first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The medial prefrontal cortex has been implicated in a variety of cognitive and executive processes such as decision making and working memory. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002825:
In 2008, Jerome J. Weis and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was effects of algal diversity on the production of biomass in homogeneous and heterogeneous nutrient environments: a microcosm experiment. Authorship is credited in the record to Jerome J. Weis and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. One of the most common questions addressed by ecologists over the past decade has been-how does species richness impact the production of community biomass?. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002925:
Thomas Fanshawe, Andrew Lynch, Ian Ellis and colleagues tackled a statistics problem in breast cancer grading in 2008. Pathologists grade tumor samples to guide care, yet past studies found only moderate agreement between raters. Missing ratings and many raters make judging that agreement harder still.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team sets out a way to assess agreement when rating data are incomplete. They apply it to a large but partial dataset of breast tumor grading. Better agreement measures help hospitals know how much weight a grade deserves and where training or review is needed most.
plos-pone-0003025:
Eliana Marengo, Luciana de Moraes, Marcella Faria and co-authors gave a leprosy heat shock protein to lupus-prone mice in 2008. Heat shock proteins guide protein assembly and transport and are highly conserved across life. The Hsp60 family is expressed at high levels and interacts with the immune system.

The treatment used Hsp65 from Mycobacterium leprae, the leprosy bacterium. It interfered with the progression of murine lupus, an autoimmune disease, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, a bacterial protein calming autoimmunity is counterintuitive but fits the idea that immune tuning can treat immune excess.
plos-pone-0003125:
Jean-Michel Benoist, Ivanne Pincedé, Kay Ballantyne and colleagues address a basic problem in pain research in this 2008 PLOS ONE study. Many tests of pain response in rats use reaction time, the gap between the start of a stimulus such as heat and the animal's response. Yet skin cannot be heated at once by normal means, which makes that timing hard to read.

The authors work out what parts of the reaction come from the body surface and what parts come from the central nervous system. Readers get a careful approach to psychophysics in the rat. It helps others judge what a simple reaction time can and cannot prove.
plos-pone-0003225:
Ting-Hua Huang, Meng-Jin Zhu, Xin-Yun Li and colleagues catalogue pig microRNAs in muscle in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. MicroRNAs play critical roles in many important biological processes such as growth and development in mammals. In this study, the team identified hundreds of porcine microRNA candidates through computer prediction and analysed their expression in developing skeletal muscle using further methods.

Readers get both a discovery list and a developmental profile for pig muscle. Pigs are a major farm animal and a medical model, so their microRNA map has dual value. Muscle microRNAs may also guide breeding for meat traits.
plos-pone-0003325:
Alexander O. Vargas, Tiana Kohlsdorf, John F. Fallon and colleagues study digit identity in the bird wing in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Comparative morphology identifies the digits of the wing of birds as one, two and three, but they develop at embryological positions that become digits two, three and four in other amniotes. A hypothesis to explain this is that a homeotic frame shift of digital identity occurred in bird evolution.

The authors examine evolution of HoxD-11 expression in the bird wing, with insights from Alligator mississippiensis. Readers see gene expression used to test a classic anatomy puzzle. Alligators, as bird relatives, provide the comparison that makes the test possible.
plos-pone-0003425:
Liran I. Shlush and co-authors checked a claimed longevity marker in this 2008 study. Studies in northern Italy and Finland tied one mitochondrial DNA group to long life. That group, haplogroup J, appeared more often among people past one hundred. The team tested the claim in Ashkenazi Jewish centenarians.

Their long-lived group showed no extra share of haplogroup J. The marker's link to long life did not hold in this population. Negative results like this keep longevity genetics honest. A marker found in one group may mean little in another. Long life likely rests on many small factors rather than one marker.
plos-pone-0003525:
Boris Schmid, Can Keşmir, and Rob J. de Boer modeled HIV escape and human diversity in this 2008 paper. MHC class I molecules vary greatly between people. That variety lowers the chance a virus arrives pre-adapted to a new host. Still, HIV might dodge shared steps of antigen processing instead.

Processing parts like the proteasome and TAP are near-identical in everyone. The model shows MHC diversity blocks global adaptation anyway. An escape that works in one person fails in the next. Diversity thus caps how far the virus can evolve ahead.
plos-pone-0003625:
Joann Mudge, Neil A. Miller, Irina Khrebtukova, and colleagues published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It searches for the roots of schizophrenia, a serious mental illness that runs in families. The team used mRNA sequencing on brain tissue taken after death, focusing on the cerebellum.

By combining gene sequence data with other genetic evidence, the study found changed activity in genes for synaptic vesicle transport. Those vesicles are the tiny sacs that carry chemical messages between brain cells. The result points to faulty message handling as one part of how schizophrenia develops.
plos-pone-0003725:
Brian B. Gowen, Donald F. Smee, Min-Hui Wong, and colleagues published this drug study in PLOS ONE in 2008. A growing list of arenaviruses cause viral hemorrhagic fever, a severe illness with leaking blood vessels. Ribavirin is the only licensed drug for some of these infections, and it has limits.

The team tested the drug T-705 in an animal model, treating late stage disease. T-705 worked against the infection and showed reduced toxicity compared with ribavirin. The results suggest an alternative for infections that are usually treated only after they are already advanced.
plos-pone-0003825:
Tzvia Abramson, Hassya Kedem, and David A. Relman published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Bordetella pertussis is the bacterium behind whooping cough. One of its surface proteins, filamentous hemagglutinin, helps it attach to airway cells. The authors asked what that protein does to host immune signaling.

They report that filamentous hemagglutinin modulates the NF-kB pathway, a master switch of immune responses. Tuning that pathway can damp or redirect the host's defenses. The result shows one way the bacterium shapes its reception while it settles into the respiratory tract.
plos-pone-0003925:
Masashi Tachikawa modeled how changing conditions split species in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Living systems always face swings in their surroundings. Species evolve under those swings and often end up robust to them. Diversity in nature also grows through evolution under change.

The author asked how swings themselves shape that growth of diversity. His mathematical model of an ecosystem shows fluctuation driving evolutionary branching. In branching, one lineage splits into distinct forms over time. The model suggests changeable worlds may breed diversity faster than stable ones. It offers theory that field studies can test against real ecosystems.
plos-pone-0004025:
Abdullah Al Mahmud, Gabriele Amore, and Giorgio Bernardi studied genome makeup and gene control in sea urchins in 2008. Gene activity is usually credited to regulatory DNA regions alone. Those regions are built from modules of transcription factor binding sites. The authors questioned whether wider genome composition also matters.

Their PLOS ONE article reports compositional contexts affect gene control in embryos. The base makeup around a gene can sway its activity. That adds a background layer to the modular control picture. Sea urchin embryos give a clear system for testing such effects. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004125:
Carlos Driscoll and colleagues published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks where the extinct Caspian tiger came from and how it relates to the living Amur tiger. The Caspian tiger once lived in river forests across Central Asia, in a range cut off from other tigers. Hunters drove it to extinction by 1970.

Because it vanished before modern genetic tests existed, its place among the tiger subspecies stayed unclear for over a century. The team read mitochondrial DNA, passed down through mothers, to place it on the tiger family tree. The study settles a long taxonomic puzzle using samples from a tiger no longer alive.
plos-pone-0004225:
Stefan Maas and Willemijn Gommans published this RNA study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cells edit some RNA messages after they are written, changing single letters in the code. This A-to-I editing adds much of the variety in the mammalian transcriptome and can recode proteins, changing what they do.

The authors report a novel exon, a coding segment, in the mammalian ADAR2 gene, one of the genes for the editing enzymes themselves. The new segment extends the gene's open reading frame, the stretch that can be read as protein. Even the editors, it turns out, had an unread page in their own instructions.
plos-pone-0004325:
Chadi Touma and colleagues published this depression model study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, the stress hormone system, plays a key role in mood disorders such as major depression. Further hallmarks of depression include disturbed circadian rhythms in behaviour, hormones, and sleep.

The team studied mice selected for extremes in stress reactivity, bred to be high or low responders. They tracked behavioural, endocrine, and sleep changes resembling endophenotypes of major depression, traits that can be measured, which underlie the illness. Such mice offer a living model of the depressed body's daily rhythm gone wrong. The mice were bred to react strongly or weakly to stress.
plos-pone-0004425:
Wolbachia bacteria live inside many insects and can rig reproduction in their favor, a puzzle explored by Arnulf Koehncke, Arndt Telschow, John Werren, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. When an infected male mates with an uninfected female, her eggs often fail to hatch. Biologists call this cytoplasmic incompatibility, and it helps the bacteria spread through a host population.

From an evolution view, the trick raises a hard question: why would hosts not evolve ways to block it? The authors model the life and death of a creature they call an influential passenger. They trace how host genes that modify the effect can appear and spread. The result helps explain how a hidden microbe and its host shape each other's evolution over time.
plos-pone-0004525:
A drink of glucose can reveal early metabolic trouble in the body's chemical profile, show Suzan Wopereis, Carina Rubingh, Marjan van Erk, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Overweight is rising worldwide, and low-grade, long-term inflammation in overweight people is thought to help drive later disease. New tools are needed to see these processes early.

The team used metabolic profiling, a broad scan of small chemicals in the body, around an oral glucose tolerance test. In that test, a person drinks glucose and the response is tracked over time. The profiling detected subtle metabolic changes that standard measures can miss. Catching such changes early could flag people heading toward diabetes long before plain blood sugar readings turn abnormal.
plos-pone-0004625:
A toolkit for building glowing reporter genes in worms is presented by Baris Tursun, Luisa Cochella, Ines Carrera, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Reporters made from large genomic clones, held in fosmid vectors, let scientists visualize when and where a gene is active in a living animal.
