pmc-13276325:
Lee Sterling and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on end-of-life care for survivors of heart attack complicated by cardiogenic shock. In this condition the heart suddenly pumps too weakly to supply the body. Survivors often decline over months or years, yet their palliative care use was unstudied.

The team followed nearly thirty-nine hundred Ontario patients who left hospital and died during follow-up up to 2024. Median survival was about three years. More than half died in hospital, and most received palliative care only in their final year. Nearly half of palliative care began in the last two weeks of life. Patients whose palliative care started earlier were far less likely to die in hospital or in intensive care. The authors argue earlier referral could improve end-of-life outcomes for these survivors.
pmc-13281925:
Roben Ohev Shalom and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a skin germ that wrecked a heart. The patient was a seventy-two-year-old man with a two-flap aortic valve from birth. He came in after a faint and blood tests grew Staphylococcus epidermidis. That germ lives on skin and is usually tame. A surface heart scan showed a growth on his valve. A deeper throat scan told a worse story.

It found a burst pouch in the tissue between two valves and an abscess behind the valve ring. A large growth also sat on the second valve, with clot attached. Brain scans showed many small strokes from flown debris. Strong drugs could not turn his course, and surgery was ruled too risky. Care shifted to comfort, and he died. The authors say it is among the first such wrecks by this germ on a natural valve.
pmc-13282225:
William Q Rios and co-authors wrote a 2026 review on a master switch protein that controls energy use in cells. The protein, shortened to PGC-1α, helps build mitochondria, the cell's power plants, in tissues that burn much energy such as heart and muscle. It works by partnering with other proteins that switch genes on. Its own activity is tuned by chemical edits after it is made, including tags that add phosphate, sugar, or marker groups.

The review maps those partners and edits, and how they affect fat burning, sugar making in the liver, and heat production. It then surveys small drug-like molecules that raise or block the protein's activity. Early compounds show promise for metabolism disorders and cancer. A core hurdle is the protein's loose, shifting shape, which makes it hard to target with drugs.
pmc-13282425:
Martina Pecoraro and co-authors present a 2026 perspective on digital twin technology for prostate cancer care. A digital twin is a virtual model of a patient, updated with their clinical, imaging, molecular, and body data. Prostate cancer is the commonest cancer in men, yet care is tangled by varied disease behaviour and the risks of finding and treating harmless tumours. The authors explore how twins could personalise decisions.

A twin could simulate how the disease will progress and how a given treatment may work for that man. That would support proactive, adaptive care, adjusting plans as new data arrive. The piece maps what such systems would need: linked data, computing infrastructure, and clinical workflows built around them. Barriers include data quality, cost, and proof of benefit. The authors argue twins could cut overtreatment and use resources better, moving care toward a predictive and participatory model, if those hurdles are cleared.
pmc-13283325:
Gut gene switches governing phosphorus uptake differ sharply between two hen strains, Yosef A Abitew's mapping team shows in 2026. The small intestine lining is the main site where hens absorb phosphorus. Gene control there may reveal key drivers of phosphorus balance in poultry.

A total of 400 hens from two high-yield strains ate feed without added mineral phosphorus. Gene activity in gut lining was paired with genome data for mapping. More than one hundred control spots were found for small RNA genes. A similar count was found for standard protein-coding genes in the study. Strain patterns differed: one strain leaned on local control, the other on distant control. Key mineral genes were among the mapped targets.
pmc-13283425:
G F Habtar authored a 2026 case report of severe lung failure linked to vaping, treated with a lung support machine. Vaping is often sold as safer than smoking, yet lung injury cases keep rising. Worst cases progress to acute respiratory distress syndrome with failing oxygen levels.

The patient was a healthy 25-year-old woman with severe vaping-related lung injury. Standard breathing support by ventilator failed to keep her oxygen safe. A vein-to-vein ECMO circuit took over gas exchange for her lungs. She recovered with that advanced support in intensive care settings. The case stresses that vaping harm can be life-threatening in young adults. ECMO can save selected patients when other support fails.
pmc-13284825:
Jerry Chen and co-authors combine case reports with a narrative review, published in 2026, on invasive Klebsiella liver abscess syndrome in critical care. The syndrome forms a liver abscess without bile disease and can seed infection to many organs. Knowledge in the United States stays limited, so the team reviewed cases at Scripps Health from 2018 to 2024.

Six patients met the criteria. Most had diabetes, none had immune suppression as defined here, and all had drainage of the abscess. Half developed spread to distant sites, including lung, bladder, brain coverings, and the eye. Those patients tended to need intensive care more often. The review gives practical points on spotting spread early and managing very ill patients.
pmc-13285025:
Asimina Lazaridou and co-authors review digital tools for shoulder replacement surgery in a 2026 narrative review. Shoulder joint replacement has grown in technique and use, and new tech now spans the whole care path. The review covers 3D planning, navigation, custom guides, robots, mixed reality, phone health tools, wearables, remote rehab, smart implants, and AI.

Planning and guidance tools improved implant placement accuracy in some studies, yet proof of better long-term patient results stays thin, the authors report. Robots and mixed reality remain at early test stages. Remote rehab and wearable checks matched standard care in hip and knee work, with only pilot data in shoulders so far. The authors urge outcome trials.
pmc-13285825:
Philip M McCarthy and David E Burdette offer a 2026 guide to programming responsive neurostimulation for drug-resistant epilepsy. The implanted device watches brain signals and fires pulses when it spots patterns tied to seizures. Good results hinge on picking the right warning patterns and then tuning pulse settings step by step for each patient.

The guide sorts target signals into groups that come before, at the start of, and during a seizure. Early pulses aim to break up a seizure as it forms, while pulses at other times may slowly retrain the network. The authors lay out a staged path for raising and shaping stimulation while keeping side effects in check. Their frame links each setting choice to a clear goal, lasting gains in seizure control with less severity.
pmc-13285925:
Masayuki Ouchi and Chika Takehara study uneven eye length and lens results after cataract surgery in a 2026 comparative study. Modern formulas predict the needed lens power well, yet eyes that differ in length from their partner may break the pattern. The pair compared the longer and shorter eye of each patient against matched control eyes.

The study held 42 patients who had both eyes done, with a gap of at least half a millimeter between them. One month after surgery, the longer eye in each pair had drifted toward short sight more than its partner had. The same drift showed against control eyes of like length, under two standard lens formulas. The gap itself stayed tied to the error after other factors were counted, a caution for planning the second eye.
pmc-13286225:
Volker Grimm, Uta Berger, and Stefano Mammola lay out ten rules for journal supplements that actually help readers in a 2026 guidance article. Extra files meant to back a study often rot into a jumble of broken links, murky figures, and stray acronyms. Their rules push authors to give those files the same care as the main text they support.

Core advice favors one tidy, self-standing master file over a scatter of loose parts. Clear signposts should link each claim in the main text to its backing in the supplement, and files should stay readable by machines as well as people. Data belong in proper public stores, not buried in a supplement, the authors add. A shared template closes the list, offered so reviewers and readers learn where to find each kind of proof.
pmc-13286425:
Julian Diaz-Moreno and co-authors describe an adult gut illness that wore Crohn's disease as a disguise in a 2026 case report. A 26-year-old man arrived with sudden belly pain and bloody stools, plus a faint raised rash on his legs from two weeks prior. Scans showed a swollen final stretch of small bowel, the classic Crohn's address, and blood tests screamed inflammation.

The camera told a stranger story: the bowel lining looked purplish blue and bruised, with deep ulcers but a normal colon beyond. Skin and bowel biopsies both found small-vessel vasculitis stamped with IgA deposits, naming IgA vasculitis instead. Steroids settled pain and bleeding within four weeks, and follow-up imaging at three months showed the bowel healed. Spotting that bruised hue, the authors argue, steers doctors away from needless Crohn's therapy.
pmc-13287125:
Francisco Glerison da Silva Nascimento and colleagues trace how a seaweed lectin calms arthritic joints in rats in a 2026 pharmacology study. The protein, drawn from the red alga Hypnea cervicornis, had already shown anti-inflammatory effects linked to macrophage signals. Here the team provoked joint inflammation with zymosan, treated helper immune cells in dishes, and dosed animals intravenously, tracking pain sensitivity, swelling, and white cell traffic.

In dishes, the lectin cut nitric oxide and interleukin-1 released by provoked macrophages. In animals, a 3 milligram per kilogram dose blunted pain, swelling, and cell influx whether the trigger was zymosan, a bacterial peptide, or fluid from provoked macrophages. Rolling and sticking of white cells along vessel walls fell, and cartilage cells survived intact. The authors pin the effect on silencing macrophage nitric oxide and interleukin-1.
pmc-13287225:
Iris Dalia Vázquez-Vargas and co-authors conditioned rats in 2026 to fear a sound cue, then measured anxiety-like behaviour and brain cell shape in two nearby prefrontal areas. Conditioned animals were compared with controls in open and light-dark test boxes and in two stillness tests.

Fear-trained rats avoided the lit side, moved less, and froze more, while one form of stillness lengthened and another stayed unchanged. Brain measures moved in opposite directions by area: one region showed enlarged cell branching, the other showed shrinkage with fewer spines. The authors link the paired changes to how the brain balances holding and releasing learned fear.
pmc-13287325:
Mitsuru Otsuka and colleagues compared two scope techniques in 2026 for removing shallow tumours from the duodenum, the first stretch of small bowel. One method works under water and the other under a clear gel. Records covered 32 water cases and 49 gel cases.

Complete removal with clean edges was more common under gel, at 47.4% against 25.7% for water cases. Gel procedures also finished faster after injection, at four against six minutes. No delayed bleeding or tearing occurred in either group. Return of tumour at three years looked similar. Larger tumour size predicted incomplete removal in both groups, the authors report.
pmc-13288025:
Aicha Gomeh-Djame and co-authors carried out field surveys in 2026 in south-eastern Cameroon. Their subject was small forest bats of the genus Glauconycteris. The group is poorly held in collections and hard to sort by looks. Ten specimens from a national park and a reserve were measured and gene-tested, yielding eight species across three species groups.

Two species proved new to science, and one was recorded in Cameroon for the first time, lifting the genus total to fifteen species. A familiar name turned out to hide a species complex. Most species tolerate moderate habitat damage, and all Cameroon species live in or beside protected land. The authors urge more regional sampling.
pmc-13288725:
Zizhen Zhou and colleagues hunt sharper COVID-19 warning signs in blood in 2026. Standard clot markers sort severity poorly. The team profiled plasma by illness grade. Three grades were used. Proteins that rose with illness were clustered. Top picks were checked in a fresh group.

Clot and complement paths grew busier as illness worsened. Two proteins stood out. They are SERPINA1 and CD59. Both ran high in severe cases. They foretold death at thirty days and twelve months. They also foretold sepsis. A joint model did best of all. Both kept value after full checks. Fresh prospective checks are still needed.
pmc-13289025:
Suzanne van der Gaag and colleagues sketch a 2026 trial plan on prostate scans. The DARO-flare trial sits at one Dutch center. It deals with hormone-sensitive prostate cancer. A drug called darolutamide may boost scan signals. That boost is called a PSMA flare.

Men with few spread spots after past cure will join. Half will take the drug for seven days. Half will take it for 14 days. All will get scans at the start. Repeat scans will run on days 7 and 14. The main check is change in spot counts. Care changes and side effects will also be logged.
pmc-13289225:
Kirsty Gray, Farhana Ahad, and Aubrey Cunnington wrote a 2026 review of heart ultrasound use in children with Staphylococcus aureus in the blood. That blood infection can seed the heart lining, a condition called infective endocarditis, but heart disease is rare in children without known risk factors. The authors pulled records from six hospitals in North West London for 2018 to 2023.

Among 101 children aged 18 or younger, 71 had a transthoracic echocardiogram, a painless heart scan through the chest, and 30 did not. Heart infection was confirmed in four of the scanned children, all with clear risk factors such as heart defects or lines in veins. Hospital stays ran longer in the scanned group. The authors favor scanning by risk rather than scanning every child.
pmc-13289425: Bo Kim and Cara C Lewis are named on a short 2026 correction notice in Implementation Science Communications. The notice fixes only the competing interests statement of an earlier commentary on a paper by Austad and coauthors from 2025. No research data, methods, or findings are presented, so the record is genuinely thin beyond that single fix.
pmc-13289925:
N. Lyons and coauthors explored a 2026 set of provider views on trauma-informed care for partner violence inside HIV and sexually transmitted infection clinics in Trinidad and Tobago. Partner violence and HIV intertwine, creating complex needs that rushed, standard care often misses. Weekly structured consultations over seven weeks gathered 13 practitioners from five public clinics, including doctors, nurses, psychologists, social workers, and peer staff.

Talks mapped current practice and gaps against national protocols and four trauma-informed principles, from grasping trauma impact to avoiding new harm. Five entry points for better care were weighed, from awareness to referral. Missing standard protocols, thin documentation, privacy worries, split referrals, and dual stigma blocked steady care.
pmc-13290525:
Long-read sequencing could catch what short reads miss in blood-based cancer tests, Grace Guzman and Analiz Rodriguez argue in a 2026 mini-review. Liquid biopsy reads tumor material shed into body fluids, but the standard short-read approach struggles with structural variants, phasing, fusion transcripts, and methylation marks.

The authors survey studies applying long-read platforms, including single-molecule real-time and nanopore sequencing, to cell-free and circulating tumor DNA. Work is most active in lung, brain, and pediatric cancers, where long reads have surfaced structural changes, methylation patterns, and tumor-of-origin signals beyond short-read reach. Barriers remain: variable sample handling, cost, and heavy computing demands. Guzman and Rodriguez expect long reads to join multimodal liquid biopsy panels rather than replace them.
pmc-13290725:
Patients with primary biliary cholangitis carry a poorer, shifted gut microbiome, Ren Qianlang and colleagues conclude in a systematic review and meta-analysis from 2026. The chronic autoimmune liver disease has been tied to gut imbalance, but small, inconsistent studies left the overall picture fuzzy.

Searching four databases, the team pooled 10 studies covering 1,057 people, 607 patients and 450 controls. Diversity ran lower in patients on the Shannon index and species counts, and most studies also found the overall community composition clearly separated from healthy controls. Certain genera, including Neisseria, Klebsiella, and Streptococcus, were enriched, while Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium were depleted. Age, region, and sequencing platform did not explain the differences between studies. The authors say the consolidated pattern strengthens the case for gut involvement in the disease.
pmc-13290825:
Cannabis, tobacco, and especially both together raise infection risk after carpal tunnel surgery, Amir Human Hoveidaei and colleagues find in a U.S. study from 2026. Using a large claims database for 2010 to 2022, they compared wrist surgery outcomes across cannabis-only, tobacco-only, combined, and non-user groups.

Group sizes were lopsided: 800 cannabis-only patients and 3,529 combined users against 167,803 tobacco-only patients and matched controls. Infection at the surgical site ran higher in every user group at six weeks and three months. Wound disruption clustered in combined and tobacco-only users but not cannabis-only users, complex regional pain syndrome tracked only with tobacco, and stiffness showed no link to any use. Hoveidaei and colleagues urge screening and counseling before surgery about these risks.
pmc-13291025:
Painful urination after prostate laser surgery is counted week by week in a 2026 prospective cohort study led by Oswaldo Oliveira Neto. Laser enucleation removes prostate tissue through the urethra, and burning pain afterward is common, yet how long it lasts and who gets it worst had not been mapped well.

Among 108 patients treated with holmium or pulsed thulium lasers, moderate-to-severe pain hit about three quarters at week one on the team’s rating scale. By week four the share had fallen below one third, and by six months almost no one still reported it. Younger age stood out as a predictor of early pain, with diabetes and clot retention also linked in the first phase after surgery.
pmc-13291225:
How well do classic life quality tools work in schizophrenia care? Max Wiessner leads a 2026 review of three interview-based scales. Good tools are vital to judge if care helps. The review used strict world standards for rating health measures.

Searches found 19 studies across the three scales. Most test results proved weak or unclear. Key checks, such as content validity, were missing for all three. Each scale landed in a middle class with promise but gaps. Newer scales were built with more modern methods. The authors suggest testing those newer tools first. That path may serve patients better than more work on old scales.
pmc-13291325:
City haze makes heat islands worse, but cool roofs can help. Minghao Dong leads a 2026 study of passive daytime cooling under haze. Such coolers shed heat to the sky without power. Dirty air changes how well they work.

Dust and soot scatter sunlight and heat rays apart. That split shifts what a good cooler should do. Heat emission in the sky window matters most. Cutting sun uptake matters less than once thought. The team tuned a clear film’s thickness for haze. Thick films won under haze, thin ones under clear skies. Tests backed the model’s odd prediction. Haze-ready designs can cool cities with no energy use.
pmc-13292325:
Simon Herbel, Guillaume Dumas, and Tomas Urbina defend a 2026 exchange about whether daptomycin still belongs in treating Enterococcus faecium bloodstream infections in intensive care. Their earlier study found more treatment failures on daptomycin than on alternative regimens, and two commentators raised microbiology and combination-therapy points. The letter answers while conceding a key gap in their own data.

Among eight failures on daptomycin, baseline drug levels existed for only four patients, and nobody rechecked sensitivity at relapse or during lingering bacteremia. The authors agree failure should trigger repeat MIC testing, since resistance can emerge on therapy, sometimes through LiaFSR pathway mutations. They also note that heavy protein binding and fluid shifts in critical illness can dilute the drug. The exchange leaves daptomycin's role unsettled pending better monitoring.
pmc-13293425:
Adding one bacterial type to larval water is the change Camden M. Dezse and colleagues tested in a 2026 study of adult male Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. Males are mass-reared for release programs that suppress wild mosquito numbers, so adult quality matters greatly.

Of three bacterial isolates tried in normal rearing water, one, a Cedecea species, slowed the shift to pupae and gave adult males with shorter wings and shorter lives. The other isolates did not show that harm. Small shifts in larval microbes can thus echo through adult life. Rearing centers may need to watch water microbes closely to keep release males fit.
pmc-13293625:
Tomoyasu Kashiwagi and colleagues report, in a 2026 surgical case, a strangulated small bowel blockage tangled with a major pelvic artery after lymph node surgery. A 77-year-old man arrived with severe belly pain after earlier bladder surgery.

Scans showed a closed loop of bowel with suspected blood cutoff near the right external iliac artery. At emergency surgery, dead bowel filled the right pelvis, and gentle freeing failed. Surgeons cut within the dead segment first to ease tension and see clearly, then found the artery as the pinching structure. About 230 centimeters of bowel were removed, the artery was saved, and recovery was smooth.
pmc-13293725:
Wenwen Liang and colleagues model, in a 2026 study, what predicts recovery from depression after stroke, a common and harmful complication. Mood after stroke swings between recovery and relapse, yet what drives each shift was unclear.

A time-based model followed 536 patients with blocked-artery stroke across 1441 check-ins, sorting them into no, mild, and severe depression states. Moves from mild depression back to none were 5.5 times more likely than moves to severe states, a ratio the authors report. Schooling of ten years or more cut worsening risk, while independence and social support favored recovery. Severe spells looked brief, though missing death data cloud that finding.
pmc-13293825:
Led by Milena Wojciechowska, a 2026 study asks which mental traits shape daily life for people living with asthma. Patients were compared with healthy controls. The team used scales for functioning in chronic illness, asthma control, self-esteem, illness acceptance, and depression, then tested which factors predicted how well patients coped.

Overall functioning in the asthma group was moderate. Acceptance of illness and self-esteem were the strongest predictors, mainly for emotional and social life. Weaker mental resources and more depressive symptoms went with poorer functioning. Poor asthma control also tended to track with worse daily functioning, which argues for routine mental health checks in asthma care.
pmc-13293925:
Qian Li and a large team build a deep learning tool in 2026 to predict heavy lymph node spread in esophageal squamous cell cancer before surgery. Standard CT rules based on node size miss many cases. Their model first learned from 3,200 unlabeled chest scans, then trained on tumor volumes from 1,060 patients across two centers with later and outside test groups.

Accuracy held up well across checks, with area values of 0.881 inside, 0.860 over time, and 0.860 externally. In the outside group, sensitivity beat a guideline-style comparator while specificity also rose. Better calibration adds trust. Such prediction could sharpen staging and treatment choices before an operation.
pmc-13294325:
Sílvia Rocha and coauthors review fat tissue growth and remodeling in a 2026 article on obesity targets. Making new fat cells, called adipogenesis, follows gene cascades led by PPAR gamma and C/EBP proteins, tuned by Wnt, bone morphogenetic protein, and insulin signals. Healthy expansion stores fat safely and renews tissue.

In obesity, excess nutrients and hormone shifts stall healthy cell creation. Existing cells swell instead, oxygen drops, inflammation lingers, and fat spills into organs, driving insulin resistance and heart-metabolic disease. Guiding growth toward fresh, well-behaved fat cells rather than swollen ones is framed as a promising route to restore balance.
pmc-13295925:
Takayuki Ando and co-authors examine, in 2026, why people with several chronic conditions end up attending many clinics in Japan, a pattern called polydoctoring. Using nationwide claims data, they track what changes when a new condition appears in the same person.

Nearly 4.7 million adults were followed, and every new condition added clinic ties, but by very different amounts. Cancer raised the count most, followed by osteoporosis and arthritis, while effects shrank among the oldest patients and those already carrying many conditions. The authors say care coordination should be tailored by condition, not one-size-fits-all.
pmc-13296225:
Jessica Hui and colleagues review, in 2026, breast findings spotted by chance on chest scans at their institution over two years. They track how often such findings appear in women over forty, what radiologists recommend and what follow-up actually happens.

Findings turned up in about one in seven scans, and dedicated breast imaging was advised in a small share of cases. Where workup happened, most results were harmless and only four cancers emerged. Wording mattered: firm recommendations led to follow-up far more often than optional phrasing. The authors call for standard reporting and follow-up rules.
pmc-13297725: Denis Bignotti and his co-authors issued a short fix to their 2026 case series on Class II bite care with bar devices and clear aligners. The fix adds a thanks section that was left out of the first print run. It thanks the Centro Ortodontico Vicentino and its head, Leonella Caliari, for their help, skill, and support through the work. The authors state the science in the paper stands as it was, and an editor signed off on the change.
pmc-13297925:
A heart scan lit up the stomach and thyroid gland but left the bones dark. That odd spread told Hiroyuki Tokue and his team the tracer dose was faulty, not the patient. Their 2026 case report tells of a 75-year-old woman with kidney disease and a slow heart rhythm, scanned for feared amyloid in the heart.

The dye left no real mark in heart muscle. Its pattern matched free pertechnetate loose in the body, a sign of a mixing or dosing slip with the technetium dose. A fresh scan 1.5 months later spread through bone as it should. It again showed no amyloid. The team warns that scans with this pattern must be read as failed tests, not as clean bills of health.
pmc-13298225:
Every day's coffee habit leaves mountains of grounds behind, and Sreehitha Pilli with colleagues review how to turn that waste into products in a 2026 article. Spent coffee grounds, produced in millions of tonnes yearly, still hold caffeine, fiber, antioxidants, proteins, and oils worth recovering.

The review surveys pretreatment, green extraction, and bioconversion routes feeding food, nutraceutical, bioenergy, and packaging uses, with multi-product biorefineries as the goal. Scaling up remains hard: the grounds vary in composition, processing eats energy, and safety testing lags behind enthusiasm. The authors call for standardized characterization, pilot-scale trials, and AI-assisted process tuning to make commercial upcycling realistic.
pmc-13298525:
Small flesh-colored bumps on a young man's penis turned out to be a benign nerve tumor, describe Phatcharawat Chirasuthat and colleagues in a 2026 case report. The 23-year-old had three firm papules on the glans that grew slowly over three years, mildly itchy but causing no urinary or sexual symptoms.

Removal and microscopy showed a neatly bounded dermal nodule of spindle cells in interlacing bundles, and staining confirmed Schwann cell origin with S-100 positivity. The diagnosis was palisaded encapsulated neuroma, a harmless growth with no known risk of turning malignant. The authors note that complete excision both settles the diagnosis and cures the lesion, with no recurrence expected.
pmc-13302725:
Routine protein levels sketch a COVID-19 patient's road ahead, Rauno Joks and colleagues report in a 2026 chart review. Of 569 adults hospitalized with COVID-19 pneumonia, sixty had the full laboratory and immune data the analysis required. Albumin, globulin, and their ratio were tested against comorbidity burden, predicted ten-year survival, severity scores, and length of stay.

Low albumin and a low albumin-to-globulin ratio each tracked with heavier comorbidity, lower predicted survival, and longer hospitalization, independent of other factors. Falling total protein meant higher severity scores. Globulin alone predicted nothing. The authors propose these cheap, standard tests as aids for sorting patients by likely course and recovery.
pmc-13303925:
Mohammad Hussein Mustafa and colleagues map research on artificial intelligence for hospital infection work in a 2026 scoping review. Software has been proposed to spot infections, sort patient risk, and guide antibiotic choices, but strong proof of patient benefit remains unclear.

Six databases were searched under standard scoping guidance, and 39 studies qualified from hundreds screened. Nearly all work built or tested models on past data, with no randomized trials and few fair tests under everyday ward conditions. Surgical wound and urinary infections drew most attention. The authors warn against reading lab accuracy as proof of clinical value.
pmc-13304125:
Kasim Akay leads a 2026 study testing whether a simple blood ratio can flag hidden spread in womb cancer. Cancer cells entering nearby lymph or blood vessel spaces worsen outlook, yet the sign appears only after surgery.

Records for 156 patients with endometrioid womb cancer treated by standard staging surgery were reviewed. Three inflammation ratios drawn from routine blood counts were kept as plain numbers rather than cut points. The platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio predicted vessel space invasion on its own, while tumor width predicted it even more strongly. A chart tool built from the model may guide surgical planning.
pmc-13304525:
Linhan Li and co-authors design cheek-sticking tablets that release a pain drug in two phases in a 2026 pharmacy study. Indomethacin dissolves poorly, breaks down in stomach acid, and needs both fast relief and lasting cover.

A freeze-dried dispersion raised the drug's dissolving speed many times over the plain powder. Two-layer tablets pressed from powders were tuned for grip and release. The best version freed a large share within twenty minutes, then kept releasing across eight hours while clinging inside the cheek for about as long. Polymer gel behavior and tablet wear govern the balance struck.
pmc-13304925:
Lisa Khairil leads a 2026 narrative review questioning whether artificial intelligence has truly improved drug discovery outcomes. Investment passed one hundred billion dollars in recent years, yet roughly nine in ten drug candidates still fail after entering human testing.

Star tools predict protein shapes with near-lab accuracy, but they falter on protein motion, chemical tags, and drug binding detail. Case studies show faster early work without matching gains in late-stage success. Weak repeatability, hidden data, and patchy regulation add risk. Stronger proof standards and shared data are urged before hype becomes trust.
pmc-13305325:
Alessandro Di Minno leads a 2026 randomized trial of a mixed-fiber blend for adults with functional constipation. Laxatives are standard care but do not suit everyone, and pairing fibers from several food sources might work better than one alone.

Fifty-four adults took two sachets daily of the blend or a placebo for 28 days in a blinded design. The blend mixed wheat dextrin, fruit pectin, citrus fibers, and oat fibers. Bowel movements rose clearly by week four, and stool form returned to normal from week two. Bloating, swelling, heaviness, and gas all eased, with no side effects reported.
pmc-13307025:
Liang Qi proposed confusing aircraft radar-cancelling systems with two separated jammers in a 2026 study. Random phase jumps between the pair swing the combined wavefront direction fast, breaking the steady null such systems track.

Simulations cut the average cancellation ratio from 26.80 dB to 20.29 dB, a drop of 6.51 dB in reported figures. Timing and phase errors between the jammers barely dented the effect in the same runs. The authors present the scheme as a lean way to gain direction agility without precise transmission control. Two linked sources are enough, which keeps cost and set up work low in use.
pmc-13307725:
Giulia Congedo and co-authors survey in 2026 what staff at an Italian university hospital know and feel about the pneumococcal vaccine, which guards older and at risk adults. Their survey ran from February to June 2024 and drew both health workers and office staff at the Gemelli hospital.

Cover was low in both groups, at 20 percent for health staff and 19 percent for office staff in the survey. Health staff knew more, while office staff showed more doubt and less awareness of the vaccine. Both groups favoured shots given at work and asked for clear teaching sessions. Doctors trusted the vaccine most, and they also advised family to take it far more often.
pmc-13307825:
Domenico Antonio Restivo and co-authors present in 2026 three cases of laryngeal adductor breathing dystonia, a rare nerve driven spasm that narrows the voice box during breathing in. Unlike the better known voice form, this form leaves speech mostly intact and instead blocks airflow, which can mimic other throat block causes.

All three cases mixed the usual throat signs with spasms in nearby head districts, which widens the known range of the condition. Standard retraining, speech work, and most drugs help little in true cases of this kind. Botulinum toxin shots into the throat muscles eased the harsh breathing noise in chosen patients, so exact typing of each case guides who should get that targeted care.
pmc-13308225:
Alvin E Lirio and co-authors run in 2026 the first gene study of asthma in a Filipino group, testing known variants in mothers from the Cebu survey cohort. Among 1678 unrelated mothers, 129 told of asthma, and 27 variants drawn from large global studies were checked one by one and as a joint score.

One variant in the SMAD3 gene passed the strict bar, with an odds ratio of 1.80 for asthma in this group. The joint score also tracked with higher odds, though the gain per step was small in size. Small numbers barred a full genome scan, so the authors call for more cohorts in groups that gene studies have long skipped over.
pmc-13308725:
Chenyang Huang and co-authors test in 2026 whether a lower oestrogen dose can hold pregnancy rates in hormone primed frozen embryo transfer cycles. Records from 2022 to mid 2025 split 1955 high dose cycles from 202 low dose cycles, all with one blastocyst moved per cycle.

Raw rates favoured the low dose group, yet the groups differed in age and egg reserve at the start of care. After matching and model fixes, the gap shrank and lost firm standing in the final checks. Early loss rates also matched between groups. A gentler dose may suit younger women, yet forward trials must prove the trade is safe and fair.
pmc-13309525:
Shinji Futami and co-authors study harmful self-directed antibodies in a rare lung disease in a 2026 article. In autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, antibodies attack a signal the lungs need to clear fatty material, yet total antibody amount does not match how sick patients are. The team asked whether the exact target spot and grip strength matter more.

From 28 patients, 186 antibodies were sorted by which spot on the signal they bind. For one binding class, tighter grip meant stronger blocking, and patients with more of these antibodies were sicker. High-grip antibodies of that class alone caused disease signs in engineered mice. The authors say target spot plus grip, not amount alone, drives harm.
pmc-13311125:
Carolynn Hare and colleagues test whether autistic and ADHD traits shape how senses combine in a 2026 study. Both conditions show sense processing differences, and they often co-occur, yet joint trait effects were unclear. A broad university sample did a fast detection task that measures gain from paired sights and sounds.

Ninety two young adults took part, with a mean age near 18 years old at testing. Trait scores showed no link to accuracy gain from paired senses. No added or joint effect of the two trait sets appeared either. When base sense sharpness is held equal, trait level alone may not drive sense combining in young adults.
pmc-13311725:
Henry Badji and co-authors lay out protocols in a 2026 article for using genome sequencing to trace gut bacteria that cause diarrhea across Africa. The GETCampy-Africa study sits inside a One Health frame.

Standard lab work shows where these germs are but cannot resolve fine strain differences, drug resistance, or spread paths. The study uses a case-control design across several countries, sampling people, animals, and the environment. Genome data will pin down which sources feed human illness and how strains move. The protocols give other teams a shared method for high-resolution gut germ tracking.
pmc-13311925:
Seungyoon Roh and co-authors in 2026 present a study on how three Toll-like receptor paths shape the inflammatory output of chicken macrophages. The cytokine IL-1 beta sits at the center of the network.

The team stimulated a chicken macrophage cell line and blood-derived macrophages through the TLR2, TLR3, and TLR4 routes. Responses differed sharply by route, with the virus-mimic route raising IL-1 beta, IL-18, and interferon beta, while the bacterial wall route answered weakly. A gene-edited line lacking IL-1 beta let the team test how the cytokine steers each route's output. The work fills a gap in bird immunology with disease-control value.
pmc-13312025:
Peishuang He and colleagues use computer models and multi-omics data in a 2027 study to explain why retinol speeds cell growth at low doses yet harms cells at high ones. Retinol is a common anti-aging ingredient in skin products, but the switch behind this two-way behavior was unclear.

Working with human foreskin fibroblasts, the team combined gene, protein, and metabolite data with a genome-scale metabolic model. Low doses switched on retinoic acid signaling and rerouted cell chemistry in ways that favor growth. High doses instead brought oxidative stress, a build-up of harmful intermediates, and signs of ferroptosis, a form of cell death. The authors name control points such as DHRS3 and GCLM that could guide safer retinol products.
pmc-13312825:
Azadeh Rakhshan and colleagues present a 2026 case report of ossifying fasciitis in a man's hand, a benign growth notorious for impersonating cancer. The lesion mixes spindle-cell growth with stray bone formation and grows fast enough, with dense imaging, to be mistaken for a sarcoma. While it usually appears on the trunk or upper limbs, the hand is an exceptionally rare site.

Their patient, aged 34, developed a painless lump on the palm of his right hand over two months, sitting beside a flexor tendon on scans. Under the microscope the removed mass showed fibroblasts in bundles within loose stroma, bone rimmed by osteoblasts, and scattered giant cells, with no malignant features. Marker tests confirmed the diagnosis. The authors stress that knowing this entity, and matching tissue, imaging, and clinical clues, spares patients needless radical surgery.
pmc-13313525:
Luana Figueiredo and Makeda Smith host a conversation piece, published in 2026, on how Canada should think about national and human security. Experts in defense studies, foreign policy, law, and human rights weigh the costs of guarding sovereignty. They also weigh the weakness of shared alliances in a shifting world.

The piece weighs the risk of American indifference or hostility. It notes a turn toward ad hoc coalitions, whole-society defense models, and strength at home. It also shows how border rules and selective law use can repeat racialized harm and wear down humane norms. The authors argue that Canada cannot outsource its safety or rest it on arms alone. Real security must rest on justice, equity, and human rights. Guarding the state means little if people inside it are not safe and free.
pmc-13314425:
Qingping Zhang leads a 2026 study of whether living high on a plateau dulls hearing. Long-term life at altitude has been floated as a factor in hearing, but proof from people who live high for years was limited.

The study drew 187 plateau residents aged 50 years or less at a Qinghai hospital health check. They were split by home altitude into three groups. The low group held 79 people at 2200 to 2499 meters. The middle group held 51 at 2500 to 3499 meters, and the high group held 57 at 3500 meters or more, by the report counts. Hearing was tested at six tones from 250 Hz to 8 kHz in both ears, with averages for low and high tones too. Early results showed the clearest group gaps at the high tones. The work weighs altitude as a quiet risk for the ears of plateau peoples.
pmc-13314625:
Ângela Alves, Rita Pombinho, and Didier Cabanes review how single-cell methods expose variety in bacterial virulence, in a 2026 paper. Cloned bacteria do not act as one uniform mass; during infection they split into unlike states across place and time.

That spread springs from random gene firing, shifting surroundings, gene change, and cell aging, the authors write. Tricks such as two-state switches, phase variation, dormant persistence, quorum sensing, and memory of past states let cells hedge bets and share labor. Groups gain fitness and staying power in hostile hosts by mixing bold and quiet members. Single-cell tools can now decode this patchwork gene by gene. Grasping it may explain why infections flare or linger and where new drugs could strike.
pmc-13315325:
C Parisi and a large oncology team report in 2026 on sex differences in side effects from new antibody-drug conjugates for lung cancer. Patients with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer got these drugs in early-phase trials at Gustave Roussy between 2018 and 2023, targeting proteins such as TROP2, HER2, and others.

Among 132 patients, about half women, three quarters had side effects of grade 2 or worse. Women had more such effects than men, with 82.8 percent affected versus 69.1 percent for men, and a higher median count of effects. Metabolic problems such as appetite loss and weight loss were also more common in women.
pmc-13316225:
Yi Lin sets out in 2026 a perspective on plant embodied intelligence, the idea that adaptive problem solving in plants emerges from the interplay of their spread-out structures with the environment. Intelligence is increasingly discussed beyond brains and nerves, and this branch of the idea was still undeveloped.

The review lays foundations and research paths, from shape change and growth to distributed memory, ecological signaling, swarm-like behavior, and decisions under risk. Global work spans plant neurobiology, systems biology, and bio-inspired materials. Mixing careful measurement, molecular tools, ecology models, and plant-inspired robots could advance both plant and intelligent systems science.
pmc-13316625:
Tristan N Samuels and colleagues built a 2026 human cell model for a rare inherited disease caused by faulty copies of NARS1, a gene needed to charge transfer RNA with asparagine. The illness strikes infants and children, hits the nervous system, and has no targeted treatment.

Two dominant faulty copies made cells sicken and switch on a stress program. Adding plain asparagine fully restored growth in patient skin cells and shut the stress signal off, a rescue the team also saw across protein patterns. A matching transfer RNA therapy and a stress-blocking drug each helped only in part. The simple nutrient result points to a low-cost treatment lead worth clinical testing.
pmc-13318725:
Ziyan Lyu and colleagues present a 2026 expert consensus on running combined cardio-oncology clinics. These clinics pair cardiologists with clinical pharmacists. Their shared task is safe, rational drug use in cancer patients. Heart damage from anticancer drugs is a leading cause of death in this group.

No established management systems existed for such joint clinics. Sichuan Provincial People's Hospital therefore led the effort, sponsored by the Clinical Pharmacy Branch. That hospital opened its combined clinic in March 2022. The consensus responds to national policy promoting pharmacist-led services and medication counselling. It aims to standardise workflows and pharmaceutical care for cardio-oncology patients. Single-discipline care, the authors argue, cannot meet these complex needs alone.
pmc-13319925:
Erik Stuchlý and co-authors test how people guess the choices of others in a 2026 study of mental copying. When we forecast what a friend will pick, we may run our own choice process in our head as a stand in. If that inner process is skewed, the forecast should skew too, a claim the team tested by first bending risk tastes.

People were tuned to high or low chance settings, which shifted their own risk values, then asked to forecast picks by three stock figures with set risk styles. Their forecasts shifted for the average and risk shy figures but not for the risk seeking one. Own risk lean also tracked forecasts for the first two figures only. Copying seems real, but who the other person is sets its limits.
pmc-13320325:
Ben-Jian Zhong and co-authors name three new mushroom species from subtropical China in a 2026 taxonomy study. The trio belongs to a brittlegill group known for mild taste and varied cap colors, sorted here by both looks and gene proof. Field finds from the region were checked spore by spore and joined to gene trees built from four gene zones.

One new species wears a dark ruby grey cap with tight gills and flesh that stays white when bruised. The second wears a pale pink white cap and a stem that yellows with age or bruising. The third shifts from red grey to purple brown and its flesh browns when bruised. Gene trees back all three as fresh branches, and full accounts with photos fix their names for future finds.
pmc-13320425:
Yuan-Qing Luo and co-authors turn roasted sesame hulls into a flavor boost for sesame oil in a 2026 food study. Hulls are a thrown away part of the seed, yet roasting loads them with prized scent compounds. Soaking hulls in plain oil was tuned to draw that scent across while also testing whether the hull goods slow oil spoilage in storage.

The best soak used one part hull to five parts oil at mild heat for eight hours, in the trials reported. That oil gained balanced caramel, roast, and nut notes from hull aromatics. In fast aged storage its spoilage marks first rose faster, then after forty days climbed far more slowly than plain oil, and off scent build up stayed lower. Waste hulls thus serve twice, as flavor and as guard.
pmc-13320825:
Bo Pan leads a large expert group setting out a staging system for children's heart function in a 2026 guidance article. Heart failure in children is rising worldwide, and the group, from the Pediatrics Society of the Chinese Medical Association, wants care to start earlier in the disease course. The system applies to all children, not only those already ill.

Three stages are defined, from full heart function through early dysfunction to outright failure. For each stage, the article sets out how to recognise it and how to manage it, forming a full care pathway. The stated aim is to make childhood heart failure more preventable and treatable and to cut its long term burden.
pmc-13321225:
Alshaimaa Tarek and colleagues report a rare artery disease found before birth in a 2026 case report from Egypt. Generalized arterial calcification of infancy hardens and narrows large arteries very early in life, often causing breathing distress, heart failure, and high blood pressure. About 300 cases have been reported worldwide.

At 29 weeks of pregnancy, ultrasound showed valve narrowing, thickened heart walls, and heavy calcium in the aorta and ductal arch of the fetus. Gene testing found a homozygous harmful change in the ENPP1 gene, written as c.749C>T in the report. The authors call it the first gene confirmed Egyptian fetal case and stress expert heart scanning plus gene tests for counselling.
pmc-13322625:
Taynara Gabriele Ribeiro Piano and co-authors test selenium and tellurium compounds against gut worms of farm animals in a 2026 laboratory study. Roundworm infections harm ruminant health, and heavy dewormer use breeds resistant parasites. Three compounds were tested on worm eggs and larvae from sheep and cattle, with cell safety checks alongside.

One selenium compound, diphenyl diselenide, stopped egg hatching best, while the tellurium compound AS-101 killed larvae best in the assays. Pairing the selenium compound with ivermectin gave a mild joint boost. That selenium compound was also gentlest on kidney cells in culture. The results mark a possible new family of worm treatments for livestock.
pmc-13322825:
Haoyu Wen, Weiwei Chen and Yuquan He explain how blood vessel walls harden with calcium, in a 2026 review of vascular calcification. The process is now seen as active, driven by smooth muscle cells in the vessel wall rather than simple mineral build-up.

Under strain from calcium and phosphate imbalance, sugar and fat toxicity, oxidative stress and long-term inflammation, those cells switch toward a bone-like state. They release tiny vesicles, break down surrounding matrix and switch on growth signals such as Wnt and BMP pathways. Other cell changes add to the effect. The authors discuss treatment ideas that target metabolic control points, block the cell switch, or alter gene regulation.
pmc-13323025:
Matteo Ricchi and a large team develop a counting method for Salmonella Infantis in poultry faeces, reported in 2026. This serovar dominates broiler production in the European Union and often colonises birds without signs, letting resistant strains spread quietly into meat.

Their method adapts a miniaturised most-probable-number approach and confirms results with a specific qPCR test. Performance checks used spiked and naturally contaminated samples, with matrix effects judged by Bland-Altman analysis and repeat testing across runs and operators. Applied to real samples, the method quantified bacterial loads well enough for risk assessment work. The authors present it as a monitoring tool for flock-level control in Italy and beyond.
pmc-13323125:
Huixian Xie and co-authors test a structured weight programme for psychiatric inpatients, in a 2026 study at Taizhou Second People's Hospital. Their 5-4-3 model joins five fields, four phases and three supports in one loop. Psychiatry, nursing, nutrition, rehab and pharmacy staff lead it jointly.

Inpatients with a body mass index of 24 or higher joined between November 2024 and April 2025. Care ran through stays of one to six months. A three-month follow-up came after discharge. Outcomes covered weight, body mass index and metabolic measures. They also covered patient knowledge and staff practice. Weight after discharge came mainly from self-report, which the authors flag as a bias risk.
pmc-13323325:
Rodolfo G Gatto, Hossam Youssef and Yuen Gao introduce a collection on imaging biomarkers for TDP-43 and tau protein diseases, in a 2026 editorial. The two abnormal proteins recur across many degenerative brain disorders and increasingly look like partners rather than separate problems.

Tau tangles and TDP-43 clumps can drive each other's build-up, harm synapses and disturb RNA handling, jointly speeding neuron loss in the editors' framing. Structural MRI shows shrinkage patterns while PET imaging traces molecular pathology in living brain. Featured work adds further clinical dimensions beyond classic symptoms. The editors argue that imaging both proteins together is key to earlier and sharper diagnosis of these mixed diseases.
pmc-13325125:
Soroush Torkamannejad, Hoi-ying Yip, and Bingyun Sun count heart ion channel proteins directly in a 2026 proteomics study. These large membrane channels set the heartbeat rhythm, and faulty levels can trigger dangerous arrhythmias.

Targeted parallel reaction monitoring with an in-sample calibration method measured copy numbers in human ventricle tissue. Extended digestion of the tough tissue fraction exposed proteins that broad surveys miss. The team quantified the main subunits Nav1.5, hERG, and Cav1.2, plus the helpers Cavβ1 and Cavα2δ1. Copy numbers let labs compare channel counts across studies and hearts on the same scale. The method should extend to systematic surveys of these hard-to-measure proteins.
pmc-13325625:
Daniele Midori Kakimoto Higa and colleagues review anesthesia for balloon heart valve repair in dogs in a 2026 retrospective study. Balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty eases severe pulmonic stenosis, but the strained heart makes anesthesia risky.

Records covered 21 dogs treated in 2024 and 2025, with a median age of 18 months. French Bulldogs made up 33.3 percent of cases, and fainting was the top sign at 42.9 percent of the dogs. Induction leaned on etomidate and midazolam in 95 percent of procedures. Low blood pressure struck 66.7 percent of dogs during surgery and often needed drug support. The balloon cut the valve gradient in 90 percent of cases.
pmc-13326425:
Fatima Gul and colleagues relate blood branched-chain amino acids to body fat in visceral obesity in a 2026 study. Belly fat ties closely to insulin resistance, yet the place of these amino acids in that link is unsettled.

The study enrolled 105 people: 52 with obesity alone, 32 with obesity plus type 2 diabetes, and 21 healthy controls. Amino acid levels ran higher in both obesity groups, with valine up most, at 43.46 micrograms per mL in the diabetes group against 30.48 in controls. Levels tracked with visceral fat area, waist size, and insulin resistance scores. Valine showed the tightest links and stayed tied to waist size in joint models.
pmc-13327025:
Yunwei Long and colleagues report a 2026 surgical series for Kümmell's disease, where a spinal bone collapses weeks after injury and bends the back. Common cement procedures often fail in late stages, so the team tested short-segment fixation paired with a leverage method to straighten the spine.

Records covered 22 patients treated from 2020 to 2023, with pain scores, nerve function grades, and spinal measurements compared before and after surgery. Operations averaged about 100 minutes with modest blood loss, pain eased, and restored bone height reached 83 percent of expected values on average, alongside a mean angle correction of 19.32 degrees across the group. Nerve grades also improved, supporting the combined approach for advanced cases.
pmc-13328025:
Krystyna Kowalczuk and colleagues measure skipped nursing care across three countries in a 2026 survey. Care rationing, leaving needed tasks undone, lowers quality and raises error risk. Between March 2024 and March 2025, 610 hospital nurses in the Czech Republic, Poland, and Slovakia rated how often 32 nursing activities were omitted.

Age, family status, schooling, and years on the job showed no clear link to overall rationing levels, which differed only slightly between hospitals. Ward type mattered far more: emergency departments reported the most omitted care, and tasks needing long patient conversation were dropped most often. Staffing fixes should target the busiest wards and protect time for talking with patients, the authors imply.
pmc-13329325:
Alba García-Viola and colleagues set out a 2026 protocol for building a chatbot to support health workers who face aggression at work. Attacks on health staff have risen worldwide, yet reporting stays low and private support is hard to reach. The planned chatbot is called Sanidad Segura.

Work will run in two phases: first building and expert-checking content from reviews and local rules, then pilot testing with emergency and critical care staff in Almería, Spain. Ease of use will be scored with a standard scale, and reading ease with a Spanish scale. Interviews will probe user experience and barriers. Blending both kinds of evidence should show whether the tool is usable and welcome.
pmc-13329425:
Siyi Wang and co-authors describe three new goblin spider species from China in a 2026 taxonomic report. All three belong to Trilacuna, a genus found only in Asia. Two species come from Sichuan Province. The third comes from Chongqing and Hubei. Both males and females are described for each species.

Each account gives detailed body form, marks that separate the species from close kin, and photos of key parts. Names reflect their places: batang, kangding, and shennongjia, each paired with the genus authors Tong and Li. The genus held 55 valid species before these additions, the authors note. Careful form records help map spider diversity and guide later field surveys in the region.
pmc-13329725:
Kai Ting Mok and a large team describe building and testing a family health app for infants and parents in 2026. The app, FamNucleus, was co-built by clinicians using behaviour theory and a complex intervention guide. A test version ran for one month from December 2024 to January 2025 with 25 parents and 6 health professionals.

Users rated the app with standard experience and quality scales, and group talks probed views on adoption. Parents rated appeal and clarity above average, but scored speed and novelty lower in the summaries given. Professionals scored it higher overall, with top marks for appeal and novelty. Content checks were mostly strong. Ease of understanding fell from early version to test version, a point for redesign.
pmc-13330525:
Juseong Kim and colleagues present a deep learning tool for codon choice in human gene designs in a 2026 study. Messenger RNA drugs need codon patterns that boost protein output and keep the RNA stable. Older methods lean on frequency tables and miss wider sequence context. The new tool, COformer, blends convolutional and transformer networks.

Contrastive learning helps the model tie codon patterns to matching amino acids while reading both local and global context. Training used sequences tuned by commercial tools. In lab tests, designs from COformer raised protein output through better codon use and stronger RNA stability, the authors report. The approach may aid vaccine and drug design where output levels matter.
pmc-13331425:
Pichatorn Suppakitjanusant and colleagues test a risk score for brain vein clots in a 2026 study. The 10-point CLOTS-EVT score bundles warning signs such as low awareness, low platelets and sodium, seizures, and wide clot spread to flag early decline and guide clot removal timing. Records spanned 12 centres from 2015 to 2017.

In total, 80 adults were scored. Headache was the top symptom, and most patients received blood thinners while 10 percent had vessel procedures in the reported care. A score of 4 or more predicted early decline with 82 percent sensitivity and 61 percent specificity in the validation values. Higher scores also tracked with worse discharge function and longer stays.
pmc-13333325:
Takashi Mikami and colleagues publish a step-by-step protocol in 2026 for profiling blood cancer samples with mass cytometry while tagging live cells so many samples can run together. The technique reads dozens of markers per cell, ideal for rare populations, but staining varies between runs and antibodies are costly.

Their workflow covers sample collection, live-cell barcoding with antibodies against β2-microglobulin and CD147, staining, data collection, and analysis for blood and bone marrow samples. Tagging living cells, rather than fixed ones, keeps surface markers in their natural state, a real concern for leukemia blasts that can look deceptively plain. The panel centers on T cell features and can include a CD19-binding fragment to spot CAR T cells when needed. Practical notes address signal spillover between mass channels and how to titrate many antibodies together. The authors aim to cut cost and technical noise for precious patient samples.
pmc-13333425:
Bora Moon and colleagues compared health curiosity across cultures in a 2026 study of Google search patterns in the United States and South Korea. Fresh starts such as New Year prompt waves of health goal setting, a pattern called the temporal landmark effect. Whether it plays out the same in individualistic and collectivistic societies was open.

Using Google Trends search data on health terms in both countries, the team found Americans showed the stronger landmark effect, with health searches clustering in the year's early periods. Korean searches instead traced an inverted U, peaking mid-year rather than at the start. The authors say the difference matters for anyone timing a health campaign: a January push fits the American rhythm, while Korean audiences may respond better later in the year. The study also stretches landmark theory by showing the fresh-start pull itself varies with culture.
pmc-13333525:
Yige Wang and Qiang Xiao argue in a 2026 review that viral pneumonia is, at root, a crisis of the body's fats as much as of its immune proteins. Severe lung infections end in respiratory distress and organ failure. The authors gather evidence that the lipidome, is remodelled along the way.

Their synthesis describes a metabolic crash: LDL cholesterol plunges, while HDL flips from shield into an inflammatory vehicle, and both shifts forecast who fares worst. Mechanistically, respiratory viruses hijack the SREBP-SCAP axis to stockpile lipid droplets for virus particles, and they exhaust the GPX4 defence system until lung cells die by ferroptosis. Gut-lung crosstalk and metabolic inflammation set the patient's threshold for barrier failure. Therapeutically, the pair back lipid-restoring strategies, pro-resolving mediators and metabolic stabilizers, and propose AI-driven typing to match treatment to the patient.
pmc-13333625:
Yuka Murofushi and co-authors built and tested an anti-doping education program grounded in values for university sport in Japan, reporting the work in 2026. The UNIVAS program aims to strengthen clean-sport decision making rather than only teach rules.

Three linked studies shaped the work. First, the team drafted 15 doping decision scenarios from theory, past literature, and Japanese disciplinary cases, then surveyed 1,000 student-athletes and support staff about them. Second, chosen scenarios became lecture slides, scripts, and worksheets, refined through five pilot classes. Third, a pre-post study checked short-term changes under two teaching formats. The process offers a tested model for universities that want ethics-based doping prevention.
pmc-13334125:
Mesud Fakirullahoglu and co-authors tested whether adenosine triphosphate can protect the stomach against damage from the cancer drug olaparib, in a 2026 rat study. Olaparib, a PARP inhibitor, causes gastrointestinal side effects that oxidative stress may help explain.

Rats were split into healthy control, olaparib-only, ATP-only, and combined groups. Stomach injury was scored by ulcer area and count, tissue slides were examined, and lipid peroxidation plus antioxidant defenses were measured. Olaparib alone produced marked mucosal injury, heavy tissue damage, and strong oxidative stress. Adding ATP shrank ulcers, preserved tissue structure, and restored oxidative balance across the measures taken. The findings suggest a simple energy molecule might shield the stomach during PARP inhibitor therapy, pending further work.
pmc-13334425:
Eduard Bezuglov and co-authors surveyed elite track and field athletes about intravenous therapy use in a cross-sectional study from 2026. IV infusions of legal substances sit in a gray zone of sports medicine, and how common they are was poorly documented.

An anonymous questionnaire drew 138 elite athletes, 73 men and 65 women, with answers collected between October 2020 and January 2021. Over half, 56.5 percent, reported receiving IV drugs not banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency, and 18.8 percent used them regularly. Actovegin led the substance list at 77.4 percent of users, followed by phosphocreatine and amino acids. International-level athletes reported IV use more often than national-level peers. The prevalence raises questions for team doctors and anti-doping educators even where no rule is broken.
pmc-13336225:
Fernanda da Costa Ferreira, Mariana Miguel Vieira, and Ângela Maria Rosas Cardoso gathered nurses' perspectives on care at Child and Adolescent Psychosocial Care Centers in Brazil in a 2026 qualitative study. These community centers anchor mental health care for young people, and nurses' preparation for them is in question.

Semi-structured interviews with nurses from the Federal District health service and residents in a child and adolescent mental health program were analyzed thematically. Three axes emerged: mental health in academic training, continuing education, and whether the nursing role there is being dismantled or built. Nurses reported that university training still leaves them unready for the biopsychosocial model and broader clinical practice, producing insecurity. Continuing education stood out as the practical remedy already within reach.
pmc-13336425:
Xiao Xu and co-authors created microspheres that can carry many kinds of radiometals for liver cancer embolization in a 2026 materials study. Radioembolization works well against advanced liver tumors, but standard radioactive spheres pose material and handling problems.

Their spheres are built from a conjugated poly(imide dioxime) ligand forming an interlocked linked network. They accept lutetium-177, yttrium-90, rhenium-188, gallium-68, and technetium-99m at just 40 degrees Celsius, serving both imaging and therapy. Spectroscopy, computing, and stability tests in vitro and in vivo showed the metal complexes barely leak radiation carriers. Lutetium-labeled spheres foretold organ shunting and delivered radiotherapy in rat and rabbit liver tumor models. One all-purpose labeling platform could ease how hospitals prepare these treatments.
pmc-13336625:
Pengfei Bai and co-authors report a 2026 light-driven method that makes hydrogen peroxide while also upgrading a plant-based alcohol. They joined zinc indium sulfide with carbon dots, forming a junction that splits light-made charges well. Furfuryl alcohol plays three roles at once: electron donor, starting material, and proton source.

In a very dry solvent mix, the system reached a peroxide rate of 24 mmol per gram per hour with high light use. The alcohol turned into furoic acid with 98% conversion and full selectivity for that product in the reported tests. Pairing a useful oxidation with peroxide output could cut waste in green chemical production.
pmc-13337825:
Huub C. Gelderblom, Glenda Gray, and Brian Kelley argue for fairer global access to antibody drugs in a 2026 perspective. Monoclonal antibodies are a major medical success, yet poorer countries get few of them. More than 130 are approved in the United States, while only sixteen sit on the WHO essential list as cited.

Long-acting prevention antibodies, starting with nirsevimab for RSV in infants, could join the essential list group and build momentum together. HIV treatment history shows prices fell a hundredfold through political action, not new technology alone. The authors frame combined demand as a wheel that could roll toward equal access.
pmc-13339225:
Yixin Chen and colleagues review contact-free detection tools for heart failure in a 2026 article. Heart failure disables and kills many older adults, yet early signs are vague and standard scans or blood tests need skilled staff and clinic visits. New sensor and algorithm systems promise continuous tracking at home.

Wearable fluid sensors and combined platforms that merge heart sounds, motion, and other signals are surveyed. Artificial intelligence and cloud tools turn those streams into risk alerts and personal plans. Policy support and industry teamwork have sped products to market as reviewed. The authors weigh promise against proof, urging validation before wide clinical trust.
pmc-13339625:
Nathalia S. de Oliveira leads a 2026 synthesis adding alkene arms to flavones at one chosen site. Flavones are plant pigments with many uses, and direct carbon-hydrogen editing avoids prebuilt handles. The flavone carbonyl itself guided a ruthenium catalyst to carbon 5.

Partners included acrylates, styrene, and vinyl ketones, giving yields up to 92 percent as reported. A carbamate group at carbon 7, normally a strong guide, did not divert the reaction. Theory showed lower energy paths for carbon 5 and a dead end at carbon 8. The work gives a clean route to 5-alkenyl flavones for further study.
pmc-13341625:
A word list for spotting cyberbullying victims online is built and tested by Xingyun Liu and colleagues, in their 2026 study. Self-reports skew victim counts, so the team mined Weibo posts, psychology lexicons, and questionnaires to construct a Chinese lexicon across methods, perceived harm, and coping responses.

The lexicon held 442 words, validated against expert ratings on 500 posts and checked for cross-platform fit on 3,442 RedNote posts. DeepSeek-R1 and GPT-4o were also made to repeat the construction steps under simple and complex prompts, their agreement with human judgments scored statistically. Machine help in lexicon building is itself part of what gets assessed.
pmc-13341925:
Macrophage metabolism is a battleground in tuberculosis, in a 2026 review by Xiaohe Lu's team. When the bacteria infect these immune cells, energy pathways rewire in ways that serve both host defense and germ survival.

Heightened glycolysis, normally a fighting trait, can be used by the germ. The original paper appeared in the Journal of Diabetes Investigation in 2026, at pages 818 to 826. A results paragraph had mis-stated how the group with albumin in their urine differed from the group without it.

The corrected sentence now reads that patients with albuminuria had a lower, not higher, share of women, alongside older age, higher body mass and longer diabetes duration. Other contrasts (higher blood pressure and lipid problems, lower kidney function) stand as first printed. The notice apologises for the error and leaves the study's data untouched.
pmc-13399225:
Sangam Yadav and colleagues asked whether letting ventilated patients breathe on their own protects the diaphragm, in a 2026 prospective study of acute respiratory distress syndrome. A ventilator can weaken the diaphragm within hours. Clinicians therefore aim to keep its thickness fraction, a measure of muscle activity, inside a 15 to 30 percent band. One hundred adults with mild to moderate lung injury were followed daily until they left the ventilator or died.

The team recorded how many days each patient spent mostly in spontaneous breathing mode, then compared that with the days the diaphragm stayed in the protective band. The two tracked each other closely, with a correlation of 0.96 across the whole group in the reported results. The same pattern held in every subgroup split by ventilation length. People who breathed spontaneously for longer also died less often. The authors encourage spontaneous modes but call for confirmatory trials.
pmc-13400825:
Filippos Anagnostakis, Michail Kokkorakis, Ilias Papadimopoulos, Junhao Wen and Christos Davatzikos link, in 2026, cochlear implants with lower dementia risk in a twenty-year national cohort. Hearing loss is a leading changeable risk factor for cognitive decline, and implants restore hearing in severe cases. Whether they change dementia rates at population scale was open.

The cohort covered 4,106 implanted adults and matched controls whose hearing loss went untreated. The group was followed for a median of over seven years. Implant users had markedly lower risk of all-cause dementia, mild cognitive impairment and memory loss than controls, with hazard ratios around half to three fifths. The pattern held in both sexes. The authors back early hearing intervention as a dementia prevention strategy.
pmc-13401125:
Weerapong Lilitwat writes, in 2026, a letter urging caution in how brain-age predictions from MRI scans are presented for young autistic children. A recent study showed ordinary clinical scans can estimate brain age in two- to six-year-olds and detect group differences in autism. Using routine sequences, not research-grade ones, brought the method closer to real practice.

The letter warns that brain age is a group statistic, not a diagnosis, a measure of intelligence or a fixed forecast, and parents may misread it as all three. Age-matched differences existed at group level, but distributions overlapped widely and age-specific effects faded after statistical correction. The cohort was also not split by severity or language level. Careful wording, the author argues, protects family engagement with proven early therapies.
pmc-13401525:
Margreet Vogelzang, Mandy Wigdorowitz, and Ianthi M Tsimpli challenge the existing Indian norms for Raven's Coloured Progressive Matrices, a standard nonverbal intelligence test for children, in a 2026 study. Norms guide how a child's score is interpreted, and a bad norm sample can badly distort those judgements.

Their sample held 1,752 children attending government schools in Delhi, Hyderabad, and Patna. Scored against the existing Indian norms, about 79 percent of the children landed in the bottom tenth percentile, with IQ scores of 80 or lower, an implausible pile-up. Reviewing the old norm sample, the authors found it five times smaller, vague about children's language backgrounds, and drawn mostly from wealthier private-school pupils. They argue it cannot represent most Indian schoolchildren and build replacement norms matched to government-school contexts.
pmc-13401625:
Alejandro Osorio-Euan, Katia Lopez Garcia, and Yoeli M Escandon Espinoza carried out a 2026 accuracy study of ChatGPT model 5.1 for sorting colorectal lesions during colonoscopy. Judging a polyp's appearance in real time decides treatment strategy and predicts its tissue type, yet human judgements vary between readers.

The retrospective study gathered 93 lesions found at colonoscopy. Written optical accounts of each lesion were given to ChatGPT 5.1, which classified them as adenomatous or non-adenomatous against set criteria. Lab study of the removed tissue served as the gold standard. It was scored with sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and overall accuracy in a two-by-two table. The study tests whether a general large language model, rather than a purpose-built image system, can carry this judgement task.
pmc-13402025:
Mariana Garcia-Arango leads a team probing why some people with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction cannot lower lung vessel resistance during exercise. Their two-step study enrolled 164 people: 80 with that form of heart failure, 57 with pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension, and 27 with breathlessness not caused by the heart. Everyone had invasive exercise testing with catheters in place.

An unfavorable response meant exercise resistance above 1.74 Wood units with a fall of less than 22 percent during effort, a pattern seen in 46 of the heart failure group. Atrial fibrillation and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease stood out as the correlates that survived fuller models, ahead of the usual metabolic risks. Heart scans showed similar chamber shapes in both response groups, pointing the finger at lung vessels and the left atrium instead.
pmc-13402225:
Johnson and team develop, in 2026, a tool that lets sports club managers audit how health-promoting their club really is, from locker rooms to food menus. No earlier tool measured health promotion in clubs objectively, so the team began with a rapid literature review. That found 11 studies covering narrower tools for injuries, coaching, or alcohol. They then ran a three-round Delphi consensus process with 69 sports stakeholders.

Round one, with 18 respondents, drafted 24 items across four observation areas. Round two, with 31 respondents, confirmed 43 items. Round three, with 21, settled 36 items kept only at 80 percent consensus or better on relevance, importance, and clarity. Experts then sorted items by the health-promoting sports club model's factors: 17 organizational, 16 environmental, 9 social, and 5 economic items in the final sort. The finished package includes a scoring checklist and a user's guide, with test-retest checks under way in European clubs.
pmc-13402925:
Jurate Civinskaite and co-authors propose reporting every tumor marker result as a pair: the level itself plus its specific growth rate, the percentage change per day between the last two readings. Clinicians now judge markers against a normal range, so a rising marker below the norm triggers no imaging and recurrence can slip past. Yet serial values already sit in electronic records, making the rate cheap to compute.

Growth rate thinking already aids radiology prognosis, the authors note, but laboratories have never adopted it as a standard report line. They review studies where velocity or doubling time could have steered therapy or caught relapse earlier. Ease of reading, low cost, and mathematical consistency headline the claimed advantages. The proposal reframes a marker from a pass-fail number into a moving signal.
pmc-13403025:
Johanna Jakobs and colleagues run a pilot study on gamma-glutamyltransferase, an enzyme of glutathione handling rich in colostrum, as a possible marker of gut maturation in newborns. Reference values and any link to breast milk intake were unclear, especially for preterm babies. Serum was measured in 84 infants, 36 born before 32 weeks and 48 later, across the first four weeks of life, with milk from 107 mothers also tested.

Serum levels held fairly steady around 110 to 130 units per liter overall. Preterm infants who received colostrum ran higher in week one and lower by week four than unexposed peers. First-week milk intake correlated with serum values across all four weeks in the preterm group. The authors present the enzyme as a window on how early feeding shapes intestinal readiness.
pmc-13403225:
