Resmi Rajalekshmi, Devendra K Agrawal, and Satabdi Datta Choudhury review three-dimensional bioprinting as the fabrication engine for stem cell regenerative medicine. Older tissue engineering, grafts and decellularized scaffolds, stalls on immune rejection, donor scarcity, and failure to copy native tissue architecture. Printing stem cells in bioinks that mimic the extracellular matrix lets builders dictate cell placement and microenvironment layer by layer.

The review weighs what printing buys: biomimetic structure, controlled spatial organization, and support for stem cell function and specialization. Two bottlenecks dominate the road to clinic, growing blood vessels into printed tissue and scaling production without losing fidelity. Newer strategies for richer tissue complexity get extended treatment. The authors frame bioprinting as the bridge between stem cell promise in dishes and organs that could one day be implanted.
pmc-13403725:
Meng-Ge Li and colleagues traced post-injury anxiety in 2026 to one overactive circuit between two front brain areas. Head injury often leaves anxiety behind, which worsens long-term recovery. Brain scans of patients with front-lobe injury and anxiety showed both areas firing more and linking more tightly.

A mouse model of front-lobe injury split into anxious and calm groups. Anxious mice showed the same hot circuit, driven by signal cells. Light and drug switches that calmed the circuit eased anxiety, while firing it raised anxiety. One potassium channel gene, KCNC3, dropped in anxious mice. Restoring calm in that gene's pathway may help future patients.
pmc-13406725:
Ghareeb O Alshuwaier compares diet and body shape between school athletes and classmates in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, in a 2026 study. One hundred twenty-four boys aged sixteen to seventeen took part, seventy athletes and fifty-four non-athletes. Athletes trained hard at least three days a week for an hour or more.

Athletes carried clearly lower body mass, averaging 23.64 against 30.28 in the reported index, with slimmer waists and lower weight as well. Eating habits across ten food groups were surveyed with a validated teen lifestyle questionnaire. Stricter statistical thresholds guarded the many diet comparisons. Whether sport itself, or the kind of student who plays, explains the gap cannot be settled by a one-time survey.
pmc-13407125:
Maria Erodotou and co-authors tracked, in 2026, how immune signalling unfolds across organs during sepsis in mice. Sepsis, the body's damaging overreaction to infection, can fail several organs at once, and two relay routes inside immune cells, named MYD88 and TRIF, sit near its centre.

The team measured gene activity in gut, kidney, liver, and lung tissue at 24, 48, and 72 hours after inducing sepsis surgically. Immune messengers, infection-fighting interferons, and hypoxia-linked genes all rose versus controls, growing stronger over time and differing by organ. Genes tied to cell identity and a longevity-related protein called Klotho were part of the panel. The time- and tissue-specific pattern, the authors suggest, could guide treatments matched to the stage of illness.
pmc-13408925:
Yuanhong Shi and co-authors slip atomic layers of magnesium into gallium nitride in 2026 to fix a stubborn weakness of power transistors. GaN switches promise efficient electronics, yet the standard gate design cannot push its threshold voltage past about two volts because magnesium doping activates poorly. Their technique, atomically confined insertion, grows self-terminating two-dimensional magnesium sheets inside the device stack.

The inserted layers strain the crystal locally and flip its polarisation, and the resulting internal fields raised the effective hole concentration several-fold. A transistor built this way held a threshold of well over four volts, nearly triple the usual figure, without the usual sacrifices in gain or output current. The familiar GaN headache of current collapse also eased, thanks to efficient vertical hole injection. The work promotes atomic-scale field design as a new dial for semiconductor engineers.
pmc-13409025:
Shuge Dai and co-authors review in 2026 how atom-thin layered materials are being drafted into every corner of the water-based zinc battery. Such batteries are safe and cheap enough for grid storage, yet zinc anodes grow dendrites and corrode while cathodes dissolve and react sluggishly. Graphene relatives, MXenes, and layered sulfides each bring flat chemistry that can intervene at several points.

The review organises their roles as anode armour, cathode hosts, separator upgrades, and electrolyte additives, explaining how each placement blocks dendrites, suppresses hydrogen gas formation, steadies the cathode, or speeds ion traffic. Remaining obstacles receive equal attention, from making the materials at scale to proving them in full cells rather than coin-cell demonstrations. The authors close with research directions aimed at commercial deployment rather than another round of record-chasing.
pmc-13409325:
Daniel Chan, Harshini Katugampola, and Mehul Dattani present in 2026 a girl whose care sits at the collision point of a genetic appetite disorder and a brain tumour. Prader-Willi syndrome brings relentless hunger, early obesity, developmental delay, and a stack of hormone failures rooted in the hypothalamus. Her medulloblastoma, a tumour of the back of the brain, demanded surgery, radiotherapy to brain and spine, and chemotherapy, each insulting the same control centre.

Afterwards she faced severe obesity and insulin resistance with impaired glucose tolerance, an underactive thyroid of central origin, adrenal insufficiency, worsening neurological decline, and severe sleep apnoea. The hardest judgement was whether to restart growth hormone, weighing its metabolic and growth benefits against oncological caution. The authors use the case to map the multidisciplinary choreography such children need, where endocrine, metabolic, and cancer teams must plan as one.
pmc-13409825:
Mislav Radić and co-authors review in 2026 how lupus affects the sac around the heart. Problems there range from mild fluid build-up to repeated painful flare-ups and, rarely, pressure that stops the heart filling well. The review asks whether a clotting-related syndrome that sometimes travels with lupus makes heart sac disease worse.

Following standard review methods, the team searched four large databases through January 2026 and found seven suitable studies of adults. Heart sac trouble tracked closely with higher lupus activity and stronger immune signals across the studies. Repeated flare-ups marked a more severe course with worse outcomes. Evidence on the clotting syndrome was patchy and uneven, so no firm link could be drawn from it.
pmc-13411725:
Qi-Ren Chen, Timothy Moural, and Fang Zhu review in 2026 the versatile enzyme family that lets insects survive chemical assaults across their habitats. Cytochrome P450 enzymes break down plant poisons and insecticides, build protective skins, and fine-tune smell. Their sheer variety underwrites the success of insects as a group.

Families of these enzymes repeatedly get borrowed for new jobs, crossing the clan boundaries that textbooks draw between them. Detox work links to skin penetration, scent detection, and even chemistry outsourced to gut microbes. The authors propose viewing the enzymes as shared hubs in one adaptation network rather than separate toolkits. That systems view may predict resistance outbreaks and guide gentler pest control.
pmc-13411925:
Dongyao Liu, Chaogu Zheng, and Roland G Roberts report in 2026 on an old toxin-antidote gene pair in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans. Such pairs act as inheritance distorters: a mother passes a toxin to all her young, and only offspring carrying the antidote gene survive. The pair named sept-1 and zina-1 turned up in a highly divergent Hawaiian strain, XZ1516.

Offspring lacking zina-1 arrest as rod-shaped larvae under the SEPT-1 toxin. Most non-Hawaiian strains carry a broken copy of the antidote, while their toxin copy has faded to a harmless form. Family-tree analysis suggests this pair is the most widespread of three known systems in Hawaii, and its decline matches the rise of two younger pairs elsewhere.
pmc-13412225:
Borriello and co-authors hunt, in 2026, for a blood biomarker signature that tracks kidney decline in long COVID, the long inflammatory condition affecting an estimated 400 million people worldwide. At a Naples-area center, survivors were recalled 12 months after discharge and split into three groups by estimated glomerular filtration rate, from above 90 down to below 30 milliliters per minute. A multiplex platform measured nine inflammatory proteins.

Of 208 patients admitted, 170 survived to the follow-up window and entered the analysis. Kidney function had declined since admission, and interleukin-6 levels rose as filtration fell across the groups. In the worst-function group, interleukin-17, interleukin-10, and the adhesion molecule VCAM-1 were also elevated, completing a four-marker signature the authors link to poorer renal prognosis. They propose interleukin-6 drives the others upward and suggest the panel could flag chronic kidney disease risk in long COVID clinics, pending larger cohorts.
pmc-13412525:
Sara Benchekroun and co-authors probe in 2026 a curcumin-like compound, PAC, against mouth cancer cells in the lab. Oral cancer of this type ranks among the ten most common cancers in the world. It is often caught late. Normal gum cells and two cancer lines, one from gum and one from tongue, were dosed with PAC for a day. The team then checked cell survival, cell death, and gene activity.

PAC slowed cancer cell growth as the dose rose. Half the cells were stopped at a set dose, while normal gum cells showed no clear harm. Both cancer lines turned on cell death, though each used a partly distinct gene set to do so. Maps of gene links showed the drug hits hubs that steer death signals.
pmc-13413225:
Junya Abe and co-authors report in 2026 a complication after bladder tumour surgery in an older man. Removing bladder tumours through the urethra, then washing the bladder with chemotherapy, is standard care meant to cut recurrence. Their patient, aged 84, had a small tumour found while doctors checked a treated prostate cancer, and he received the drug epirubicin into the bladder right after resection.

Two days later, abdominal pain led to scans showing the bladder had perforated, leaking into the space behind the abdominal lining. A drainage catheter alone failed to heal the hole, so surgeons repaired it and cleaned the area, finding pale dead-looking tissue blamed on escaped drug. A dye test twenty-eight days after repair showed no further leak.
pmc-13413625:
Sharon Ong and co-authors map the indicators hospitals use to measure the environmental performance of their food services. Their 2026 scoping review looks for measures of emissions, waste, and sustainable diets, and checks how far Australian standards and policies already include them.

Following standard scoping methods, the team searched three databases and included fifty studies. They extracted 51 indicators spanning buying, facilities, staffing, menu design, production, delivery, waste, and quality systems. Gaps included reporting of indirect supply-chain emissions, inconsistent ways of measuring waste, and weak links to quality audits. Mapping against Australian policy showed most indicators were absent or only partly embedded. The authors conclude that without an agreed, feasible indicator set, hospitals cannot benchmark progress toward sustainability goals.
pmc-13413825:
Xiang Wu and co-authors study in 2026 how hot an atmospheric microwave plasma jet runs while it etches fused silica, the glass of precision optics. Contact-free plasma finishing avoids the scratches mechanical polishing leaves, yet temperature steers the removal rate. Infrared cameras watched the working zone in real time while the team varied microwave power, argon flow, and carbon tetrafluoride flow one factor at a time.

Plasma temperature climbed in step with microwave power across their experiments. Argon flow showed a sweet spot, peaking near 3 standard litres per minute before cooling again. Etching sped up as the surface grew hotter, and long dwells piled up heat until removal turned nonlinear. Splitting the job into segments tamed that drift, and the method checked out on a fused quartz sub-mirror.
pmc-13415425:
Jianan Li, Minjie Hu, Lu Ding, and Yongyu Wang review the signaling pathways that drive heart regeneration, in 2026. After a heart attack, adult mammals mostly scar instead of regrowing muscle. Pathways named Hippo, Wnt, NRG1-ErbB, MAPK, and Notch each control whether heart muscle cells divide again or stay locked in maturity.

Blocking Hippo frees cells to multiply and reshapes their inner skeleton. Wnt signals help or hinder depending on timing and injury phase. Matrix proteins and growth factors in the tissue surroundings also steer repair. New grafts, short lived modified RNA, and low oxygen tricks are covered as routes toward treatment.
pmc-13416625:
Alyssa Sanchez and colleagues write to the editor in 2026 about where Americans with kidney failure die, using the CDC WONDER mortality database. Death certificates from 1999 to 2023 listed kidney failure as an underlying or contributing cause. Places of death were grouped as inpatient facility, outpatient or emergency setting, home, or hospice and nursing facility.

Yearly deaths tied to kidney failure more than doubled, from about twenty-six thousand to about fifty-two thousand. Inpatient deaths fell from sixty-nine percent to about forty-nine percent of the total. Home deaths climbed from about eleven percent to about twenty-three percent. Patterns were split by year, sex, urbanization, and race.
pmc-13416825:
Alvaro Guimaraes Paula and a large team report outcomes for lung cancer patients whose tumours carry a RET fusion, in a 2026 brief report. Targeted RET drugs are the usual first treatment, yet cancers often learn to resist them. The team compares chemotherapy paired with a RET drug against chemotherapy paired with immunotherapy after resistance appears.

Only 12 patients were included in this real world group. Time without growth was longer with the RET pairing, at a median near 7.8 months versus 3.5 months. Response rates were also a little higher. Blood related side effects at severe grade were more common with the RET pairing, so benefits came with added risk.
pmc-13416925:
Ryan N Baugher and co-authors describe a lab test for a hidden gene change in von Hippel-Lindau disease, published in 2026. People with this inherited condition grow tumours in many organs. Standard gene tests miss some large structural changes, leaving families without a firm cause despite clear symptoms.

The test targets a flipped DNA segment of 291 kilobases, found near the VHL gene, using polymerase chain reaction and fragment sizing. Validation in their certified lab matched expected results in every case. A confirmed cause supports earlier checks for relatives and sharper care planning. The authors argue that custom tests remain vital for rare structural changes.
pmc-13417025:
Emelie Obi and co-authors map insect records for Nigeria held by the Global Biodiversity Information Facility, in a 2026 appraisal. Insects support ecosystems and signal their health, yet Nigerian records are scattered. The team pulled 49,854 occurrence records from that global database to chart orders, families, and where collecting has focused.

Records covered 19 orders, 305 families, and 5,880 species. Estimation suggests that tally is only about a fifth of the true total. Diversity differed by biome and followed latitude, with clear gaps in places and groups. The authors call for wider surveys, local effort, and stronger support to close the record gap.
pmc-13417225:
Indira Karibayeva and colleagues chart HIV and AIDS burden in Kazakhstan from 2010 to 2023 and project trends to 2030, in a 2026 analysis. Data come from the Global Burden of Disease 2023 study, covering new cases, people living with HIV, deaths, and years of healthy life lost. Kazakhstan is compared with Central Asia and world patterns.

Prevalence more than tripled and new cases more than doubled, while world incidence fell. Deaths and years lost to early death dropped, yet years lived with disability rose sharply, marking a shift to chronic illness. Gains clustered in adults aged 30 to 69. Stronger prevention and testing are urged.
pmc-13417725:
Adhikari and colleagues report a 2026 study of gut parasites in one-horned rhinos living outside Chitwan National Park in Nepal. The species is classed as vulnerable, and parasite disease is one threat to its health. The team collected 60 fresh dung samples from five sites near the park without disturbing the animals, then checked them with standard lab methods.

Every sample held at least one parasite, and the team found 16 kinds in all: five single-celled types and eleven worm types. No rhino carried just one kind, and infection with four kinds at once was the most common pattern. Anoplocephala and strongyle worms were the most frequent worms, while Entamoeba and Eimeria led the single-celled group. The authors call for prompt parasite treatment and routine checks, since heavy mixed infections can drain their health.
pmc-13418725:
Sophia Knudson and colleagues review ways to give the hepatitis B vaccine birth dose to babies born outside health facilities. Their 2026 rapid scoping review covers low- and middle-income countries, where home births can miss the shot that must arrive within a day of birth. Global coverage within that window sits at 45 percent, well under the global target of 90 percent set for 2030.

The team searched PubMed and selected websites for work published from 2005 to 2025, then charted what each source reported. Three broad routes stood out: finding and tracking home births, helping caregivers accept the shot, and bringing the vaccine to the home or linking families to a facility. Home visits, phone reminders, small payments, and flexible cold storage all played a part. Program planners can use the map of options when they design outreach for newborns.
pmc-13418825:
Gustavo Alarcón-Nieto and colleagues compare flight effort across three movement strategies in oilbirds, fruit-eating birds that roost together in colonies. Some birds commute back to the colony often, while others wander far in the non-breeding season. The team fitted 21 adult birds with small loggers weighing 22 grams each, recording place and body motion from August 2008 to February 2009.

Night flight time served as the measure of effort for each strategy across the study months. Birds on long intra-tropical trips spent less total time in flight than colony commuters. Staying away cut the costly nightly round trips that commuting demands. The contrast shows how personal movement choices shape energy use inside one bird population.
pmc-13421325:
S. Corradini and thirteen colleagues describe, in a 2026 paper, a drug candidate called CBPD-409 that destroys two proteins multiple myeloma cells depend on. CBP and p300 switch on growth programmes driven by the gene MYC and keep the malignant plasma cells alive; existing blockers only mute their enzyme activity, leaving their structural roles intact.

CBPD-409 instead uses a PROTAC design — a molecule that tags a target protein for the cell's disposal machinery — to remove both proteins entirely. Earlier blockers showed early clinical promise but incomplete effect, which the authors attribute to those leftover scaffolding functions. In their experiments, full degradation produced strong anti-myeloma activity, supporting complete protein removal as the stronger strategy.
pmc-13421425:
Desislava Stoianova, Gayane Karagyan and Snejana Grozeva survey, in a 2026 study, the DNA repeats capping chromosome ends across the insect infraorder Nepomorpha, a group of true bugs. Only the oldest branch had been checked before, by microscope methods, leaving the remaining families' telomere sequences unknown.

Mining 32 public genome datasets spanning 24 genera and all 13 families, the team recovered the classic arthropod repeat in the two basal superfamilies. The more derived groups instead carried longer, ten-letter repeats, most sharing a common core segment. Their screening tool was validated on species with known telomeres first. The authors read the pattern as an evolutionary switch in telomere makeup within the group.
pmc-13421825:
Andrew Laitha, Anna Fabry, Bart Minten and Eva-Marie Meemken survey hired farm workers in Myanmar, in a 2026 study. They ask how violent conflict around the workers relates to mental health and to how much work gets done. Hired labourers live precariously on daily wages, and evidence about conflict's toll on this group was thin.

Phone interviews reached 1,504 workers, and answers were matched to a database of conflict events. Thirty-nine percent had been exposed to conflict and twenty percent met criteria for trauma. Exposed workers fared worse on several measures, and statistical mediation analysis tested whether mental health carries part of conflict's effect on time lost and on-the-job productivity. The authors connect the findings to agricultural output and food security under instability.
pmc-13422825:
Amber Hussain, Tanya Park, Zahid Ali Memon and Salima Meherali explore, in a 2026 ethnographic study, what becoming a mother does to a teenager in rural Pakistan. Twenty-five adolescent mothers in Matiari, Sindh, shared their experience through interviews, observation and objects that prompted their stories, with transition theory guiding the questions.

Five themes ran through the findings. Schooling was cut short and ambitions redirected. Caregiving ran round the clock with patchy support. Care was hard to reach. Distress and strain were common, and identity itself was reshaped. The burdens piled together and deepened the mental-health toll, yet the young mothers also showed real resilience. The authors call for care shaped for teenagers, with private distress screening and clear referral routes in underserved districts.
pmc-13422925:
Cole and colleagues described in 2026 the GreenME project, a multi-country study of green care and mental health equity. Green care ranges from nature in daily life to formal nature-based therapy. The protocol covers seven countries across the Global North, a term for wealthier world regions.

The project has three strands: mapping current green care, testing its effects, and building tools with stakeholders. The team will catalogue successful models and design a shared protocol for trials of nature-based therapies. Population surveys will link exposure to green and blue spaces, such as parks and water, with mental health across social groups. Modified randomised trials will test effectiveness and cost-effectiveness in real settings. Outputs include policy guidance for national and European levels and online resources for therapy providers.
pmc-13424025:
Feng Gao and six colleagues follow patients for two years after a combined cataract and angle-opening operation for angle-closure glaucoma, a disease where the eye's drainage angle is blocked. The operation removes the cloudy lens and peels open stuck drainage tissue, and the team compared results between the acute form of the disease, which strikes suddenly, and the chronic form.

Of 213 patients treated between 2019 and 2022, 116 had the acute form and 97 the chronic. Complete success at two years reached 72.4% in the acute group against 65.0% in the chronic, while broader success rates matched near 82%. Baseline vision loss, chamber depth, and disease type predicted the outcome.
pmc-13424325:
Yanfei Liu and nine colleagues introduce a fully automated droplet test that measures how well a bacteriophage kills its target bacteria within three hours, a speed phage therapy badly needs. Choosing a virus that attacks a patient's drug-resistant infection currently relies on slow, crude spot tests, and standardised selection tools are missing.

Their method counts DNA spilled from burst bacteria using droplet digital PCR aimed at a conserved bacterial gene. Across 122 phage–host pairings from nineteen strains, the test agreed with spot tests 95.9% of the time while exposing weak or patchy killing the older method blurs. It also registered bacterial defence systems at work. The authors pitch automated profiling as a route to routine phage matching.
pmc-13424525:
Xu and colleagues ask in 2026 whether markers of biological aging actually cause osteoporosis, the thinning of bone that raises fracture risk, or merely travel with it. They use Mendelian randomization, a method that treats inherited gene variants as a natural experiment.

The team tested eight aging-related measures in both directions using European genetic data. The measures included telomere length, a mitochondrial DNA count, a growth factor, three amino acids, and a bone-related protein. Three signals appeared at first glance: higher growth factor and higher isoleucine each linked to lower risk, and higher Dickkopf-related protein 1 to higher risk. None of the three survived strict correction for multiple testing, though two extra methods kept supporting the Dickkopf protein. Osteoporosis itself showed no effect back on any marker.
pmc-13425025:
Elaine N Clarke and Rachael J Thorneloe survey 130 people living with psoriasis about how faithfully they use their prescribed skin treatments and how kindly they treat themselves. Skipping topical therapy is a well-known problem in psoriasis. In other long-term conditions, self-compassion has been linked with better adherence. Here it means being supportive toward oneself in distress. That connection had never been tested in this disease.

Recruited through patient charities, dermatology bodies, and social media, participants completed an online cross-sectional survey. The headline result is simple: people who scored higher on self-compassion tended to stick closer to their topical regimen. The authors present the finding as a first step toward kinder, psychology-aware adherence support in psoriasis care.
pmc-13425625:
Hassnain and Azhar published a 2026 study on fast quality checks for sandalwood oil. Sandalwood earns high prices, yet testing its oil has meant slow, destructive lab work. The team built a system pairing infrared light scans with learning software. Scans covered logs, chips, powders, oils, and extracts from the same tree species.

The system guessed oil yield with very high accuracy in outside check samples. It also nailed the share of heartwood, the fragrant core buyers prize most. Two scent compounds central to oil value were predicted nearly as well. Even a handheld scanner gave strong results on mixed emulsion samples. Such tools could speed grading all along the sandalwood supply chain. Fast, non-destructive checks could also curb fraud in the high-value trade.
pmc-13425925:
Huifang Liang, Junqin Li, and Kaiming Zhang review cellular senescence in chronic inflammatory skin disease in a 2026 article calling it a hidden driver. Senescent cells stop dividing permanently and release inflammatory signals known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, alongside mitochondrial problems and DNA damage. Traditional explanations for these skin disorders center on immune dysregulation, while newer evidence places senescence upstream of progression and recurrence.

Coverage spans hallmarks, regulators, and triggers of senescence, its role in representative skin disorders, and therapies aimed at senescent cells. Dermatology readers gain a framework linking aging cell biology with barrier failure and repeated flares. Skin that flares for years wears down sleep, work, and mood. The skin is the shield of the body, and when that shield cracks, germs and stress rush in with ease day by day in sick men and women.
pmc-13426025:
Kosola and colleagues published a 2026 study on a protein that may forecast kidney cancer outcomes. Clear cell renal cancer often returns after surgery, even when caught early. The team measured a protein called PML inside tumor cell nuclei. Two hospital groups in Finland gave them 364 surgical cases to test.

Patients with high PML levels saw their cancer return far less often. They also lived longer in both hospital groups over long follow-up. In the second group, high PML held its value after adjusting for known risk traits. Follow-up stretched to a median of eight and nine years in the groups. A simple tissue stain could one day sharpen risk talks after surgery. Risk talks after surgery could soon include a PML result as well.
pmc-13426225:
Siyan Che and colleagues built a dose framework for the chemical colitis model used in mouse research in a 2026 study. Dextran sulfate sodium, called DSS, in drinking water injures the gut lining. Laboratories use widely varying doses, which blocks comparison between studies. Groups of C57BL/6J mice received plain water or one of four dose levels, from one and a half percent up to three percent, for five days plus two recovery days. Tissue, microbe, gene, and immune profiling followed.

Low doses caused mild, mostly reversible injury with early microbe shifts and CD8 T cell build-up. High doses drove lasting inflammation, deep mucosal damage, and strong cytokine signals. Shared pathways including TNF and NF-kappaB rose with dose, guiding rational model selection.
pmc-13426325:
Sarah Elizabeth Troy and Charles Mitchell tested how warming and plant age change disease when two fungi infect the same grass. They grew tall fescue, a common pasture grass, at two ages and two temperatures in a controlled experiment.

One fungus rots tissue outright, while the other lives inside the plant first and turns harmful later. Against expectations, hosting both fungi at once changed symptoms only slightly across the measures used. Higher heat eased lesion severity from the rotting fungus, and older plants also showed milder damage from it. For the second fungus, older plants resisted better in cool air but lost that edge under warming, Troy reports.
pmc-13427625:
Boccino, Grieco, and Merlino review how chemists have rebuilt the temporins, a family of short bacteria killing peptides from the skin of the common frog Rana temporaria. The peptides attack membranes broadly, a trait that slows resistance, but they are fragile in the body and only modestly selective. Their 2026 review sorts the strategies tried across the A to L family members and draws out the rules that link structure to killing power and safety.

Tactics include swapping in mirror image building blocks that enzymes cannot chew, reversing the chain, retuning charge and greasiness, and adding unusual residues. Locking the shape paid off: ring closed, stapled, and double ring versions often gained stability and activity at once. The review maps which positions tolerate change and which break the peptide. It closes on the hurdles left, chiefly safe delivery and proof in animals, before a temporin drug can reach patients.
pmc-13427825:
Manzoni and colleagues published a 2026 study on tracking many chronic diseases over time. Older adults often carry several long-term illnesses that shift in tangled ways. Past tools handled uneven check-up gaps and missed data poorly. The team built a hidden-state model that runs in continuous time.

Test runs showed the hidden model cut bias far below simpler versions. The team then applied it to 2,716 Swedish elders followed for up to 18 years. The model sorted people into disease patterns with clear death-risk steps. It also flagged traits tied to faster slide into complex illness mixes. Such forecasts could help aim care at those sliding fastest. Irregular visit gaps, common in elder care, no longer break the math.
pmc-13428025:
Tailei Nie and colleagues characterise reports of anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction, linked to glatiramer acetate, a drug used for multiple sclerosis. Their 2026 pharmacovigilance study mines the United States FDA adverse event database and the Canadian vigilance database after regulators required a boxed warning for the drug.

The FDA database held 9,816 relevant reports with 29 statistically significant safety signals, and the association with anaphylaxis held up across age, weight, sex, and reporter groups. Younger patients accounted for a higher share of serious reports. Reported reactions tended to appear earlier rather than later after treatment started, with median onset around five to six months depending on signal priority. The Canadian database added 711 reports, including respiratory arrest, a signal not seen in the FDA data. The authors frame the results as groundwork for future validation studies.
pmc-13428625:
Aditya Jain and colleagues scrutinize, in a 2026 methods paper, how hospitalization rates are defined and estimated in health research. Hospital data feed countless studies and quality rankings, yet the quantity being measured is often left vague. The authors test three common rate estimators against a model of health as a stock that people build and lose over time. They show that healthy time outside hospital can be bounded using stay lengths alone, with no assumptions about life at home.

One widely used admission rate turns out to be a weighted average whose weights lack a clear basis. The team proposes an alternative built on weaker assumptions. They also show that the readmission scores used to penalize United States hospitals can shift with patient mix rather than care quality. Their fix reads quality straight from the model's hospital effects.
pmc-13428725: Kamigaichi and colleagues correct their earlier study in Cancer Immunology, Immunotherapy on lymph node removal in early lung cancer. The right side of Figure 2 was cut off in the first version. Some data points and labels could not be seen. The note prints the full figure. It shows how CD4 T cell groups in blood changed after surgery. It also shows disease-free survival curves. The test results and the main claims stay the same.
pmc-13429125:
Wenchen Zhao and Xinxia Li investigate, in a 2026 study, why some sleep apnea patients use online health information well and others do not. Obstructive sleep apnea repeatedly closes the airway during sleep, and managing it leans heavily on patient learning. The team surveyed 241 diagnosed patients during 2025 with five validated questionnaires. Measures covered digital health skill, information-seeking habits, confidence, social support, and self-management.

Average digital health skill scores sat low. Skill rose alongside information seeking, confidence, support, and self-management in simple comparisons. A combined model pinned down eight significant influences, including family education level, time spent seeking health information online, access barriers, and life management skills. The authors suggest clinics coach patients on finding and judging online information, with family involvement and support networks treated as part of the prescription.
pmc-13429225:
Enes Karakaya and colleagues present, in a 2026 case report, severe liver injury where two treatments overlapped. Their patient was a 66-year-old man with widespread small-cell lung cancer. He received atezolizumab, an immunotherapy that releases the immune system against tumors. At the same time he took isoniazid, an antibiotic given to prevent dormant tuberculosis from waking during cancer care.

His liver injury reached grade 4, the second-highest severity band. Doctors stopped the isoniazid and started steroid treatment to calm the immune attack. Liver tests then improved steadily. Immune hepatitis from checkpoint drugs is known, and isoniazid alone can also injure the liver, so the pair may have added their risks together. The authors add their case to a small literature warning that preventive antibiotics deserve a second look beside immunotherapy.
pmc-13429525:
Celine Kadesch and co-authors run, in a 2026 German trial, a phone app meant to keep bariatric patients from dropping out before surgery. Candidates must clear a long multidisciplinary assessment, and many fall away along the route. The trial enrolled 223 adults with severe obesity at one major center. Half received standard team care alone, while half also got an app with checklists, reminders, and automatic alerts to staff when appointments were missed.

About 65 percent finished the assessment overall, with no meaningful gap between the app and control groups as randomized. A deeper look told a different story: patients who actually used the app often finished at about 76 percent, while rare users finished at only about 20 percent. Lower starting body weight also predicted finishing. Quality of life improved in every group. The lesson is engagement, the authors say, not the download.
pmc-13429925:
Jin Sun and colleagues upgrade, in a 2026 engineering study, a nature-inspired search algorithm and put it to work on dams and pipes. The nutcracker optimization algorithm mimics how nutcracker birds cache and recover seeds. The team first benchmarked 26 rival meta-heuristic algorithms on standard test problems. Their improved version layers six tricks onto the base method, including chaotic starting points, a swooping flight move, and two kinds of random mutation.

The base algorithm already ranked best overall among the 26 tested. The improved version searched more accurately, settled faster, and ran more stably. Two water engineering jobs followed: spotting broken wires inside concrete pipes from sound signals, and forecasting dam deformation over seasons. The improved optimizer beat baseline rivals at both tasks. Dam safety monitoring is the intended home for the method.
pmc-13430025:
Pell and a large team investigated why APOL1 risk variants, gene changes common in people of African ancestry, promote kidney transplant rejection beyond their known effects on kidney cells. Working with transgenic mice expressing the normal gene or the G1 and G2 risk versions at natural levels, they focused on T cell behavior.

Mice carrying either risk variant showed stronger CD8 T cell activation and an expanded pool of central memory T cells, the long-lived sentinels of immune memory. Stimulated G1 cells multiplied more and produced more cytokines, effects reversed by blocking APOL1 in the experiments. In mismatched heart transplants, G1 mice accumulated more graft-infiltrating T cells and lost grafts sooner than controls. The mechanism ran through calcium signaling: G1 cells started with depleted internal calcium stores and surged higher on stimulation, making them unusually sensitive to calcium blockers.
pmc-13430525:
Maryam Darestani-Farahani and Peter Kruse reviewed the material hurdles that face solid sensors built to track ions in water around the clock. Clean water checks have long relied on taking samples to a lab, which gives brief snapshots and can miss fast shifts. Solid sensors promise steady readings with low power use and easy links to electronics.

The review surveys many working materials, from metal oxides and carbon tubes to new layered compounds and soft plastics. It weighs ways to sharpen a sensor's aim, such as tuned flaws in a surface, added tiny particles, or special films that admit one ion only. Gains, weak points, build methods, and test scores all come under review. Groups of sensors that read many ions at once close the survey.
pmc-13431325:
Tomas Ulloa-Guerrero and co-authors ran a six-week trial in 2026 that set sled-pulled sprint drills against free sprint drills for young soccer players. The trial enrolled 44 players in two age bands. Each band split into groups that trained twice a week under watch, one group pulling a sled load near a fifth of body weight.

Jump height barely moved in any group. Sprint times improved across the board. The sled group gained more on force-linked measures, such as peak push and top power, which shape the first steps of a sprint. Top speed rose in both groups. In the older band, the balance between force and speed shifted in unlike ways by group. The authors read sled work as the better pick for raw push off the mark.
pmc-13431425:
Nisa and co-authors compare two preventive antibiotics for gynecologic surgery at an Indonesian teaching hospital, in this 2026 retrospective study. They ask whether the broader-spectrum ceftriaxone beats the narrower cefazolin at preventing surgical site infections. Stewardship principles favor the narrow drug when outcomes are equal, since heavy broad-spectrum use breeds resistance.

Records from 366 patients showed no significant difference in infection rates between the antibiotics, with the comparison landing at p equals 0.097 in the analysis. Patient factors predicted infection far better than drug choice. A body mass index above roughly 24.9 carried an odds ratio of 4.27 for infection in the analysis. High white-cell counts, a high neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, and anemia each roughly doubled or tripled the odds. The authors endorse cefazolin as first-line prophylaxis and flag the risk profile for closer monitoring.
pmc-13432225:
Edward Young and co-authors tested in 2026 whether adding computer-aided spotting to a color-and-texture boost view lifts polyp finds during colon checks. Early removal of bowel growths blocks their march toward cancer. The boost view alone had already beaten plain white light in past trials, yet the extra worth of a computer helper stayed untested.

The study folded 263 patients, with a hundred in the paired-tool arm and the rest drawn from a past trial arm that used the boost view alone. Growths found per check tied exactly between arms, and the share of checks with at least one growth showed no firm gap. Doctors with low base find rates did gain from the helper. The paired arm cost near a minute more per check and cut out more harmless growths.
pmc-13432625:
Moothedath and colleagues improved a zinc-iodine redox flow battery, a rechargeable system that stores energy in liquid electrolytes for grid use, by adding cheap ammonium chloride to both sides of the cell. Zinc-iodine chemistry is inexpensive and safe but suffers from iodine loss, zinc dendrite spikes, and dead zinc that shorten battery life.

The additive forms a complex that curbs iodine precipitation and unwanted polyiodide formation on the positive side of the cell. On the negative side it suppressed dendrite growth and stabilized zinc deposition during repeated charging in their tests. The full cell ran beyond 1,000 cycles at 30 milliamps per square centimeter, holding a coulombic efficiency of 93.83 percent and energy efficiency near 75 percent across cycling. Peak power density reached 74.8 milliwatts per square centimeter, far better than the additive-free version of the same cell.
pmc-13432825:
Hernández-Calderón and co-authors test a pollutant pairing in this 2026 toxicology study: polypropylene microplastics, plastic fragments under five millimeters, fed to fruit fly larvae together with an arsenic compound, dimethylarsinic acid. Microplastics can ferry other contaminants through the environment, so the team asked whether the combination harms flies differently than each agent alone.

Plastic particles alone, at 0.01 grams per milliliter of food, did not much change survival to adulthood, visible abnormalities, or fecundity, though tissue damage was detectable under the microscope. The arsenic-plus-plastic mixture behaved against intuition, looking milder for survival and tissue damage, meaning less harm than expected, yet harsher for fecundity loss and abnormality rates, meaning more. The authors frame the mixed pattern as a warning that co-exposure harm cannot be predicted by simply adding single-agent results.
pmc-13433725:
Yvonne Gaddy and co-authors graded a light-touch help plan in 2026 for town health coalitions, groups that anchor local prevention work yet often lack cheap, steady coaching. Thirty-two coalitions in two states took yearly data reports, then picked one weak skill per year to build with coach aid. A check three years out closed the arc.

Skills picked in year one grew across the years that came after, by a small but firm step. Skills picked in year two grew by a like step. Year three picks leapt by the widest step of all. The plan's loop is plain: read the report, pick a gap, plan acts, then read fresh data next year. The authors say light coaching can steer real growth in group skill.
pmc-13436025:
Stefania Andrea Rosso Villanelo and coauthors use antibiotics as a weeding tool to culture shy sludge bacteria in 2026. Sewage sludge germs clean water, yet many kinds refuse to grow in the lab. Brief antibiotic pressure thins rivals so rare kinds can claim a plate.

Eleven antibiotics at three strengths each reshaped plate communities in distinct ways. Two winning settings yielded seventy four pure isolates across twenty eight species. Thirteen look new to science by genome checks. Nineteen fall in core sludge genera found world wide. Genome guesses about sludge jobs can now face bench tests.
pmc-13437925:
Sewa, Yang, and Khosla review a newly recognized route by which modified food proteins become immune targets in this 2026 article. Chemical alterations to proteins can create neo-epitopes, new shapes the immune system has not learned to tolerate. In celiac disease, the enzyme transglutaminase 2 converts a specific amino acid in gluten fragments. That makes the fragments bind strongly to HLA-DQ2. This molecule presents them to T cells.

The puzzle was delivery: such modified fragments are scarce in the gut lining, yet dendritic cells capture them efficiently. The review explains that the enzyme-fragment complex docks onto a receptor called LRP1, which ferries it into the cell's processing compartments and releases the altered fragment there. A similar alteration-driven mechanism may operate in rheumatoid arthritis, and the authors discuss exploiting this selective pathway in vaccine design.
pmc-13439725:
de Beijer and a large team compare sexual health in young cancer survivors and the general population in this 2026 Canadian study. Sexual health is part of overall well-being but is rarely assessed in survivors of childhood, adolescent, and young adult cancers. The team used repeated assessments from routine survivorship care for 305 survivors, median age about 22, and compared them with age-matched respondents from a national health survey.

Nearly half of survivors, about 47.5 percent, were not sexually active, compared with about eleven percent of controls, a large and significant gap in the reported analysis. Condom use was less frequent among sexually active survivors than controls as well. Not using any birth control was similar in both groups. Among survivors, though, more intensive cancer treatment was tied to lower contraceptive use. The authors suggest this may reflect mistaken beliefs about fertility.
pmc-13439925:
Pfortmiller and colleagues tracked gene activity over time in 2026 in lab-grown heart muscle cells exposed to doxorubicin, a strong cancer drug that can damage the heart years later. Most models study only the immediate hit. The team treated heart cells from six donors for one day, then sampled responses right after treatment and after one and six days of recovery, alongside a DNA damage marker.

Damage signals rose after treatment and cleared by the final time point, but gene activity did not simply reset. A lasting signature of about five hundred genes stood out, rich in targets of the guardian protein p53, DNA damage response genes, and cell aging genes. The p53 targets stayed switched on while repair genes faded steadily over time. The authors read this as a new, altered cell state after repair, and offer the persistent genes as candidate early warning markers or drug targets.
pmc-13440125:
Sugahara and colleagues report real-world results for bladder-preserving chemoradiotherapy in Japan. Their 2026 paper reviews 175 patients treated with combined chemotherapy and radiation between 2010 and 2023 at seven institutions, an approach offered instead of bladder removal surgery. Nearly half the patients were judged unfit for that surgery in the first place.

Five years after treatment, 52 percent of patients were alive overall, and 73 percent had not died from bladder cancer. The bladder itself was preserved in 69 percent of patients at five years. Poorer general fitness predicted worse overall survival, while more advanced tumour stage predicted worse cancer-specific survival. Removing as much tumour as possible through the urethra beforehand was linked to better bladder preservation, supporting thorough local treatment first.
pmc-13441725:
Jinhua Yuan and colleagues ask whether a pre-treatment immune signal can flag which brucellosis patients will turn chronic, in a 2026 retrospective study. Brucellosis, a bacterial infection caught from livestock or unpasteurised dairy, can linger with lasting symptoms and organ damage. Records came from one Ningxia hospital covering diagnoses between January 2021 and June 2025. The team centred on interferon-gamma, an immune messenger measured before treatment began.

Higher pre-treatment interferon-gamma tracked with lower risk of chronic progression, and the link survived full adjustment. The relationship bent rather than running straight, with a turning point near the middle of the measured range. Patterns held across age, sex, exposure, occupation, and comorbidity groups. Adding the marker to a baseline prediction model sharpened its discrimination modestly but significantly. The authors present interferon-gamma as an objective early warning candidate for a disease that lacks such markers.
pmc-13443325:
Jeong and colleagues test a stain as a tie breaker between psoriasis and atopic dermatitis. The two skin diseases can look alike under the microscope when both show thickened, psoriasis like growth. The stain targets EMA, a marker of skin cell maturity, rarely checked in inflamed skin. Their 2026 study reviews fifteen patients with each disease and compares signs, microscope features, and stain strength and spread.

The diseases split on several signs. Thickened, leathery skin favored dermatitis, and wide tiny vessels favored psoriasis. A white cell type called eosinophils appeared in dermatitis only. The stain split them best. Strong EMA staining showed in three quarters of dermatitis cases but almost no psoriasis cases. Wide spread staining across the skin layer also favored dermatitis. Average stain strength ran about twice as high in dermatitis. Because weak staining overlaps, the authors advise using the stain as support, not a verdict.
pmc-13444125:
Zhuohui Liang and colleagues build fake patient histories for HIV research that keep real privacy in a 2026 paper. World HIV cohorts span decades, yet strict and clashing privacy rules block data sharing. Their model, MeLD, learns to spin mixed-type care paths of varied length, gaps and all.

Training drew on CCASAnet, a network with near 50,000 people and more than 30 years of follow-up. Head-to-head tests show MeLD beats top rival generators on use, likeness, and privacy marks. Death timing and risk factor effects came back close to real in the fake cohort. The team releases a large open fake cohort for free study. Such data may let labs worldwide test ideas without touching real records.
pmc-13444225:
Margot Gumbau and colleagues catalog parasitoid wasps that attack the melonworm moth in the Neotropics in a 2026 paper. The moth, Diaphania hyalinata, plagues squash kin crops across the region. No full list of its wasp foes had been pulled together before this work.

The review found 37 parasitoid wasps tied to the moth across its range. Field work in Guadeloupe reared eggs, larvae, and pupae, and turned up eight of them, all new island records. Each wasp was photographed and DNA-barcoded for future control use. Two leads stand out: an egg wasp, Trichogramma pretiosa, and a larval wasp with fresh promise. The authors urge care for side effects on local fauna in any release plan.
pmc-13444625:
Richard I. Joh and colleagues ask whether genes that sit close together on a chromosome help separate body processes switch on and off in step, in work published in 2026. Cells often need thousands of genes, spread across the genome, to act in concert when stress hits or growth programs start. The paper tests gene clustering as one way that such wide coordination stays in tune.

The group compared genomes from yeast to plants to people and found thousands of clustered gene pairs, some kept across species and some unique to one. Many pairs rose and fell together in normal human tissue. Control genes for one process often sat beside control genes for another, a layout the authors say lets cells build shared, tunable control units.
pmc-13445525:
Yuru Shui and colleagues stir pre-treated egg liquid into yogurt and track how the mix changes texture, nutrition, and small-molecule content, in a 2026 food study. Egg could enrich yogurt, yet its effect on the ferment and the final gel needed proof. The team compared plain milk, egg milk, and both yogurts after fermenting.

Egg raised the nutrition of milk and yogurt and gave a thicker mouthfeel with a tighter gel structure. Chemical profiling found nine hundred thirty-five small molecules in the products. Egg yogurt ran richer in amino acid products, fatty chains, and a class of membrane fats, with gains that held after fermenting. Pathways for membrane fat handling stood out, giving makers a base for egg-dairy goods with added function.
pmc-13445625:
Ganguly and a large team test grafts made from human placental tissue for segmental bone defects, injuries where a whole chunk of bone is lost. Their 2026 study creates a two millimeter gap in the thigh bone of male mice. It fills the gap with salt water, a standard growth protein called BMP-2, or one of three forms of the placental matrix: paste, membrane, or both. Healing and pain behavior are tracked for thirteen weeks.

BMP-2 grew the largest callus, the healing lump, yet its bone share of the defect ran lower than in untreated mice. The membrane plus paste graft raised that bone share above controls and matched BMP-2 on twist strength in lab tests. Pain behaviors, though, stayed high in every group and never returned to baseline, even where bone healed. The placental graft aided bone repair without adding pain, the authors conclude.
pmc-13446325:
Kausar Sadia Fakhruddin and colleagues review what the film on the tongue can say about gut disease, in a 2026 scoping review. The tongue's back is a rich biofilm shelf, long read in folk care as a mirror of body health. Modern microbe and multi-omics tools now let that claim be tested with rigor.

Twenty-five studies with more than four thousand five hundred people, mostly in East Asia, met the rules. Three patterns recurred: microbe shifts that grow more ordered from mild inflammation to cancer, shared fat-handling signals across study layers, and strong shaping by the coating's own color and thickness. All proof was snapshot in kind, with no outside checks, so the authors hold clinic use at bay for now.
pmc-13447725:
Massimo Imazio weighs blood microRNAs as a possible test for heart muscle inflammation in a 2026 commentary. Myocarditis, inflammation of the heart muscle, ranges from silent lab changes to sudden death, and no single current test is both safe and decisive. Tiny RNA molecules that tune gene activity circulate stably in blood, raising hope for an informative liquid biopsy.

A pooled analysis covered here gathered twenty-six studies in viral myocarditis, finding forty-two altered microRNAs. Combined accuracy looked strong on headline measures, including for the fulminant form. Imazio cautions that the pool mixes different molecules, sources, platforms, thresholds and patient groups, so the result describes a promising class, not a ready test. Standardised assays, defined cut-offs and prospective validation must come before clinic use, he argues.
pmc-13447825:
Juanru Guo and colleagues present a soft segmentation framework for spatial transcriptomics, gene mapping that keeps tissue location, in 2026 work. High-resolution platforms capture RNA at spots that do not align with cell borders, so assigning messages to the right cell is a core challenge. Curved tissues such as gut lining also resist flat analysis, hiding gradients along their length.

Their deep learning method gives probabilistic assignments from capture spots to nearby nuclei, then unrolls folded tissue onto flat coordinates for analysis. Accuracy beat existing approaches across platforms in the authors' tests. Applied to mouse small intestine, the method segmented over four hundred thousand cells and revealed zoned gene programmes along the maturing villus, the finger-like absorptive surface. Signals from the gut lumen reshaped upper villus identity in their findings.
pmc-13448025:
Treah Haggerty and colleagues explore whether adult medical weight treatment changes health habits for the whole household in a 2026 interview study. Family-based programmes help children with obesity, yet little was known about spillover when a parent joins a clinic programme and starts obesity medication. Parents living with at least one child were asked what shifted at home.

Ten adults enrolled in a medical weight clinic between late 2024 and mid 2025 were interviewed in depth. Four themes emerged, covering deliberate personal food choices, unplanned family diet changes that followed, and wider awareness of health behaviour across the household. Parents also voiced optimism about lifelong change alongside worry over insurance coverage for medication. Household dynamics deserve a place in childhood obesity care, the authors conclude.
pmc-13449925:
Bryant and a large team present a developmental brain atlas for the baboon, in this 2026 resource paper. The baboon is an Old World monkey prized in neuroscience for its large brain. Comparing brain growth across species requires a standard reference that changes with age, so they built one that follows baboons from infancy to adolescence.

Their atlas, named BaBa21, combines structural MRI scans and tissue probability maps. The maps come from 21 olive baboons imaged at four timepoints. Imaging started about two weeks after birth. It ended at sexual maturity around five years. The method, called BABACOOL in the paper, can also generate a template for any age in between, so researchers are not limited to the four scanned ages. The team releases the resource openly to standardize baboon neuroimaging and to support comparisons with human and macaque development.
pmc-13450025:
Shubham Lodha and co-authors recount in 2026 an advanced HIV case from central India that punished the idea of one tidy diagnosis. In tuberculosis country, body-wide illness in a patient with weakened defenses defaults to tuberculosis in most clinicians' minds. Their patient, a 35-year-old man, carried three separate processes at once. Parvovirus B19 was suppressing his bone marrow. He also had an inflamed, stone-like kidney infection called xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis, and HIV-driven cognitive disorder with spinal cord involvement.

The kidney infection held a surprise, growing both a carbapenem-resistant Escherichia coli and Mycobacterium chelonae, the latter never before reported as a cause of this kidney disease in HIV. Each condition demanded its own treatment, and finding one explained nothing about the others. The authors use the case to argue in advanced HIV, rival diagnoses should be chased side by side, especially where the TB reflex is strongest.
pmc-13452125:
Ao-Men Lu and co-authors follow in 2026 a blood-and-belly index and later heart disease in older Chinese adults with early metabolic risk. The index blends a sugar-fat score with a belly fat gauge. Data came from a long-running national aging study, with 7,132 adults in the early stages of a heart-kidney-metabolic web and no open heart disease at the start.

Across a median nine years, 1,688 of them had a first heart event. The team set starting index values, a two-reading burden score, and rise-or-fall patterns from grouped readings against those events. The design tests whether a cheap index, read more than once, can flag who in this wide risk pool needs care first.
pmc-13452225:
Rihab Fannouch and Said Tounsi sort in 2026 what drives carbon output in rich and poor lands, using three decades of World Bank data. They trained three deep learning models on macro, energy, people, and trade factors for 1990 to 2023, then read which inputs drove the scores with a forest model and link checks.

One model, a layered perceptron, read the patterns best. In poorer lands, emissions tied most to the energy mix and raw resource wealth. In mid and rich lands, trade exposure, fuel reliance, factory work, and crowd pressure rose to the top. The authors stress these are forecast links, not causes, and they urge climate plans cut to each group's shape.
pmc-13453725:
Erickah Mary Therese R Dy-Calayag and Claudine Yap Silva test a cheap trick for proving nail fungus under the microscope. Confirming the infection matters since the oral cure runs for months. Their 2026 study uses 84 archived nail clipping slides from 2019 to 2023, half proven fungus positive by the standard special stain and half negative.

Reading the routine stain under fluorescence light, a method that makes fungus glow, caught 80.95 percent of the true cases. It wrongly flagged almost none of the clean slides, for a specificity of 97.62 percent. Misses came mostly where fungus was sparse or in yeast form without the usual threads. The authors offer the trick as a fast, low cost helper for labs that already own a fluorescence scope.
pmc-13453825:
Natalie Rajabi and Prakash V A K Ramdass pool published studies on how often irritable bowel syndrome and chronic fatigue syndrome strike the same people. Both conditions drag on for years, sap life quality, and drive heavy health care use. Their 2026 review searched four databases through February 2026 and kept 22 studies, with 18 feeding the pooled math.

People with the fatigue syndrome had 7.20 times the odds of bowel syndrome compared with controls. Across studies, about 37 percent of fatigue patients also had the bowel condition, though estimates swung widely. Which rule book defined each condition shifted the numbers a lot, the team found. The authors read the tight overlap as a sign of shared roots, such as immune and gut brain signaling faults, and urge joint screening.
pmc-13454125:
Duanduan Liu, Jiayi Wan, Shuo Gao, and Hongye Li review a strategy that pairs heat with electric fields to split water for hydrogen more cheaply. Plain electrolysis stalls on the slow oxygen making half and eats power. Their 2026 review gathers work on thermo electric coupling, where waste heat from factories or power plants joins the electric drive.

Heat helps in several ways beyond speeding flow: it damps a charge imbalance fault, steers electron spin states, and strains catalyst surfaces into better shapes. Matched with renewable power, the pairing raises energy efficiency while using heat that would otherwise be thrown away. The authors also map the roadblocks, from materials that must survive heat and current together to system design. They frame the approach as a practical route to cheaper green hydrogen.
pmc-13454325:
Nicolás Padilla-Raygoza leads a ten-author team reporting, in 2026, a test of sound waves for finding hip problems in newborns. Hip dysplasia is common in early life, and standard hand checks catch only hips that slip out of place. The team tried a small device that sends sound through the hip and reads what comes out the other side.

One hundred babies aged 4 to 27 days were tested at a hospital in Guanajuato, Mexico. Two examiners each ran the sound test three times per hip, and ultrasound served as the reference check. Ultrasound found dysplasia in 15 right hips and 18 left hips out of 200. The sound device scored above 90 percent on the main accuracy measures, and repeat readings agreed well. The authors say the device can aid, not replace, standard checks.
pmc-13454825:
Xiaokang Zeng and four colleagues report, in a 2026 mouse study, that a mitochondrial helper protein keeps natural killer cells numerous and sharp. These killer cells form a first line of defense against tumors and viruses. The protein, Hspa9, guards the energy hubs inside blood cells. The team deleted it only in blood-forming cells and watched the killer cells.

Killer cell counts fell sharply across the spleen, bone marrow, and liver in the altered mice. The remaining cells released less of a key attack signal and showed weaker killing marks. Surface sensors tied to growth and maturity shifted as well, suggesting stalled development. A central growth pathway, Akt with mTOR, ran quieter in the deficient cells. The authors name Hspa9 a promising handle for tuning killer cell strength in future immune therapies.
pmc-13457125:
Ming Diao, Yaxi Zhu, and Hailing Tang compare, in a 2026 meta-analysis, artificial intelligence against the dermatologist's magnifier for judging whether a pigmented skin spot may be malignant. Sorting such spots well catches melanoma early and spares healthy skin needless cutting. The team searched four databases and kept ten studies with seventeen test arms.

Performance overlapped heavily. Dermoscopy sensitivity ranged from about 42 to 97 percent across studies, and AI landed in a similar span. AI specificity likewise overlapped the clinicians' range. In the single study of clinicians aided by AI, sensitivity was perfect and specificity solid, a hint that partnership may beat either alone. Spread between studies was wide, reflecting varied algorithms and settings. No publication bias showed. The authors conclude that today's AI matches standard dermoscopy on average, with consistency, not peak skill, as the open problem.
pmc-13457725: HPV vaccine health beliefs — latent profiles and their links to vaccination intention among college students, globally. Ya Liu, Haiming Cao, Jiaqi Li, and others profile the beliefs. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is HPV. It profiles students' HPV vaccine beliefs. Beliefs, latent.
pmc-13459925:
Yanhua Luo and co-authors used single cell gene reading to watch how inhaled hydrogen gas reshapes immune signals in the gut during sepsis recovery. Sepsis, the body's runaway response to infection, damages the gut barrier early, and hydrogen has shown protective hints without a known mechanism. In their 2026 mouse study, animals with surgically induced sepsis received hydrogen or not. Gut tissue underwent cell by cell reading alongside barrier leak tests and inflammation measures.

Hydrogen significantly reduced gut injury and barrier leakage, shown by lower leak markers in blood, and calmed whole body inflammation in the treated animals. The reading revealed sepsis had expanded a non functional B cell population and skewed T cell development, and hydrogen restored both toward normal balance. Analysis of signals between cell types showed the gas reshaping the web that coordinates mucosal immunity. Hydrogen's gut effects can now be targeted more precisely, the authors argue.
pmc-13460225:
Xin Qiao, Jing-Jing Zhang, Bin Liu, and Jian-Wen Qin searched in 2026 for factors that predict survival in pleural mesothelioma patients. In this cancer of the lung lining, malignant fluid builds up around the lung. Their Tianjin cohort held 71 patients diagnosed between 2015 and 2025, followed by regular telephone checks. Survival averaged a median of thirty months, and models tested clinical and lab measures, especially tests on the pleural fluid itself.

Four routine measures stood on their own. High lactate dehydrogenase in the fluid and high fibrinogen each multiplied the death hazard several-fold. Larger average platelet size also worsened outlook, and a higher lymphocyte count proved protective. All four come from ordinary baseline testing, though the authors want confirmation from larger future studies before clinical use.
pmc-13461325:
Alexandra Grigoreanu and colleagues surveyed veterinary students and teaching staff in Romania on dog-assisted support programs for campus wellbeing. Such programs bring trained dogs into study settings to cut stress, yet their acceptance inside veterinary education was untested.

The survey drew 200 students and 99 staff, who answered questions on dogs, program knowledge, and their own mental health. Both groups liked dogs and strongly backed the programs, seeing gains for stress, mental health, and the learning climate. One in five students, 20.5 percent, reported a diagnosed mental health condition, underlining the need for support. Women answered more warmly and saw less risk than men, Grigoreanu notes, though logistics and anxiety concerns remained.
pmc-13461725:
Jingna Tao and colleagues built machine learning models that stage autoimmune gastritis from scope images and blood tests. Autoimmune gastritis is a slow stomach disease where the immune system destroys acid-making cells, and staging today depends on observer judgement.

The study enrolled 203 patients classed into three stages by how much healthy stomach lining remained. Seven algorithms were trained on five feature sets, mixing standard scope views, magnified imaging, and a serum panel. A random forest using scope plus blood features staged best, with a macro-AUC of 0.878 across the three stages. Lost stomach folds and two blood markers ranked among the strongest staging signals, Tao reports. Barrett's oesophagus, a risky throat-lining change, appeared in 66.8 percent of patients, backing routine checks in this group.
pmc-13461825:
Pastorino and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how to free natural killer cells, immune cells that can kill cancer without prior training, to attack solid tumors. Two braking systems dominate their control: KIR receptors and the NKG2A axis, which keep the cells tolerant of healthy tissue. Tumors exploit these brakes, in part by keeping or raising levels of a surface tag, HLA-E, that presses the second brake.

Pastorino notes that blocking either brake alone has brought only modest gains in most solid tumors, despite strong lab logic. The surrounding tumor tissue adds more blocks: physical barriers, low oxygen, metabolic stress, and suppressive networks that limit entry and staying power. Future plans, the authors argue, should combine brake release with hand-picked or engineered killer cells that resist exhaustion. Added treatments should remodel the tumor niche so the cells can reach it and keep fighting.
pmc-13462225:
Kanvinde, Khurana, and Mudaliar wrote a 2026 clinical guide to vitamin B12 deficiency in children, a common yet often missed nutritional disorder. Shortage can damage brain development for good, stunt growth, and disturb blood formation, above all where mothers are deficient or diets are vegetarian. Brain symptoms often appear before blood changes do.

Diagnosis blends the clinical picture with blood counts, blood film review, and B12 testing, Kanvinde explains. Extra markers such as methylmalonic acid and homocysteine sharpen the picture when results sit near the cut-off. Inherited faults in B12 handling can now be found by gene testing and need lifelong care. Oral B12 works for most diet related cases, while injections suit severe anaemia, nerve damage, or poor uptake from food. Delayed treatment may leave lasting nerve damage.
pmc-13463825:
Viraj Bandsode and ten co-authors read Salmonella genomes from soil and water to track virulence and drug resistance worldwide. Lab data skew toward rich countries, leaving wild strains from poorer regions poorly mapped. The team sequenced fifty-four fresh isolates from India and set them beside global collections.

The joint set held 1,399 genomes, and over half of the Indian isolates resisted many drugs at once. Rare genes for colistin resistance, a last-line drug, already circulate in wild strains. Core attack genes stayed alike across groups, while extra resistance and plasmid loads shifted by family line. Wild waters and soils, the authors warn, form one linked global pool of risk genes.
pmc-13465125:
Mengying Guan and Hua Hao review CDK4/6 blocker drugs in hormone-driven breast cancer, where the drugs have redrawn the treatment map. Three drugs in the class serve both early and spread disease. The review weighs them side by side rather than as interchangeable copies.

Real gaps in benefit appear between the three drugs across trial settings. Resistance grows through two broad routes: loss of the drug's target machinery, or detours that bypass the block entirely. Sorting resistance that way can guide what to try next, the authors argue. Protein shredders, new hormone blockers, and antibody-guided drugs lead the next wave. Sharper patient picking may gain more than yet more drugs, they conclude.
pmc-13465325:
Haoqun Zhang and four co-authors pair eye tracking with taste panels for three red bean and coix seed drinks. Self-report scores can bend under memory and wording ease, so the team also logged where eyes lingered on the answer scale. Twenty-four volunteers rated scent, taste, feelings, and liking for each drink.

The score a person picked and the score their gaze held longest agreed strongly, and both ranked the drinks in the same order. Gaze scores, though, swung too widely person to person to swap for picked scores. Warmth and sweetness tracked with pleasant feelings and with liking across both read types. One feeling word, good-natured, clung most steadily to liking, which marks gaze as a helpful side channel.
pmc-13465925:
Root-Bernstein published a 2026 study linking two diseases long thought separate. People with type 1 diabetes face a higher risk of multiple sclerosis, and the reverse also holds. Both diseases involve immune attacks, but the shared trigger has stayed unclear. His work tests whether diabetes-linked immune proteins also target myelin, the nerve coating.

Lab searches matched immune receptor codes from patients with both diseases. Tests then showed diabetes-linked antibodies sticking to myelin basic protein in samples. Most patient blood samples reacted to myelin, while healthy samples did not. Certain gut bacteria proteins also mimic myelin, a fresh clue in the data. Such cross-reactions could explain nerve damage seen in long-term diabetes. More lab work is still needed to prove this chain of cause in patients.
pmc-13466425:
Ruixiang Yuan and eleven colleagues published this 2026 study of a gene that helps the fungus Verticillium dahliae attack cotton plants. This fungus causes Verticillium wilt, a serious cotton disease, and it uses secreted enzymes to break down plant cell walls. The gene, named Vdbgl1, makes an enzyme that digests glucan, a wall sugar, and it switches on strongly during infection. The team tested what happens when the gene is removed or silenced.

Deleting the gene slowed colony growth by about a fifth and cut spore production and germination. The mutant fungus was also more sensitive to wall stress and salt stress. On cotton, the mutants caused a disease index roughly 19 to 28 percent lower, and fungal biomass fell by 42.7 to 61.8 percent in the plants tested. Silencing the gene from inside the plant gave similar protection. The authors present Vdbgl1 as a promising target for wilt control.
pmc-13466525:
Yung-Yi Lan, Rujith Kovinthapillai, Andrzej Kędzia, and Elżbieta Niechciał review how to cut dangerous acid buildup at the start of type 1 diabetes in children, in a 2026 article. This crisis, diabetic ketoacidosis, often strikes because early symptoms get missed, and poorer or rural families face it more. Screening blood for early autoantibodies can flag the disease before symptoms begin.

The review gathers evidence on who faces the highest risk, how screening programs run, and which early treatments might slow the disease itself. Sources span trials, guidelines, and pooled analyses from 2011 onward, plus classic older work. The authors argue that finding the disease in its quiet stage is the strongest lever against a preventable emergency.
pmc-13466825:
Ziliang He, Junlong Ma, Yun Liu, and Zhanhong Du review how the body reacts against electrodes implanted in the brain, and how surface treatments might calm that reaction, in a 2026 article. Long-term implants power brain-machine interfaces and deep brain stimulation, yet the tissue response slowly degrades signals: resistance climbs, noise grows, and usable channels vanish.

The chain starts with insertion injury and protein coating, runs through barrier leakage, immune activation, and reactive support cells, and ends in scar tissue with lost neurons nearby. Countermeasures reviewed include non-stick coatings, helpful molecules fixed to the surface, drug-releasing designs, and interfaces that actively soothe immunity. The authors insist on linking each chemistry to the exact step it interrupts.
pmc-13466925:
Malak Ahmed Almalki and colleagues present two children with a rare bacterial infection of the middle ear that masquerades as ordinary chronic ear discharge, in a 2026 case report. Only about fifty such cases appear in the literature. The germ usually travels up the Eustachian tube from the throat and demands surgery plus long antibiotic courses.

The first child, a seven-year-old boy with Joubert syndrome, kept draining from one ear six months after a ventilation tube was placed; a second cleaning plus three months of antibiotics cleared it. The second, a ten-year-old girl, drained for four months despite several drug courses. Tissue from surgery gave the diagnosis in both, underlining that stubborn ear discharge deserves a biopsy.
pmc-13467125:
Abdulaziz Alshomrani, Anum Hussaini, and Elhadi Miskeen run a national survey of long COVID in Saudi Arabia, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. The team reached 1,790 adults with confirmed infections across all thirteen regions between mid-2023 and late 2024. Long COVID followed the World Health Organization definition: symptoms lasting at least three months with no other explanation.

About a third of respondents met that definition. Fatigue dominated the symptom list, followed by breathlessness and thinking problems. Being female roughly doubled the odds after adjustment, and a harder initial illness also predicted lasting symptoms. The study adds healthcare use and daily burden measures, giving planners the first nationally framed numbers for the kingdom.
pmc-13467525:
Isabella Peetz and colleagues review what the fruit fly brain teaches about repairing injured nervous systems. The fly, Drosophila melanogaster, offers a rich toolkit of genetic tricks for watching neurons and support cells regrow after damage.

Evidence from crush, cut, and stab injury models shows flies can regrow nerve fibres, support cells, and even neurons. New support cells clearly arise from existing ones in the central brain and the eye lobes. Where new neurons come from is murkier: in eye lobes they spring from sleeping stem cells, unproven for the central brain. Peetz frames these open questions as the manual's missing pages, guiding the next repair experiments.
pmc-13467725:
Sadaf Memon and colleagues scan the genome in 2026 for regions tied to grain protein content in hulless barley, a nutritious cereal grown in the Tibetan regions of China. Protein content decides much of the grain quality but shifts strongly with environment.
