The team analyzed 1,453 patients with blocked front-brain arteries treated in a first-pass device registry, comparing scans a day after treatment and modeling risk factors for each bleeding pattern.

Four in ten patients showed some bleeding on imaging, though only a small share, just over three percent, had symptoms from it. Diabetes, severe stroke scores, and high blood sugar at arrival raised the overall risk, while a healthy early scan score and having atrial fibrillation lowered it. Specific scan and sugar patterns predicted particular subtypes. The authors urge trials to report bleeding by subtype, since lumping them hides who is truly at risk.
pmc-13550025:
Morató, Peña-Salazar, Grande, and the STRESSURG group measure surgeons' trauma after patients die unexpectedly. Their 2026 paper reports the first international validated survey on this burden. Unexpected deaths during or just after surgery devastate operating teams. The psychological fallout was poorly quantified until now. A forty-two item questionnaire went to surgeons worldwide.

Three hundred fifty-four surgeons responded. The survey used the Impact of Event Scale-Revised instrument. Nearly half scored in the clinically relevant distress range. About twenty-nine percent met the threshold for probable PTSD. A quarter showed severe distress levels. Acting as the primary surgeon raised distress sharply. Mid-career surgeons suffered more than juniors or seniors. Only eight percent had received institutional psychological support. Over half believed such support should be mandatory. Structured support programs are urgently needed, they argue.
pmc-13550525:
Harriet L. S. Lawford and colleagues run a single blood survey that reads immunity to seventeen pathogens at once across Tonga, in a 2026 serosurveillance study. Dried blood spots from nearly eighteen hundred people aged five and up, collected in mid-2024 across three island groups, were tested on a bead platform carrying twenty-six antigens. The design hunts immunity gaps and transmission hotspots in one pass instead of seventeen separate studies.

Lymphatic filariasis antibodies climbed with age and peaked in the Ha'apai group. Dengue exposure topped ninety percent in people over fifty, highest on the main island. Vaccine-preventable coverage ran high overall, yet measles immunity, at about eighty-six percent, sat below the level elimination requires, despite historically strong vaccination. Most pathogens clustered significantly by village. The authors argue the platform lets Pacific health teams aim campaigns precisely.
pmc-13551825:
ZhenKun Xiao, LiangJie Deng, YongHong Duan, Bing Wang, and AiHua Liu published a 2026 study pairing global burden estimates with individual cohort data on stroke tied to blood sugar and cholesterol dysfunction. Global Burden of Disease figures traced Chinese stroke deaths and disability from high fasting glucose and high LDL cholesterol between 1990 and 2023. A Chinese aging cohort served for discovery, with a United States cohort validating biomarker findings.

Age-standardized death and disability rates fell over the period, yet absolute numbers stayed large in 2023 in the reported estimates. A biomarker called eGDR, reflecting estimated glucose disposal, consistently tied to lower stroke risk and topped the predictor rankings in machine learning analyses. Adding it to standard risk models was tested for discrimination and clinical benefit.
pmc-13556025:
Yuanwu Zou and six colleagues studied in 2026 how eating patterns relate to chronic disease among people living at high altitude in Tibetan areas of China. National nutrition surveys rarely reach these regions, where food habits differ sharply. The team used food frequency questionnaires with 606 residents, extracted five dietary patterns statistically, and compared disease rates across low, middle, and high adherence to each pattern.

About four in ten participants reported at least one chronic disease. Patterns heavy in salt, carbohydrate, and fat, and a meat-heavy high protein pattern, both linked to more disease, as did smoking and local tea drinking. A traditional Tibetan pattern and regular physical exercise linked to less disease. The results give local health planners a picture of which habits to encourage and which to challenge.
pmc-13556325:
Qian Sun and ten colleagues found in 2026 that a widely used immune-suppressing drug, mycophenolate mofetil, also blocks poxviruses such as monkeypox. Approved antivirals for these viruses are scarce and resistance is a concern. Because vaccinia virus is a close, safer relative of the monkeypox virus, the team screened ten approved drugs that target nucleotide building enzymes in host cells, using vaccinia first.

The drug hit both viruses hard and acted after the virus had entered the cell. It works by stopping a host enzyme the virus needs for making DNA building blocks. The drug breaks that enzyme's partnership with a protective partner protein and forces it into inactive rod-and-ring bundles, draining the pool of building blocks. The authors propose this host-directed route as a template for broad poxvirus defences in future outbreaks.
pmc-13559125:
Bowen Liang and three colleagues compare two open operations used to fix vesicoureteral reflux in children, a condition where urine flows backward from bladder toward kidney. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis weighs the Cohen technique against the Lich-Gregoir technique using only studies that compared them directly. Three databases were searched through March 2026.

Nine retrospective studies covering 655 children met the criteria. Persistent reflux after surgery, overall complications, reoperation, and later febrile urinary infection occurred at similar rates under both techniques. Lich-Gregoir operations finished faster and meant shorter hospital stays. Urinary retention after surgery, though, struck more often after Lich-Gregoir, while blood in the urine was more common after Cohen. The authors rate their certainty low to very low, weakened by retrospective designs and uneven complication definitions. Choice, they conclude, should weigh these trade-offs family by family.
pmc-13559625:
Ruizhe Yue, Zheng Wang, and Hao Zhang ask whether removing the primary tumor helps women whose triple-negative breast cancer has already spread to organs by the time of diagnosis. Their 2026 study uses the US SEER registry for patients diagnosed between 2010 and 2020 with metastases in liver, lung, or brain. Propensity matching paired operated and unoperated patients with similar profiles.

Of 1,827 patients, 543 had primary tumor surgery. After matching formed 507 pairs, median overall survival reached fifteen months in the surgery group against nine months without. Breast cancer-specific survival showed the same pattern. Adjusted models kept surgery tied to longer survival, and several sensitivity checks agreed. The authors caution that healthier patients may simply be chosen for surgery more often, so the link may reflect selection rather than a true treatment effect. They call their results hypothesis-generating.
pmc-13560125:
Virginia Vigiano Benedetti and colleagues profile the fibroblasts that surround breast tumors and uncover a previously unrecognized subset tied to immune suppression. Their 2026 study integrates three single-cell sequencing datasets from 29 patients and cross-checks patterns in cancer atlas bulk data. Cancer-associated fibroblasts shape progression and treatment response, but their flavors differ between breast cancer subtypes.

Alongside three known stromal populations, the team found a cluster they name metabolic stressed CAFs. These cells run programs for antigen presentation, stress response, sugar burning, and matrix remodeling. Their abundance rose as T cell presence and function fell. Triple-negative tumors held immune-infiltrated yet constrained environments rich in these cells, while Luminal A tumors showed weaker infiltration and mixed patterns. Several of the subset's genes predicted prognosis and chemotherapy response. The authors propose the cells as targets for improving immunotherapy.
pmc-13560425:
Yuqing Liu and three colleagues review how extracellular vesicles carry messages between the brain and the body's organs in Alzheimer's disease. Their 2026 article questions the brain-only picture of the illness, synthesizing evidence across six organ axes: liver, heart, gut, lung, bone, and fat. Vesicles move proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids across fluids and barriers.

Evidence runs strongest for the gut-brain, liver-brain, and fat-brain routes, while other axes rest mostly on animal models or engineered vesicles. Organ-derived vesicles may sway brain inflammation, blood vessel health, metabolism, barrier integrity, and amyloid or tau processes, and brain vesicles may in turn disturb peripheral organs. Translation faces stubborn obstacles: vesicle mixtures are heterogeneous, their organ of origin is hard to prove, and isolation methods lack standards. The authors frame vesicles as one signaling layer inside a wider systemic network.
pmc-13560625:
Svitlana Pidoprygora and three colleagues show how global comics made Ukraine visible yet distorted before 2014. Their 2026 article reads three case studies across comic traditions: Hergé's Tintin in the Land of the Soviets from 1929. The others are a 1976 Nestor Makhno comic by Spain Rodriguez and the Italian Ivan Karine series from the early 1960s. Visual and story analysis meets a postcolonial lens.

The authors name the mechanism distorted visibility: Ukrainian land, figures, and symbols appear, but folded into Soviet, Russian, or imperial stories. Hergé homogenizes Soviet space with Russian cultural markers. Rodriguez frames the anarchist Makhno through Russian Revolution mythology, leaving Ukraine a backdrop. Ivan Karine borrows Cossack imagery for a Russian imperial adventure. Naming, spatial framing, iconography, and narrative position each do part of the displacing work. The authors offer the case as a lens on cultural erasure in transnational storytelling.
pmc-13561225:
Angad Tiwari and five colleagues published this 2026 case report of one patient with mast cell leukaemia, the rarest and most aggressive form of systemic mastocytosis, a cancer of mast cells. Their patient was an 86-year-old man previously treated for a sinus lymphoma, in remission since 2017, and for prostate cancer in 2019. He arrived with acute pancytopenia, a drop in all blood cell types, first presumed to be lymphoma returning.

His serum tryptase, a mast cell marker, exceeded 11,999 nanograms per millilitre, and marrow sampling showed 20 percent abnormal mast cells, confirming the leukaemia. Gene sequencing revealed pathogenic variants in six genes, including TP53, plus a rare KIT variant; the usual KIT mutation was absent. He declined treatment with the targeted drug midostaurin, deteriorated and died two weeks later. The authors stress that unexplained low blood counts warrant suspicion of this disease, and that genomic profiling clarifies tangled cases.
pmc-13561725:
Hernandez and co-authors ask whether earlier injections change later surgery in this 2026 study of Peyronie's disease, the scarring condition that bends the penis and impairs sexual function. Collagenase injections dissolve plaque non-surgically, but clinicians worried that prior treatment might compromise the tunica tissue and worsen outcomes of plication, the tightening operation used when injections fall short.

From 926 men in their hospital series, 322 had received them, and 7.8 percent of those later needed plication against 5.6 percent of injection-naive men. Starting curvature was similar between surgical groups, and correction was near-identical, ending at 4.6 degrees against 3.0 degrees on average after surgery, both over ninety percent reductions. Early problems ran numerically higher after treatment, 20.0 versus 2.9 percent, without reaching that bar, and revision rates matched. The authors reassure that prior collagenase should not deter indicated surgery.
pmc-13562625:
Yifei Feng and six colleagues put a new surgical robot, the Carina platform, through preclinical trials for rectal surgery. Robotic help promises steadier work in the narrow pelvis, but each new system must prove itself before human use. The 2026 team first planned port and cart positions on three-dimensional reconstructions. Six pigs then underwent robot-assisted rectal removal, split into acute and longer-term groups. Working times, device errors, and complications were logged, and the longer-term pigs were examined after four weeks.

Every pig operation finished successfully with no device-related problems during surgery. The follow-up animals recovered well, and their joined bowel ends healed favourably by the 28-day check. Port and cart layouts were then confirmed on three human cadavers, where a full rectal resection could be simulated. The authors judge the platform feasible and safe at this stage, while noting that patient trials remain ahead.
pmc-13562725:
Saman Chalaki and four colleagues show that dairy cows which slim down too fast after calving are, at gene level, dismantling their own muscle. The weeks around calving push high-yielding cows into energy deficit, and they raid body reserves to fill the gap. The 2026 study followed 200 multiparous Holsteins giving at least 30 kilograms of milk daily, grouping them by condition-score loss to day 42. Muscle biopsies from 40 cows at days 21 and 42 measured genes for protein breakdown and building, while blood carried the chemical fingerprints of muscle loss.

Cows losing half a condition unit or more switched on the tagging machinery that marks muscle protein for destruction, including MuRF1 and Atrogin-1, and dialled down a synthesis regulator. Their blood held more creatinine and 3-methylhistidine, both in step with how much condition was lost. The authors urge tight condition management across the transition weeks to protect muscle and metabolic health.
pmc-13562925:
Wimalasena and colleagues present a systematic review, published in 2026. A bibliometric analysis accompanies it. The topic is research on micro-influencers. These are social media creators with small but engaged followings. Brands use them instead of celebrities. The team followed PRISMA methods. They analysed sixty-eight papers from the Scopus database. The papers ran from 2020 to 2025. Mapping software charted themes and connections.

The analysis maps how the field is structured. It shows which topics and methods dominate. It also shows where the gaps lie. Community-driven and authentic engagement distinguish these creators. The authors use the map to propose future research directions. Marketing scholars studying this fast-growing promotional channel are the audience.
pmc-13563725:
Congcong Yan and six colleagues trace molecular conversations between the meninges, the immune-active membranes wrapping the brain, and the hippocampus in Alzheimer's disease. How those membranes talk to the vulnerable memory region was largely unknown. Their 2026 study used two mouse models, one for amyloid disease and one for tau disease, layering bulk gene sequencing, protein measurement, and spatial gene mapping across disease stages. The design separated true disease signals from ordinary ageing.

A sturdy 19-gene hippocampal signature emerged, repeating in an independent dataset from each model. Spatial maps defined a progression axis along which meningeal spots clustered at the advanced end. Message-and-receiver analysis nominated signalling pairs between the tissues, tied to the states of microglia, the brain's immune cells. The authors are explicit that these computer-inferred channels, drawn from mice, are hypotheses. Human tissue checks and perturbation tests must come before any treatment talk.
pmc-13564125:
Shaun Shadaker and thirteen colleagues published this 2026 report of a population-based hepatitis C survey in Uzbekistan, carried out in 2022 to guide the country's national elimination programme. Earlier estimates of infection rates ranged wildly, up to 9.6 percent. The team sampled blood from adults and children across seven regions covering nearly 60 percent of the country. They measured both antibodies, which mark past exposure, and viral RNA, which marks current infection.

Antibody prevalence came out at 3.9 percent in adults and 1.1 percent in children, while active infection measured 2.0 percent and 0.5 percent respectively. Rates in Tashkent city ran higher, at 6.6 percent antibody prevalence among those surveyed there. Past surgery, invasive medical procedures and incarceration were tied to exposure, while invasive dental work and tattoos were tied to active infection. The authors present these as the most robust national estimates available, considerably lower than the older pooled figure yet above modelled estimates.
pmc-13572325:
Ravit Pertez-Machluf and colleagues ask, in a 2026 retrospective study, whether a past cesarean birth predicts failure of drug treatment for first-trimester miscarriage. Records covered 716 patients treated with mifepristone and misoprostol at a major center between 2019 and 2022, comparing those whose treatment completed against those needing further intervention.

Treatment failed in just under thirty percent. A prior cesarean nearly doubled the adjusted odds of failure, and each extra day of pregnancy age added a little risk. Failure rates ran higher still in the cesarean subgroup analysis. Among women without a cesarean history and earlier pregnancies, bleeding during treatment oddly marked lower failure. Counselors can now give cesarean-scarred patients a more honest estimate before choosing drug treatment.
pmc-13573425:
Hafiz Muhammad Obaid Kazmi, with 12 colleagues, reports a 2026 mouse study of glycine as a shield against brain harm from a cancer drug. Cisplatin cures many cancers but inflames the brain, above all the memory centre and the front cortex. Glycine, a simple amino acid, fights inflammation and oxidation and costs little.

Twenty-five male mice were split into five groups with varied timing of the drug and glycine over 14 or 28 days. Blood levels of a key inflammatory signal rose most in the long drug-only group. Glycine given alongside the drug held that signal lowest, and late glycine still helped. Brain slices showed nerve cells better preserved in glycine groups than in drug-only groups. The authors back wider preclinical tests of glycine as an add-on shield.
pmc-13575225:
Nebahat Sahin leads a 2026 hunt for drugs that block AXL, a protein found at high levels in many cancers and tied to poor survival. AXL helps cancer cells grow, spread, and resist treatment, and genetic studies support it as a drug target. The team screened compound libraries on the computer first.

Virtual screening, docking, and motion simulations narrowed the field, pinpointing contact spots inside the AXL binding pocket. Three lead compounds then went into lab tests on four breast cancer cell lines. Each slowed cancer cell growth, with the compound coded STOCK1N-80636 the strongest. One lead was nebivolol, a known drug from another field. The authors present the trio as starting points for AXL-focused drug development.
pmc-13576125:
Ji-Hyung Park leads a 2026 postmortem study of an Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphin watched for years off Jeju Island, South Korea. The dolphin carried a mouth mass and a deformed jaw, noted over six years with three years of close monitoring. After death, the team combined scans, tissue work, microbe studies, and gene activity profiling.

Scans showed a jaw fracture at the mass site. Tissue checks ruled out viral growths and one tumour type, supporting a trauma-caused fibroma, a benign scar-like growth. Lung findings pointed to aspiration pneumonia as the main cause of death, with the bacterium Parvimonas micra dominant in a mixed infection. Chemical pollutant levels matched those typical of aged dolphins, with no sign they drove the final illness. The authors frame the case as a first for marine mammals.
pmc-13578325:
Prashantha Murahari and co-authors dope cadmium sulfide films with antimony to build a better ultraviolet light sensor, in a 2026 materials study. The films were sprayed onto glass by a mist based method. Crystal checks showed the same basic structure in every film, with the two percent antimony mix giving the cleanest crystals and the biggest, tightest grains.

That same mix soaked up more light and answered UV rays most strongly in current tests. Its response and recovery both landed near a second, and repeated cycles held steady over long runs. Too much or too little antimony did worse, so the middle dose carried the day. The authors offer the film as a durable pick for UV sensing in fields from flame alarms to space work.
pmc-13578425:
B Madhana and colleagues survey what builds trust in online banking in India, in a 2026 study of more than five hundred university students. Fast growth in digital banking has raised fears about fraud and data theft. The team asked how safety knowledge, felt threats, and teaching support from schools shape trust, then built predictive models on the answers.

Safety knowledge and school support both raised trust, while felt threats dragged it down. Knowledge also carried much of the effect of teaching, since students who learned more knew more and trusted more. A forest model predicted trust best among the tools tried. How students viewed AI tools strengthened the link from knowledge to trust, a point the authors press on banks and colleges alike.
pmc-13578725:
Deshraj Singh Thakur and Santosh Narayan Chadar turn teak wood waste into nano scale charcoal for cleaning dirty water, in a 2026 study. Plain charcoal from farm waste is cheap, yet it grabs only modest amounts of pollution. Shrinking the char to nano size after a controlled burn gave a far more porous material, rich in surface groups that can bind contaminants.

Lab checks mapped the pore web, surface chemistry, and charge of the new powder. Heavy metals and organic pollutants stuck through three routes at once: surface binding, charge pull, and filling of tiny pores. The authors present the teak char as a low cost, scalable option that gives sawmill waste a second life. Field scale proof and cost work remain ahead.
pmc-13579725:
Chiyoko Bando and colleagues report an 80 year old man whose fixed belief that mites infested his body traced back to a vitamin shortfall, in a 2026 case report. He misread lint and skin flakes as bugs, a visual illusion that fed the belief. Testing showed mild thinking decline and a marked lack of vitamin B12, and brain scans showed weak blood flow at the back of the brain. His wife had come to share the belief over time.

Care paired a low dose calming drug with the missing vitamin in its active form. The illusions cleared fast, the infestation belief faded after them, and the drug was stopped without relapse. Follow up scans showed better brain flow. His wife's shared belief eased as he improved and the pair spent time apart.
pmc-13582725:
Samantha Gaidula and colleagues build bite size nutrition lessons for medical students and test the reception, in a 2026 report from a Pennsylvania medical school. Doctors lean on food advice daily, yet training leaves most students unsure of their nutrition skills. The team's micro lessons, called Nutriments, slot food guidance into the case based frame students already learn in, so nutrition rides along with disease teaching rather than standing apart.

Students at the school reported a clearer grasp of nutrition in care after using the resource. They also backed wider adoption of the tool. The authors pitch the lessons as a portable patch any school can drop into its platform, while noting that survey warmth is a first step, not proof of bedside skill.
pmc-13588925:
Watanabe Yoichi and six colleagues reconstruct how three rare herbs survived the ice ages in Japan's snow country. The plants are living relics, sole survivors of ancient lineages now confined to regions of heavy snowfall. Reading the full chloroplast genomes of many populations, the team traced each species' family history and past population swings in their 2026 study.

The three lineages split from their nearest relatives at wildly different depths, from about twelve million to about sixty-four million years ago, all long before the ice ages. Within each species, family trees stretched back anywhere from thirty thousand to three million years. Yet all three boomed in numbers between roughly one hundred thousand and ten thousand years ago, as the heavy-snow climate itself took shape. Present diversity patterns reflect each plant's powers of spread and where its refuges lay.
pmc-13592325:
Huihui Xu and seven colleagues bottle, in 2026, a boron vinyl anion carrying an unusually heavy negative charge. Such anions pair a boron carbon double bond with a vinyl anion, a pairing so charge rich that only one example had ever been caught. A phosphorus ylide arm steadies the center carbon here, letting the team isolate the species and test its temper.

The anion proved fiercely reactive, grabbing hydrogen gas within minutes and attacking a fluorinated ring in the cold. Its reactions with other partners install a bulky, strongly donating group that can calm wild intermediates such as germanium fragments. Carbon dioxide took a surprise path, inserting twice into the boron carbon bond to close a fresh ring, Xu and the team report.
pmc-13593725:
Vanessa Almonti leads a twelve-author team hunting for early warning signs that mineral fibers can set lung tissue on the path to cancer. Their 2026 study exposed a three-dimensional human bronchial model, grown to mimic real airway tissue, to crocidolite asbestos and to short and long chrysotile fibers, then tracked the tissue's responses.

Tests in the first two days showed only brief toxicity that the tissue shook off, which would make a poor early test. By twelve days, though, fiber-treated tissue showed lasting changes matching known hallmarks of carcinogens. Inflammatory signals kept firing. DNA break markers persisted without much cell death. Scarring and identity-shifting programs had begun in the cells. The authors propose these signatures, combined with physical fiber measurements, as a faster way to judge the cancer risk of inhalable fibers.
pmc-13595325:
Xiaoxu Na and colleagues test whether a mother's body fat during pregnancy relates to her newborn's brain cortex development. Their 2026 prospective study follows 169 mother and newborn pairs, measuring maternal fat directly rather than relying on body mass index.

Fat mass percentage was measured at 12 and 36 weeks of pregnancy using air displacement, a method that estimates body composition from displaced air. At about two weeks old, babies had brain scans during natural sleep. Higher maternal fat at both time points was linked to smaller cortical volume in memory-related regions, including the left entorhinal cortex and parahippocampal gyrus. Late-pregnancy fat was also linked to the right temporal pole. One region showed a sex-specific effect, suggesting boys and girls may be affected differently.
pmc-13596825:
Joon Sang Baek and co-authors asked tuberculosis patients and the professionals who treat them what a conversational agent, a chat-based digital assistant, should actually do. Their mixed-methods study surveyed 107 healthcare professionals and thirty-one patients, then interviewed ten patients in depth about treatment experiences and expectations.

Professionals named drug side effects as their top challenge, followed by drug-resistant disease, drug interactions, and poor adherence. Patients wanted side effect consultation most, then general information and diagnostic help, and a majority were willing to use mobile health tools. Interviews deepened the picture: patients asked for steady contact with providers, trustworthy information, emotional support, and services they could afford and actually operate. The authors convert these needs into design directions, from adherence support and visible treatment progress to psychosocial features, for a user-centered TB companion.
pmc-13599325:
Katarzyna Filip-Hutsch leads a ten-author team reporting in 2026 on germs carried by ticks and other biting insects in moose calves in Finland. Moose make good sentinels for these infections because they range widely across northern forests. The team tested blood from 23 calves in their first season of life, most taken by hunters, to see how early exposure begins.

At least one target germ appeared in 44 percent of the calves. Trypanosoma DNA showed up in 35 percent, and every find belonged to one known family line of that parasite, including three new gene variants. Anaplasma phagocytophilum appeared in 17 percent, and Bartonella bacteria in 9 percent. Family-tree analysis placed the finds within wide-ranging populations rather than local oddities. The authors say early infection is common in young moose, and they frame the work as a base for wider wildlife monitoring in northern Europe.
pmc-13600925:
Olayinka Oladosu and four colleagues report in 2026 a deep learning shortcut for detailed brain imaging in children. High angular resolution diffusion imaging reveals fine structure in the brain's wiring, but needs long scans that young children struggle to sit through. The team asked whether software could predict the richer dataset from a shorter scan, halving scan time.

Brain scans from 95 children aged 2 to 10 supplied the material. A model learned voxel by voxel to predict high-strength scan data from low-strength data. Bigger training samples, wider windows, and added tissue maps all improved accuracy. Eight white matter tracts in the remaining 71 children were then analyzed, and outcomes from predicted data followed the same age patterns as real data, including consistent sex differences in tract volume. The authors conclude that generated imaging is workable for studying how children's brains develop.
pmc-13602625:
Nadieh Rouhani and four colleagues describe in 2026 building and piloting a clinical dashboard for kidney inpatients in Iran. Kidney disease demands constant monitoring, and dashboards promise that picture at a glance. Working at Imam Khomeini Hospital in Urmia between 2022 and 2023, the team ran a two-round Delphi with 25 nephrologists to pick key performance indicators. They then built the system on common web and Android tools, with barcode access at the bedside.

The panel agreed on 58 indicators grouped into demographics, medical history, clinical and laboratory values, and discharge information, with electrolytes and blood pressure drawing the strongest consensus. Ten experts rated usability as acceptable on most principles, though orientation scored lower and was improved. After a three-month pilot, 40 clinical staff rated system quality, information quality, satisfaction, and net benefit highly. The authors conclude the dashboard is ready to support real-time monitoring and decisions on the ward.
pmc-13612225:
C D'Souza and a large Australian team report a single-cell study, published in 2026. It covers a rare lymphoma that can grow around textured breast implants. The team sequenced individual cells from these tumours. They asked where the cancer cells come from. They also asked what in their surroundings keeps them alive.

The cancer cells differed from patient to patient. They traced back to memory T cells. These are the long-lived immune cells that remember past infections. The surroundings held immune cells that appeared to support the tumour. Fluid around implants carried raised levels of immune messengers. A secreted form of the checkpoint protein PD-L1 was present too. Active immune suppression likely helps the lymphoma survive.
pmc-13612425:
Edukondalu Mullapudi leads a four-author team photographing a molecular machine that breaks the symmetry rules in 2026. Acyl-CoA carboxylases build fatty acid precursors, and every known version was a tidy, symmetric complex. Mycobacteria, wrapped in waxy mycolic acids, seemed to run something stranger. The team fished natural complexes out of Mycobacterium smegmatis cells and solved one's structure by cryo-EM.

The catch was a sixteen-subunit hybrid with two carboxyl transferase parts, one for short-chain and one for long-chain substrates. A two-layered transferase core wraps around a dimer of the epsilon subunit, whose folded segment builds an asymmetric nine-stranded barrel. On each face sits a tetramer of the biotin carboxylase part, able to rotate about ninety degrees. The architecture explains how one machine services varied chain lengths mycobacteria need. It also hands drug hunters a structurally distinct target in a pathogen family that includes tuberculosis.
pmc-13614425:
Stephen Bonett and colleagues report a 2026 survey of how well adults from racial and ethnic minority groups in Philadelphia know and use the city's community health worker program. Such workers help neighbours reach care, cut hospital stays, and support healthy habits, yet awareness of their services is uneven. Data came from a web health survey run in February and March 2024 with 522 participants, most of them Black and women, with an average age of 39.

Fewer than half, 44.6 percent, had heard of the program, and only 13.6 percent of all participants had used it. Among users, 80.3 percent were satisfied with the help they got. Some groups, including Asian and Hispanic residents and people with private insurance, were less likely to know the program exists. The authors say outreach, not service quality, is the weak link.
pmc-13615225:
Lu and colleagues examined in 2026 how brain age shapes the links among sleep quality, brain waste clearance, and thinking in healthy adults. Brain age estimates how old a brain looks on scans compared with the calendar. The glymphatic system flushes waste from the brain, largely during sleep, and a scan index called DTI-ALPS tracks how well it works. The data came from 582 adults aged eighteen to eighty-seven in a Cambridge aging project.

The clearance index leaned lower on the left side across groups. People whose brains looked older than their years showed a tighter link between the clearance index and sleep quality. Those with younger-looking brains showed the index tied more to thinking scores instead. Statistical modeling put brain age in the middle of the path from clearance to sleep efficiency.
pmc-13616125:
Singhal and colleagues present a 2026 scoping review of acceptability in dental care, . Canada's dental care plan, launched in 2023, cut cost barriers, yet only about half of enrolled people had used services by late 2025. The team reviewed existing reviews of barriers and aids to acceptable care, from both patient and provider views.

Findings were sorted by theme to build a framework. Cost clearly is not the whole story: trust, communication, cultural fit, and past experience shape whether people book and return. Providers' willingness to treat certain groups also matters. The synthesis gives the new national plan a map of the non-price problems to fix, and gives researchers shared terms for a concept that dental studies have used loosely.
pmc-13619325:
Lucas Rezende and six colleagues describe rebuilding a kneecap tendon that had failed twice before. Their patient, a forty-one-year-old farmer, first tore the tendon on its own after a period of tendon pain. Two repairs broke down, leaving the kneecap riding high and bone lost at its lower edge, a mix that makes standard fixes unreliable.

For the third attempt, surgeons combined suture anchors with a block of the patient's own shin bone and an added tendon graft taken from the lower leg. Twenty-six weeks later he could fully straighten the knee and bend it across a wide range, with kneecap height improved and function much better. The authors offer the combined bone-plus-tendon approach as an option when both tissue and bone are missing in hard revision cases.
pmc-13623625:
Ramaditya Srinivasmurthy joins a large team pooling trial evidence on adding immune checkpoint inhibitors to standard chemoradiotherapy for locally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma. The cancer sits in the upper throat and is most common in East and Southeast Asia. The immune drugs had already shown activity in this cancer, but their value alongside the standard combined treatment was untested as a body of evidence.

Three randomised trials covering 1,022 patients met the rules, with just under a thousand in the safety pool. Adding the immune drugs cut the risk of disease progression or return by roughly half on the combined measures. It also halved the risks of spread to distant sites and of local regrowth. Overall survival leaned the same way without reaching firm statistical ground. Immune side effects rose, while most chemoradiation harms did not. The authors say longer follow-up must show whether better disease control becomes longer life.
pmc-13623825:
Toby Hopkinson, Liam R Cox, and Andrew J Wilson review traceless ligand-directed labelling, a chemistry trick for tagging proteins inside living cells without leaving the tagging tool attached. A guide molecule homes to the target protein, hands over a small label to a nearby spot, and then floats away. That vanishing act lets researchers mark natural proteins in their real setting.

The review traces how the method developed, covering both direct transfer designs and catalyst-tethered designs where the guide carries a tiny chemical worker. Recent advances widen which proteins and label types the approach can reach. Working examples include watching proteins glow in live cells, mapping protein partnerships across the cell, adding natural-style chemical marks on demand, and even rewiring cell signalling. The authors also list what still blocks wider use, from delivery into cells to controlling exactly where the label lands.
pmc-13625025:
Miki Takahasi and Reiko Mazuka review how babies learn to time voice and breath together, a skill speech depends on. Babies babble in bursts of sound and silence, and those bursts must ride on steady airflow past the voice box. The authors trace two settings: solo babbling and face-to-face exchanges. They mark a shift in the second half of the first year. Timing then steadies with breathing, and later it turns flexible for social use.

To explain the shift, they compare songbirds and marmosets and weigh swallowing, which needs the same tight timing to keep food from the airway. Early spoon feeding and a sinking voice box may have raised the stakes for safe timing in human babies, laying groundwork for speech.
pmc-13626325:
Adam Viktorisson and colleagues chart sick leave around a transient ischemic attack, a brief stroke warning that clears within a day. Using Swedish registers, they followed 347 working-age adults treated in Gothenburg between 2014 and 2019 and 1,388 matched neighbors. Patients already took more sick days than controls in the year before the attack, a sign that ill health gathers before the event itself.

After the attack, sick leave jumped by a mean of thirty-nine extra days in the following year. Over a third were on leave two weeks out, with the attack itself, stroke, and mental health the top recorded reasons, and one in ten remained on benefit a year later. Higher income and holding a job predicted taking leave, a reminder that return to work after a warning stroke is a long road.
pmc-13627225:
Aysenur Pac Kisaarslan and five colleagues, publishing in 2026, probe a quiet arm of the immune system in children who carry two inflammatory diseases at once. Familial Mediterranean fever, caused by MEFV gene faults, often overlaps with spondyloarthritis, a joint and spine inflammation. The team compared blood and joint fluid cells from children with either disease, both together, or neither, counting innate lymphoid cells and reading the signals those cells make.

Cell counts looked the same across groups, so the difference lay in behavior. Cells from doubly affected children leaned hard into a type 2 program, raising two signature signals, while joint fluid in spondyloarthritis alone carried its own distinct signal mix. Overlap disease, the authors conclude, rewires what these cells do rather than how many gather.
pmc-13630225:
Nazia Thakur and thirteen colleagues screened bat sarbecoviruses, the family that includes the COVID-19 virus, for how widely they can use the ACE2 doorway protein across mammal species. Receptor breadth hints at spillover risk, and the team tested binding and cell entry against a panel of thirty-four ACE2 variants from bats, humans, livestock, and possible intermediate hosts.

Viruses from the SARS-CoV-2 branch behaved as generalists, entering through many receptors, while two other branches stayed specialists with narrow tastes, a split traced partly to specific spike residues. Generalists were also the most antigenically similar to SARS-CoV-2, showing strong cross-neutralisation by patient sera, though faint cross-reactivity spanned the whole subgenus. The authors link receptor generalism to pandemic potential.
pmc-13631225:
Kaile Ma and five colleagues review the two-way talk between gut microbes and the brain. They trace how its breakdown feeds obesity and type 2 diabetes. Their review appeared in 2026. The microbes send chemical messengers. They include short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, and neuroactive compounds. These reach the brain and body through nerves, hormones, and the immune system.

When that signalling goes wrong, several failures follow. The brain's appetite centre malfunctions. Fat tissue inflames. Gut hormones falter, and insulin-making cells fail. The authors map therapies that try to retune the axis. They span diet, microbial transplants, and targeted drugs. They also weigh honestly why animal results have been slow to become clinic-ready treatments.
pmc-13632725:
Kieran Sparkes and five colleagues reviewed what is known about fetal DNA floating in a pregnant person's blood. Tests on this DNA screen for fetal genetic problems without risking the pregnancy. Yet the test stays a screening tool, partly because fetal DNA is scarce beside the mother's own loose DNA and hard to tell apart from it. The reviewers ask a basic question the field skipped: where exactly does this DNA come from, and what shape does it take?

The review weighs evidence on the DNA's origin, its release into the mother's circulation, and its physical structure. Knowing the structure could help engineers separate fetal from maternal fragments more cleanly. Better separation might cut false positives and widen what testing can diagnose. The authors argue that basic biology, not just faster sequencing machines, is the missing step toward fuller prenatal diagnosis from a blood draw.
pmc-13635225:
Kh Tohidul Islam and twelve colleagues published this 2026 resource of average brain templates for ultra-low-field MRI. Portable low-field scanners are cheap and can work at the bedside or in rural clinics. Their images are grainier than hospital scans, and no standard reference brains existed for aligning them. The team scanned one hundred healthy adults on a low-field machine across the adult lifespan and averaged the images into shared templates.

Separate templates cover three age bands alongside a whole-population version, in two common image contrasts. Example tissue segmentations and the full processing scripts come with the release, which is posted openly for anyone to reuse. Standard preprocessing was used to tame intensity differences between scanner software versions. The authors expect the templates to anchor alignment, measurement, and method testing for the growing low-field community, making results easier to compare between studies.
pmc-13635525:
Briggs and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a rare cancer of the nail bed. Onycholemmal carcinoma grows slowly under the nail and is often misread. Fewer than twenty cases appear in the medical literature so far. Most past patients lost the fingertip to clear the cancer fully.

Their patient, a 67-year-old man, had a warped thumbnail for ten years. Antifungal pills had failed, hinting the problem was no infection. A biopsy showed an invading tumor under the crumbling nail plate. He chose Mohs surgery, which checks tissue edges layer by layer. The cancer cleared fully while he kept his thumb and its function. Function-sparing care marks a shift from the older amputation standard.
pmc-13640025:
Tobias Reinberger and seven colleagues present a study of chemical modifications on RNA in vascular smooth muscle cells, the cells that help drive artery disease. These cells can switch between a calm, contractile state and an inflamed, energy-hungry state, yet the RNA marks guiding that switch were unexplored.

Using nanopore direct RNA sequencing on human cells pushed into each state, the team found distinct modification landscapes. Changed uridine marks clustered in a repeating sequence motif and in tail regions of messages, near spots where small regulatory RNAs bind. The authors link these marks to control of protein output during the cells' change of character.
pmc-13649325:
Joy L. Taylor and eleven colleagues report a 2026 pilot trial of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, a non-invasive brain stimulation technique, for memory problems in mild cognitive impairment. Which scalp site works best was unknown, so the trial compared stimulation over the frontal lobe, over the parietal lobe, and a sham procedure.

Forty participants with the memory-predominant form of the condition received twenty guided sessions and were followed for six months. The parietal group beat sham on a standard word-list learning test one week later and on delayed recall, while the frontal group showed no clear advantage. The authors call the parietal site promising and ask for larger definitive trials.
pmc-13650925:
Xiaojuan Shi and nine co-authors study how potassium fertilizer coordinates carbon and nitrogen metabolism in cotton fibers when irrigation water runs short. Cotton dominates natural fiber production, drought constrains arid growing regions, and potassium is known to soften water stress, yet the mechanism tying potassium to fiber building was uncharacterized.

Field trials from 2021 to 2023 crossed two drip irrigation levels with three potassium doses. A middle potassium dose under reduced irrigation raised the activity of sugar-handling enzymes that stockpile sucrose and a related glucan, the raw materials for cellulose. Nitrogen-processing enzymes also rose, lifting amino acid and soluble protein supplies and balancing the fiber's carbon-to-nitrogen allocation during wall thickening. That treatment produced a strong gain in cellulose content and the highest average lint yield across three years, while using irrigation water far more efficiently. The authors frame potassium as a metabolic coordinator, not just a nutrient.
pmc-1564025:
Kramer, Schwebke, and Kampf review how long hospital germs survive on dry surfaces. Surfaces in wards are often blamed as sources for outbreaks of hospital-acquired infection. Knowing survival times helps staff judge real risk and set cleaning rules.

The authors searched the medical literature in a systematic way and gathered data for each major pathogen. Different germs persist for very different spans, from hours to months. Their summary gives infection control teams an evidence base for cleaning schedules, ward design, and handling of shared equipment.  Ward staff can act on it without waiting for fresh lab work.
pmc-3867325:
Győrffy, Surowiak, Budczies, and co-authors present online software for testing survival markers in non-small-cell lung cancer. In the prior decade, better treatment had improved prognosis for this cancer, yet overall survival remained very short. Understanding the disease's molecular basis requires markers tied to survival.

Their software lets researchers test, online, whether a gene's activity level predicts patient survival using gene activity data. Quick public tools open up outlook research, letting any lab check a candidate marker against real patient cohorts before spending on costly checking studies.  Users can test several candidate genes in minutes through the web site.
pmc-3872725:
Gramfort, Luessi, Larson, and co-authors present MNE-Python for analysing MEG and EEG data. These methods measure the weak electric and magnetic signals that brain cell activity generates. Using those signals to describe and locate brain activation is a genuine challenge.

It demands expertise spanning physics, signal processing, and statistics. MNE-Python turns that expertise into open-source Python tools with a documented workflow. The library made advanced brain signal analysis accessible to many more labs, and it anchors a large open community in neuroscience.  Hospitals use the same toolbox when mapping seizure activity before brain surgery.
pmc-4188125:
Arango Duque and Descoteaux reviewed macrophage cytokines in 2014. Macrophages are immune cells that shape body development, eat dead cells, and kill germs. Cytokines are small proteins that carry instructions between cells and guide these actions.

The review covers the main cytokines that macrophages make and respond to. It explains how these signals help the cells fight infection and how they can also drive harmful inflammation. Imbalances in these signals are tied to many infectious diseases. A clear map of who signals what helps researchers design treatments that boost defense without adding damage.
pmc-4893825:
McLaren, Gil, Hunt, and their co-authors described the Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor in 2016. Known as VEP, it is a toolset for analyzing, annotating, and ranking variants across the genome, in genes and outside them. Every genome study produces far more variants than anyone can judge by hand.

VEP draws on a vast store of genome annotation, offered through several interfaces, from web to local software. It predicts the effect of each variant on genes and proteins and flags known disease links. That ranking lets researchers focus on the few variants most likely to matter. VEP is a standard step in clinical and research genomics worldwide.
pmc-5385025:
Singh, Chang, Yan, and their colleagues reviewed diet and the gut microbiome in 2017. Recent studies suggested the intestinal microbiome helps modulate risk of several chronic diseases. These include inflammatory bowel disease, obesity, type two diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.

Diet is now understood to be one of the strongest forces shaping that microbiome. What a person eats changes which microbes thrive and what they produce within days. The review covers how dietary patterns shift the gut community and what that means for human health. It supports using food as a lever to steer microbes toward lower disease risk.
pmc-6250425:
Jasenko Zivanov, Takanori Nakane, Bjoern Forsberg, and coauthors described RELION-3 in 2018. RELION is leading software for building three-dimensional structures from electron microscope images. High-resolution work needs fast, automated steps that users can trust.

The third release adds speed on standard processors as well as graphics cards. New tools pick particles without a starting template and polish particle motion frame by frame. These steps sharpen fine detail in the final maps. Structural biology labs worldwide adopted the release for routine work on viruses, ribosomes, and drug targets. Benchmarks in the paper compare speed and resolution against the previous major release.
pmc-6970225:
Kristina Rudd, Sarah Johnson, Kamara Agesa, and coauthors estimated global sepsis in this 2020 analysis. Sepsis is organ failure caused by a disordered response to infection. It is a major cause of health loss, yet global counts were scarce.

Because sepsis is a syndrome rather than one disease, standard cause lists had missed it. Modeling from death records across many countries, the team finds the toll far larger than once thought. Deaths concentrate in young children and in low income regions. The authors argue sepsis deserves a place among top global health priorities.
pmc-8005925:
Matthew Page, David Moher, and colleagues published in 2021 the companion guide that explains the PRISMA 2020 reporting statement item by item. Systematic reviews should be reported in enough detail for readers to judge whether the findings can be trusted and where they apply. The main statement lists what to report, but authors often need help seeing how each item looks in practice.

This explanation and elaboration document walks through every checklist item, giving the reasoning behind it and worked examples of good reporting drawn from real reviews. It is the document reviewers open when the short checklist leaves them unsure. Together the pair set the working standard for transparent evidence synthesis.
principia-mathematica-vol-1-1925:
Alfred North Whitehead and Bertrand Russell sought to ground all mathematics in logic in Principia Mathematica. Volume one appeared first in 1910, and the text here is the second edition of 1925. Russell wrote a new introduction for that edition. The volume runs through the sections numbered from star one to star forty-three.

Inside, the authors build numbers and classes from pure logical notions. Their dense symbols fill page after page of careful proof. Even simple truths take long chains of steps to secure. The project, called logicism, set the terms for later work on foundations. Few books match its ambition or its rigor. Volume one opens a three volume set.
proust-guermantes-way-moncrieff-1925:
The Guermantes Way, third volume of In Search of Lost Time, appeared in French in 1920. C. K. Scott Moncrieff's English translation followed in 1925. The narrator, now older, longs to enter the world of the Guermantes, the grand family whose name has charmed him since childhood.

Inside their salons he finds wit, cruelty, and hollow ritual in place of magic. The Dreyfus Affair splits dinner parties and friendships across Paris. His grandmother's decline and death give the volume its grave, tender core. Proust dissects snobbery with a surgeon's patience and a poet's eye. The book shows high society as a theater where everyone performs and few connect.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-158-19:
February 25, 1920, opens in Punch, volume 158, with Charivaria, the weekly column of brief jokes on the news. American affairs stand out this week, from Mexico to whisky, beside the usual London targets.

A Washington report of another American captured and held to ransom in Mexico draws a call for plain speaking from President Carranza. A claimed proof that burning ears mean talk about you leads to asbestos ear-guards crocheted for Mr. Churchill. The man who claims he invented revues is advised to delay his English holiday, and the Allies' note to Holland on the former Kaiser's trial gets a firm nod.
rohde-psyche-1925:
Erwin Rohde was a German classical scholar and a close friend of the young Nietzsche. His Psyche, in this 1925 English edition, studies the cult of souls and belief in immortality among the Greeks. The book is his life's work and a landmark of classical studies.

Rohde traces hero cults at tombs, the mysteries of Eleusis, and the wild worship of Dionysus across Greek lands. He argues that faith in an undying soul entered Greece from outside and grew against the older Homeric gloom. His rich, somber learning still sets the terms for studying Greek religion.
russell-abc-relativity-1925:
The ABC of Relativity, published in 1925, is Russell's popular account of Einstein's special and general relativity. Einstein had remade physics, and the public needed a guide who could write clearly. Russell, a philosopher of mathematics, took the task.

He explains why events called simultaneous may not be, how gravity becomes geometry, and what the famous tests showed, using trains, lifts, and clocks instead of equations. The book avoids false simplicity: Russell admits where the ideas strain common sense and says why they must be accepted anyway. It became the standard lay introduction of its era and still serves readers well.
santayana-dialogues-limbo-1925:
Dialogues in Limbo, published in 1925, sets Santayana's arguments among the dead, in the Platonic manner. In limbo, shades of Alcibiades, Democritus, Dionysius, and a modern stranger debate philosophy, religion, and the modern world without the heat of the living.

Santayana speaks largely through the Stranger, testing his views on nature against ancient thought and modern faith. The dialogue form lets doubts be voiced that a treatise would suppress. Death gives the speakers leisure and honesty in equal measure. The book is playful, serene, and quietly radical, a favorite among his readers for its ease of manner.
scott-hermetica-vol-2-1925:
Volume two of Walter Scott's Hermetica appeared in 1925 as pure commentary. Scott works through the Corpus Hermeticum tract by tract in these notes. The first volume's texts and translations are assumed open beside it.

He explains dark passages, traces sources, and wrestles with damaged Greek. Competing readings get weighed with patience and learning. Readers who want to grasp what the Hermetic sermons actually say need this guide. Scott can be exacting, and his rearrangements of texts drew later criticism. Even so, the commentary's depth rewards patience. It remains a serious companion to the Hermetica.
shahnama-warner-vol-9-1925:
Volume 9 of the Warner brothers' Shahnama of Firdausi appeared in 1925, completing the first complete English version of the Persian national epic. Firdausi finished the Book of Kings around 1010, after some thirty years of work. The Warners' own labor ran to nine volumes over twenty years.

Final chapters close the Sasanian story and the epic itself, with indexes and notes to guide readers back through the whole. Firdausi's own words about his task and his patrons appear in the closing sections. The completed set gave English readers Persia's founding story entire for the first time. It remains a monument of translation and of the epic it carries.
shinn-game-of-life-1925:
Florence Scovel Shinn wrote The Game of Life and How to Play It in 1925. Shinn was a New York art hand turned faith guide. The book teaches the laws of wealth, health, and right life. Tales from her own work with folk fill its pages.

Words have power, Shinn holds, and what a man speaks he draws to him. Fear is the great foe, and faith the cure for all lack. Short, sharp tales show her rules at work in shops and homes. The book is one of the most read faith works of its age.
spence-atlantis-in-america-1925:
Atlantis crossed the ocean in Lewis Spence's telling of 1925. Atlantis in America makes the case that the lost land's heirs, or its kin, stood in the New World. Spence pairs Plato's old account with the ruins and myths of Mexico and its neighbors.

He reads Maya and Aztec tales, temple forms, and flood myths as echoes of an Atlantic source. The book is the key statement of the American school of Atlantis thought. Spence wrote it as the New World half of his wider Atlantis work. Readers met here a bolder, more concrete version of his claim.
spence-problem-of-atlantis-1925:
Writer Lewis Spence made a scholarly case for Atlantis in The Problem of Atlantis. Spence was a Scottish poet and occult writer of wide learning. He treated Plato's island tale as garbled history, not mere myth.

He gathers geology, myth, and reports of Atlantic lands into one brief. Cro-Magnon culture in Europe and America anchors his argument. He answers rival theories point by point in calm prose. Mainstream scholars never granted his case. The book still stands as the most reasoned fringe brief for Atlantis, useful to readers on either side.
spr-proceedings-vol35-1925:
Parts ninety three through ninety six make volume thirty five, printed in 1925. The Society for Psychical Research nears the end of the span its archive is known for. Telepathy trials take their place beside reports of sittings and cases. Mediums old and new face the society's practiced tests.

Records of sittings run long, with sitters testing claims against private facts. Apparition reports continue under the old standards of proof. Skeptics within the society publish beside the convinced. Volume thirty five keeps the journal of record true to its founding bargain. Evidence and doubt share the binding. The long debate of the era breathes in these pages.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5025:
Andrew Johnson gives four yearly addresses in one set. Their dates run from December 4, 1865, to December 9, 1868. Three stars part each address from the next. The first makes thanks its first duty. It thanks God in the people's name for the Union's keeping. Thought turns next to the late president's death. An act of kin-slaying treason caused that death.

Some balm lies in one set of facts. Lincoln lived to take up his renewed term. He had won that term at the polls. He brought the civil war in the main to a close. All parts of the Union mourned his loss. Foreign nations did justice to his fame as well. His fall cast a heavy weight on Johnson. He pledges frank speech on the rules that guide him. He asks the backing of government and folk alike.
stein-making-of-americans-1925:
The Making of Americans, published in 1925, is Stein's thousand-page novel of everyone. Begun as a history of one family, the Herslands, it swells into an attempt to describe every kind of person who has ever lived.

Stein's prose circles and repeats, working out her idea that character shows itself in the bottom nature of each person, endlessly restated. Whole chapters turn on tiny variations of a single sentence. Few readers finish it; many writers have been changed by trying. It is the long laboratory of her continuous present, the experiment behind all her later work.
stendhal-charterhouse-parma-moncrieff-19:
Fabrice del Dongo rides into Waterloo half understanding what he sees, in Stendhal's Charterhouse of Parma. C. K. Scott Moncrieff's 1925 translation, complete in two volumes, carries Balzac's praised masterpiece of court life at Parma. Balzac himself called it among the century's greatest novels, and his study of Stendhal rides along in this edition.

Prison, a great-aunt's schemes, and a forbidden love shape Fabrice's path through a petty, sparkling court. Stendhal writes fast and dry, letting politics and passion share every scene. The charterhouse of the title waits at the end as refuge, the quiet close of a life spent chasing joy.
sur-les-fonctions-du-cerveau-et-sur-cell:
Sur les fonctions du cerveau, printed at Paris in the eighteen twenties, is a French treatise on the functions of the brain and of each of its parts. No author's name is printed on the pages at hand; the title page is followed by long lists of medical books offered by the same Paris house.

The full title promises observations on the possibility of knowing the instincts, leanings, talents, and moral and mental dispositions of men and animals from the shape of their brains and heads. That claim marks the work as a founding text of phrenology, the doctrine that character can be read from the skull. Lists of new medical works, from treatises on medicine to a pharmaceutical code, fill the opening leaves.
tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontaine-vol:
Volume 25 of The Tales and Novels of J. de La Fontaine contains The Dress-Maker, The Gascon, The Pitcher, To Promise Is One Thing, to Keep It, Another, The Nightingale, and an Epitaph of Fontaine. The set closes the long series of verse tales.

The Dress-Maker opens in song. A cloistered nun has a lover in the neighboring town. The pair rack their wits for a way to crown their love. Getting past the convent door is the hard part. A nun in such a spot, the poet says, is never beaten. The youth must dress in woman's clothes. He must win entry as a seamstress. Shut in a small barred cell together, the pair sew through the day. The hours slip past unnoticed. The epitaph at the end lets the poet sum up his own idle, easy life.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-:
Vol. 1, No. 25 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is dated April 29, 1897. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Its lead item reports that the quarrel of Greece and Turkey is still unsettled. The war clouds look lower, the paper says, but the storm has not yet broken. One thing has become clear. A Concert of the Powers, it turns out, does not exist.

Greece refused the Powers' demand that she pull her soldiers out of Crete. The Powers threatened a blockade of the Piraeus and the ports of Greece. Greece chartered every ship she could and sent men and arms to the frontier. She would declare war on Turkey if her ports were blockaded. The Powers did nothing. England, France, and Italy had stood out against forcing Greece to obey.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2-part:
Miguel de Cervantes' Don Quixote, rendered by John Ormsby, stands at Volume 2, Part 25 here. Chapter twenty-two relates the grand adventure of the cave of Montesinos in the heart of La Mancha, which the valiant Don Quixote brought to a happy termination. Thanks from the newly married couple open the part.

The pair feel bound to Quixote for defending their cause, and they rate his wisdom level with his courage, as a Cid in arms and a Cicero in speech. Sancho, for his part, enjoys three good days at their expense. Praise and feasting give way to the descent into the famous cave, where report and wonder will be hard to part.
tob-10825:
Mead edited Five Years of Theosophy in 1885, picking the best early pieces from The Theosophist, the movement's own magazine. The book shows a young creed finding its voice in print. Karma and rebirth, the astral plane, and the hidden masters said to guide the work all get long, full treatment.

The pieces teach the creed to new readers and fight its critics in the same breath. Mead later won fame as a scholar of Gnosticism, and his picks show what the first Theosophists truly taught. For those who study the group's roots, this book keeps the first five years in the words the members chose.
tob-13325:
Claud Field's translation presents al-Ghazali's Deliverance from Error, the famed teacher's own account of losing and remaking his faith. Al-Ghazali held a prestigious post in Baghdad, then suffered a crisis that left him unable to lecture. He gave up the post, left the city, and found peace as a wandering Sufi.

His narrative sorts the ways people claim knowledge, theologians, philosophers, and mystics among them, and explains why only lived experience finally cured his doubt. V1 evidence calls it Islam's most personal tale of doubt and healing. A medieval mind tells of its own crisis with a frankness modern memoirists would recognize.
tob-13725:
G. R. S. Mead, an English scholar and theosophist, completed his Thrice-Greatest Hermes in 1906 with this third volume. The set presents the writings tied to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage of Egypt and Greece. Mead translated, ordered, and explained texts few English readers could reach.

Volume three gives the remaining fragments, the Kore Kosmou, and sayings preserved by later writers, with Mead's notes. Together the volumes made the Hermetica open to general readers in English. Scholars now use newer editions, but Mead's labor first carried these texts of late antique religion to a wide public.
tob-4025:
William Molyneux's early English translation presents René Descartes's Six Metaphysical Meditations, the founding text of modern philosophy in its most concentrated form. Over six days of imagined solitude, Descartes retraces his search for certainty. An evil demon, invented to make doubt total, gives way to the cogito: I think, therefore I am.

Proofs of God's existence, the mind's distinction from the body, and the route back to trusting the senses occupy the later meditations. Molyneux, an Irish philosopher and friend of Locke, carried Descartes to English readers in their own tongue. Doubt as a road to truth has rarely been walked more carefully.
tob-4125:
Herbert A. Giles presented Chuang Tzu under three titles at once: mystic, moralist, and social reformer. Giles's lively translation made the butterfly-dreamer a favorite Chinese sage for English readers. Chuang Tzu dreams he is a butterfly and wakes unsure which side of the dream is real, and the book keeps that playful uncertainty throughout.

Mystic of the Tao, Chuang Tzu dissolves fixed distinctions; moralist against convention, he mocks scholars and rulers; reformer, he imagines freedom from useless striving. Talking skulls, giant trees, and Cook Ding's effortless knife carry the lessons. Often called the most entertaining classic in Chinese literature, it earns the title by laughing while it philosophizes.
tob-4225:
The Arbatel of Magick, a slim Latin grimoire of 1575, reaches English readers in Robert Turner's translation of 1655. Unlike the dark pacts of other grimoires, the Arbatel promises wisdom through prayer and a clean life. Its seven Olympic spirits rule 196 provinces of the unseen world between them.

Aphorisms lay down the magician's conduct: honor God, harm none, keep the hours of the spirits, and hold knowledge humbly. The tone is gentle, almost pastoral, for a book of magic. Verified from the 1919 edition, the Arbatel stands as the Renaissance gentleman's magic, complete in a few dozen pages.
treaty-of-rio-1825:
Portugal and Brazil signed the Treaty of Rio de Janeiro in 1825, formally settling Brazil's break from Portuguese rule. King John of Portugal accepted Brazil as an independent empire under his son, Dom Pedro. Brazil had declared its independence three years earlier, but Lisbon's legal recognition still had to be won at the negotiating table.

The text records Portugal's recognition, the titles each ruler would keep, and the financial terms that came with the settlement. Unlike the wars that freed Spanish America, this separation was closed by agreement between father and son. Brazil became a sovereign nation with its monarchy intact and its new status accepted in Europe.
trotsky-literature-revolution-1925:
Literature and Revolution, published in English in 1925 in Rose Strunsky's translation, is Leon Trotsky's theory of art after the Russian Revolution. The exiled revolutionary, then still a leader of the Soviet state, surveys Russian literature and asks what culture the new order should want.

Trotsky defends artistic freedom against party bureaucrats, arguing that art must work by its own laws, while he judges writers by their stance toward the revolution. Futurists, formalists, and fellow travelers are weighed with wit and severity. The book is a paradox: a Marxist classic against socialist realism. Its intelligence survives its moment.
un-doc-address-to-the-united-nations-gen:
Han Seung-soo, prime minister of the Republic of Korea, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on 25 September 2008. He had led the Assembly itself when the 2001 attacks shook New York. This year marked sixty years since his country's founding. A world money crisis was deepening as he spoke.

He urges a shift to low-carbon, green growth. Korea will back that path with aid and a new East Asia climate fund. Seoul will give 100 million dollars in food aid over three years. He presses North Korea to restart the shutdown of its nuclear plant under the six-party talks. His warning on the cash crisis is plain: do not turn to trade walls.

President John F. Kennedy of the United States addressed the United Nations General Assembly on 25 September 1961. The Secretary-General, Dag Hammarskjöld, had died in a plane crash days before. The Soviet Union was pressing to replace him with a three-man team. The Berlin crisis hung over the hall.

Kennedy rejects the troika plan in plain terms. One driver, he says, or the machine stalls. He lays out an American plan to end all armies save a UN peace force. Cuts would come in checked stages, with watching built in. A test ban pact sits ready for signature. He challenges Moscow to a peace race and asks that space stay free of weapons.

Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, leader of Bangladesh, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on 25 September 1974. His country had just taken its seat at the world body. Its people, 75 million strong, had won freedom in a brutal war three years before. Floods that year had pushed the young state toward famine.

He frames the fight for Bangladesh as part of a world fight for self-rule. He backs the Arabs, the Palestinians, and the freedom drives of Africa. The rich world must help build a fairer trade and money order, he argues. He notes his grant of mercy to 195 prisoners of war. Peace with Pakistan, he says, should rest on fair play.
un-ga-res-25:
Where should the United Nations plant its flag for good? Resolution 25, passed in February 1946, picks the ground: Westchester County in New York, or Fairfield County in Connecticut, close to New York City. A headquarters team must go to the area at once. It is to study the ground in full and report back, with a firm pick of the site, at the next part of the session.

The team must draw plans at five sizes, from two square miles up to forty. For each, it must price the cost of buying the land and the buildings on it. It must also ask what steps the U.S., state, and county chiefs will take to guard how the land around the site grows. In the end, the UN rose instead in Manhattan.
un-ga-res-2625:
How states must treat each other was spelled out in full in Resolution 2625, adopted by the General Assembly in 1970. Its annex holds the Declaration on Principles of International Law concerning Friendly Relations and Cooperation among States. A special team had worked on the rules since 1962, meeting last in Geneva in the spring of 1970. Their report lay before the Assembly.

The rules rest on the Charter. States are equal in rights. None may use force against the land or freedom of another. Rows must be settled by peaceful means, and no state may meddle in the home affairs of another. Peoples hold the right to rule themselves. States must also work with each other in good faith. The text is still a base stone of world law.
un-ga-res-44-25:
Children hold rights of their own. The world wrote them down in the Convention on the Rights of the Child. The General Assembly adopted it in Resolution 44/25 on 20 November 1989. The pact grew from the Charter's faith in the worth of each human person. It recalls the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the two great rights pacts, which hold that all are born to the same rights and freedoms.

The pact sets out the civil, civic, trade, and social rights of each child. States that join it bind themselves in world law to guard those rights. It took force on 2 September 1990. Ratified by more states than any other rights pact in the UN shelf, it is the base text for the rights of children across the world.
un-ga-res-a-69-25:
Israel's hold on the Syrian Golan is condemned in Resolution A/69/25, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The heights have been held since the war of 1967. The text recalls the Security Council's 1981 vote, which found Israel's bid to impose its laws on the Golan void. It also states again the core rule that land may not be taken by force.

Deep concern runs through the text that Israel has not pulled out, in breach of UN votes. The building of Israeli settlements on the Golan since 1967 is called unlawful. The 1949 Geneva pact on the safety of civilians in war is held to apply to the held land in full.
un-ga-res-address-to-the-united-nations-:
Han Seung-soo, prime minister of South Korea, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on September 25, 2008. He spoke days after a bank collapse in the United States shook markets across the world. Leaders at the general debate that year all faced the same spreading financial crisis.

Han set out Korea's view of the crisis and the joint response it demanded. He also spoke on climate change, aid to poorer states, and peace on the Korean peninsula. The speech shows a mid-sized power arguing that shared problems need shared rules, stated at a tense moment.

John F. Kennedy, president of the United States, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on September 25, 1961. It was his first speech to the body, given months into his term and days after the death of Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjöld in a plane crash. The Cold War hung over every word.

Kennedy called for an end to the arms race and a ban on nuclear tests. He proposed that weapons of war be dismantled step by step under strict checks. He also pledged support for new states winning freedom. The address remains a high point of Cold War oratory.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 25, adopted on 14 February 1946, chose the ground for the permanent headquarters of the United Nations. The Assembly settled on Westchester County in New York and Fairfield County in Connecticut, near New York City. It set the temporary headquarters in New York City itself.

A nine-state Headquarters Commission was sent to study the region closely and report to the second part of the first session. It was to price sites from two to forty square miles. It was to ask United States authorities how nearby building would be controlled. It was to leave the final choice of place and size to the Assembly, with no money promised yet.

General Assembly Resolution 2625 (XXV) was adopted on 24 October 1970. It marked the twenty-fifth anniversary of the United Nations. It approved the Declaration on Principles of International Law concerning Friendly Relations and Cooperation among States. The annexed declaration restates the Charter's core rules as seven linked principles for how states must treat each other.

The principles bar the threat or use of force against any state's land or freedom. They require disputes to be settled by peaceful means. They forbid meddling in another state's home affairs. They also demand cooperation between states. They affirm equal rights and self-rule for peoples. They affirm the equal standing of all states. They require promises made under the Charter to be kept in good faith.

Hosted under the Resolution 44/25 label, the text here is the Convention on the Rights of the Child. The General Assembly adopted it and opened it for signing through resolution 44/25 of 20 November 1989. The preamble holds that childhood deserves special care. It holds that the family is the natural setting for a child's growth. It holds that a child needs legal protection before and after birth.

The articles define a child as a person under eighteen. They set out wide rights: life and fullest growth, a name and nationality, care by parents, and a voice in matters touching the child. They guard against unfair treatment and abuse. They cover schooling, health, play, and protection in war and in the courts.

General Assembly resolution 69/25 (2014), 'The Syrian Golan,' declares that Israel has failed to comply with Security Council resolution 497 (1981). It declares that Israel's 1981 decision imposing its laws and administration on the occupied Syrian Golan is null and void. The Assembly says the continued occupation and de facto annexation block a just regional peace. It demands Israeli withdrawal from all the occupied Syrian Golan to the line of 4 June 1967. It calls for peace talks on the Syrian and Lebanese tracks to resume.
